blocks.text: People picture Bondi as a beach; I see a stage — where surf lifesaving was born, where giant kites fill the sky each spring, and where the world's largest fun run comes pouring over the hill. These are the ten biggest events that, to me, turned an ordinary bay into the most famous beach on earth.

items.label: Oldest institution
items.value: Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club

blocks.text: The moments that made Bondi Bondi
Some are grand and global, others gloriously silly — but together they're why Bondi feels the way it does when you reach the promenade.
1. The birth of surf lifesaving

The Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club is recognised as the world's oldest surf life saving club, and it changed how the country goes to the beach. It long celebrated a 1906 founding, though its own historians later settled on a formal establishment date of 21 February 1907. Either way, this is where the reel, line and red-and-yellow flags began.
2. Bondi Icebergs (club formed 1929)

That emerald pool at the southern end, waves crashing over the lane ropes, is the most photographed corner of Bondi. The Icebergs Club was formed in 1929 by local lifesavers wanting to stay fit through winter — hence the rule about swimming through the cold months. The pool is still a working ocean bath, so check the Icebergs website for current public-swim times and prices.
3. City2Surf comes over the hill

First run in 1971, the City2Surf pours 14 kilometres from the Sydney CBD down to Bondi Beach and has grown into the world's largest fun run. If you've never watched the finish, do it — tens of thousands of runners cresting the hill on a winter Sunday.
4. Sculpture by the Sea

In 1997 someone dotted the Bondi-to-Tamarama coastal walk with sculptures for a single day. It's now the world's largest free-to-the-public outdoor sculpture exhibition, drawing huge crowds each spring. Dates shift year to year, so confirm this season's run on the Sculpture by the Sea site before planning.
5. Festival of the Winds
My personal favourite. First held in 1978, this Waverley Council event has been Bondi's most colourful day ever since — the whole beach turned upward to giant kites, music and multicultural stalls.
6. Beach volleyball at the Sydney 2000 Olympics
For the Sydney 2000 Games, a temporary stadium rose on the sand and the world watched Olympic beach volleyball at Bondi. Locals argued about it, but it cemented Bondi's image as Australia's beach.
7. Bondi Rescue hits the screen (2006)

When the reality series following Bondi's lifeguards began airing in 2006, it carried the beach into living rooms worldwide. Half the visitors I meet came because they watched it — and yes, the lifeguards really are that busy.
8. The pink bikini fundraiser (2007)
In 2007 a mass beach shoot packed the sand with women in pink bikinis for a record-setting breast-cancer fundraiser. Peak Bondi: a serious cause wrapped in something wonderfully over-the-top.
9. The graffiti (art) wall

The long sea wall along the promenade doubles as a legal, ever-changing art canvas — layers of murals painted by locals and visiting artists for decades. It's one of the few places where you can watch a piece being made and see it painted over within the month.
10. Bondi as a place to gather
From climate and community rallies to spontaneous dawn services, Bondi has become the beach Sydney comes to when it wants to be together. That, more than any single day, is what shaped it.

The big free events — Festival of the Winds, Sculpture by the Sea and the City2Surf finish — all bring road closures and packed buses. Leave the car at home: take the train to Bondi Junction, then a bus or walk down to the sand.

blocks.title: Dates move — always double-check
blocks.text: Annual events shift their dates every year, and some founding dates are still debated by the institutions themselves. The official organisers are linked in the sources below; confirm this year's programme with them first.

items.q: What is the oldest event or institution at Bondi Beach?
items.a: The Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club, the world's oldest surf life saving club. It long marked 1906 as its founding year, though its historians later settled on a formal date of 21 February 1907.

items.q: When is the City2Surf and where does it finish?
items.a: It runs in winter and finishes at Bondi Beach after 14km from the Sydney CBD. First held in 1971, it's now the world's largest fun run. Check the official City2Surf website for this year's date and entry.

items.q: What is the Festival of the Winds?
items.a: Bondi's annual kite festival, first held in 1978 and now presented by Waverley Council. Expect giant kites, live music and multicultural food stalls, usually in early spring — confirm the date on the council's events page.

items.q: Can I still see Sculpture by the Sea at Bondi?
items.a: Yes. It runs each spring along the free Bondi-to-Tamarama coastal walk and began in 1997. Dates change annually, so check the Sculpture by the Sea website before you go.

items.q: Is the Bondi graffiti wall legal?
items.a: The promenade sea wall is a long-standing public art space where murals are painted openly and change constantly. It's one of Bondi's most photographed backdrops, but the artwork is temporary by design.

blocks.text: Ten events, one beach — and the list keeps growing. Stand on the promenade during any of them and you'll feel why this place matters.

blocks.text: If you've ever wondered who the aerobics instructor in Eric Prydz's "Call On Me" film clip actually was — and whether you can take her class here in Bondi — here's the short answer. Her name is Deanne Berry, she's a Sydney-born professional dancer, and after that leotard-and-legwarmers routine made her one of the most recognised faces on British TV, she came home to Australia and has taught high-energy dance-fitness right here on the beach. I went looking for her story, because a local link to one of the 2000s' most talked-about music videos is far too good to keep quiet.

items.label: The video
items.value: "Call On Me" by Eric Prydz, released 2004

items.label: Bondi link
items.value: Has taught dance-fitness classes in the Bondi area

items.label: Best for
items.value: Anyone who loves moving to music — no dance experience needed

items.label: Booking
items.value: Check her current classes via her own website and social channels

blocks.text: The most talked-about aerobics video of the 2000s

You almost certainly remember it: a room full of dancers in high-cut leotards, legwarmers and sweatbands, working through a suggestive aerobics routine to Eric Prydz's thumping club track. Released in 2004 on Ministry of Sound, and built around a sampled vocal from Steve Winwood's "Valerie", the song became a UK number-one hit and the video one of the most recognised — and most debated — dance clips of the decade. At the time it was about as risqué as a mainstream music video got. And the instructor front and centre? A Bondi local in the making.
Who is Deanne Berry?

As Deanne tells it, her career began in Sydney at 16, dancing and performing before touring interstate and through Asia with musicals and artists. That work eventually took her to the UK, where a tour backing Sir Cliff Richard led to a stint in London — and, during a break between concert dates, to a casting call for an eighties-inspired Ministry of Sound video. She landed the role of the instructor, and a few days later found herself in that now-infamous black thong leotard, legwarmers and not much else.

She didn't expect it to go anywhere. "I thought not too many people would see it," she told me — so jumping around and pelvic-thrusting felt harmless enough. Then the track shot to the top of the charts, the video spread around the world, and almost overnight she went from working dancer to accidental fitness guru. She took the moment and ran with it: enrolling in fitness courses, choreographing and presenting a Ministry of Sound fitness DVD that sold strongly, and later waking up Britain as a fitness presenter on breakfast television.
The Bondi dance-fitness class

Back in Australia, Deanne has channelled all of that into a dance-conditioning class — each workout themed to a different pop artist, so you sweat your way through the sounds of the likes of Rihanna, Kylie, Beyoncé and Michael Jackson while building stamina, flexibility and strength. Her pitch is simple: leave your inhibitions at the door, come with an open mind, and don't worry if you can't dance. She's had mums and daughters in the same session; the only real requirement is a love of moving to music.

blocks.title: Classes and studios change — check before you go
blocks.text: This interview dates back a few years, and dance-fitness timetables and studios move around. Rather than turn up on spec, look up Deanne Berry's current classes and locations on her own website and social channels for what's actually running now.

Fancy recreating the routine? Deanne told me she still gets asked to bring back the "Call On Me" moves at parties and events, and clearly still loves performing the track — so if you're planning an eighties-themed do, she's the person who danced the original.

items.q: Who was the aerobics instructor in the Call On Me video?
items.a: Deanne Berry, a Sydney-born professional dancer. She was cast as the instructor for Eric Prydz's 2004 "Call On Me" clip and later returned to Australia, where she has taught dance-fitness in the Bondi area.

items.q: Is the Call On Me clip really by Eric Prydz?
items.a: Yes. "Call On Me" was released by Swedish producer Eric Prydz in 2004 on Ministry of Sound and built around a sampled vocal from Steve Winwood's "Valerie". It became a UK number-one hit.

items.q: Can I take Deanne Berry's class in Bondi?
items.a: She has run dance-fitness classes in the Bondi area, but timetables and studios change over time. Check her current website and social channels for what's on now rather than relying on this older interview.

items.q: Do I need dance experience to join?
items.a: No. Her classes are pitched at all levels — she's had complete beginners, and even mums and daughters, in the same session. The only thing you really need is a willingness to move to music.

items.q: Did the Call On Me video top the charts?
items.a: Yes — the track was a UK number-one hit and the video became one of the most recognised and talked-about dance clips of the 2000s.

blocks.text: It's a lovely little piece of Bondi trivia: the face of one of the era's most famous music videos quietly getting people dancing a few streets back from the sand. If the story's tempted you to try a class, do check what she's running before you go — and either way, next time that Eric Prydz track comes on, you'll know the instructor is one of our own.

Here's the short version so you can get on with your day: in Sydney, clocks go forward one hour on the first Sunday of October, at 2:00am, which instantly becomes 3:00am. You lose an hour of sleep but gain a summer's worth of long, golden evenings — and down here at Bondi, that trade is the best deal going. Here's my quick local guide to making the October clock change work for your trip.

items.label: In 2026
items.value: Sunday 4 October (check NSW Government for the exact year)

blocks.text: When the clocks actually change

Daylight saving in New South Wales runs from the first Sunday in October to the first Sunday in April, and the switch always happens in the small hours of Sunday morning so it barely interrupts anyone's week. At 2:00am you skip straight to 3:00am. The original version of this article was written for 1 October 2023, but the rule is the same every year — only the calendar date shifts. For the coming season the NSW Government has it landing on the first Sunday of October, which falls on Sunday 4 October in 2026 (handily, right on the October long weekend). If you want the exact date for the year you're visiting, the NSW Government daylight saving page is the source I trust.

blocks.title: Not every state joins in
blocks.text: Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia don't observe daylight saving. So for roughly six months of the year, Sydney is an hour ahead of Brisbane — worth remembering if you're booking a connecting flight, a phone call home, or a Zoom with the Gold Coast.
Why it's brilliant for a Bondi trip

The whole point of shifting the clock is to push an hour of daylight from the early morning — when most of us are asleep — into the evening, when we can actually use it. For a beach town, that's transformational. Suddenly the sun is still up well into the evening, and Bondi shakes off its daytime crowds to reveal my favourite version of itself: warm light on the sand, the promenade humming, and the water often at its glassiest.

items: An after-work (or after-sightseeing) swim while it's still bright and lifeguard-patrolled hours are longer through summer.
A slow walk along the Bondi to Bronte coastal path with the cliffs glowing gold — early evening is the sweet spot for light and cooler air.
Dinner outdoors on Campbell Parade or up in North Bondi without the midday heat.
Sunset from the Icebergs headland, which drifts later and later as summer deepens.

blocks.text: The flip side of long evenings is early, punishing sun. On daylight-saving mornings the UV climbs fast — I'd rather swim at 7am or after 5pm than bake between 11 and 3. Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags, and check current Bondi conditions on Surf Life Saving's Beachsafe before you go in.
Practical stuff so the change doesn't catch you out

Your phone, laptop and most modern devices update themselves automatically overnight, as does a recent hire car. The things that catch people out are the analogue holdouts: a wristwatch, an oven clock, a hotel-room alarm, an older car dashboard. Nudge them forward on the Sunday and you're sorted.

blocks.title: Double-check time-sensitive bookings
blocks.text: The morning of the change is the classic trap for early flights, airport transfers, tours and ferries. Devices usually handle it, but if you're relying on a manual alarm, set two — and confirm any pre-booked pickup runs on the new local time.

Public transport runs to the new time automatically, though overnight timetables around the changeover can shift — if you're travelling in the small hours of that Sunday, check with Transport for NSW. For everyone else, daylight saving asks very little: lose an hour of sleep once, and enjoy the longest evenings Bondi has to offer.

items.q: When do the clocks change in Sydney in October?
items.a: On the first Sunday of October, clocks go forward one hour at 2:00am, becoming 3:00am. The exact date shifts each year — it's Sunday 4 October in 2026 — so confirm on the NSW Government daylight saving page for the year you're visiting.

items.q: Do I move the clocks forward or back in October?
items.a: Forward. In spring you 'spring forward' one hour, which is why you lose an hour of sleep but gain lighter evenings. In April you 'fall back' an hour when daylight saving ends.

items.q: What time zone is Sydney on during daylight saving?
items.a: Australian Eastern Daylight Time (AEDT), which is UTC+11. For the rest of the year Sydney is on Australian Eastern Standard Time (AEST), UTC+10.

items.q: Does all of Australia use daylight saving?
items.a: No. New South Wales, Victoria, the ACT, Tasmania and South Australia observe it, but Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia do not. That's why Sydney sits an hour ahead of Brisbane over summer.

items.q: When does daylight saving end?
items.a: On the first Sunday of April, when clocks go back one hour and Sydney returns to AEST. Right up until then you'll get those long Bondi evenings.

blocks.text: So set your watch forward, forgive yourself the lost hour, and come find me on the sand around six. Daylight saving is the unofficial start of Bondi's best season — and there's nowhere better to spend a long summer evening.

sources.label: Bureau of Meteorology — Sydney sunrise/sunset times

blocks.text: Bondi has a rhythm, and the quickest way to enjoy your day is to fall into step with it. The etiquette isn't complicated — swim between the red and yellow flags, keep your music to yourself, take your rubbish home, and remember the beach belongs to everyone. Get those right and you'll blend in like a regular. Here's how we actually do things on our patch of sand.

items.label: Golden rule
items.value: Swim between the red & yellow flags

items.label: Alcohol
items.value: Not permitted on the beach or in Bondi Park

items.label: Dogs
items.value: Not allowed on the beach at any time

items.label: Smoking & vaping
items.value: No — keep it off the sand

items.label: Rubbish
items.value: Bin it or take it with you

blocks.text: Safety first: swim between the flags

If you take one thing from this guide, make it this. The red and yellow flags mark the patrolled swimming area, and the lifeguards move them to wherever is safest that day, which shifts with the surf and the rips. Swim between them and you're in the eyes of the professionals; wander outside and you're on your own, often right where the rips run. Surfers stay well clear of the flagged zone; boards and swimmers don't mix.

blocks.title: Respect the lifeguards
blocks.text: The lifeguards are here to keep everyone safe, so follow their instructions without argument — if they wave you in or move the flags, there's a reason. And if they're too busy to stop for a chat, don't take it personally.
New to ocean swimming or travelling with kids? The northern end near the flags tends to be gentler and shallower, which is why families cluster there, along with the surf school.
Sharing the sand
Bondi gets packed in summer, and the unwritten rules are really just common courtesy dialled up for a crowd. The ones that matter:
Leave the speaker at home. There's nowhere on this beach your playlist won't carry, and the person next to you didn't come to hear it. Headphones instead.
Choose your spot with the crowd in mind. For breathing room, the middle of the beach or the southern end gives you more space than the busy northern corner near the flags.
Set up your tent or umbrella toward the back of the beach so you're not blocking anyone's view of the water — and if someone parks in front of you, let it go. It's public sand.
Be sun smart. Our UV is fierce even on cool days, so slip, slop, slap and reapply; that first-day-in-Australia sunburn is brutal and entirely avoidable.
Watch for the little ones. Kids dart in and out everywhere in summer, so keep an eye out when you're moving around or bodysurfing in.
The things that'll actually get you in trouble

Some Bondi rules aren't just etiquette — they're enforced by Waverley Council, and rangers do patrol. Alcohol isn't permitted on Bondi Beach or in Bondi Park, so leave the esky at home. Smoking and vaping don't belong on the sand either. And dogs aren't allowed on the beach at any time, though you can walk them on a lead along the promenade and through the park.

blocks.title: Parking: don't risk the big fine
blocks.text: After circling for a park it's tempting to chance it — don't. Blocking a driveway or a no-parking zone can land you a hefty fine, and boxing someone in can mean a call to the police. Don't idle at the entrance stalking a spot, either; it gridlocks Campbell Parade.
Rules and specifics can change, so if you're unsure about alcohol zones, dog areas or seasonal restrictions, the Waverley Council beach pages are the source of truth — I've linked them below.
The little local courtesies

Beyond the official stuff, there's the Bondi finishing school. Take your rubbish with you — bins line the promenade, so use them; the gulls and the ocean will thank you. And if you've left a pram in the North Bondi rack, check you're grabbing your own before you wheel off; near-identical black prams are everywhere, and a mix-up ruins two families' afternoons.
The ethos is simple: the beach isn't here to watch you, it's here for everyone. Come to have fun, not to be seen.

items.q: Can you drink alcohol on Bondi Beach?
items.a: No. Bondi Beach and Bondi Park sit within Waverley Council's alcohol-free zones, so drinking isn't allowed and rangers do enforce it. Check the Waverley Council website for the exact zones and current rules.

items.q: Are dogs allowed on Bondi Beach?
items.a: Dogs aren't permitted on Bondi Beach at any time. You can walk a dog on a lead along the promenade and through the park; for nearby off-leash areas, check Waverley Council's dog rules.

items.q: Why does everyone say to swim between the flags?
items.a: The red and yellow flags mark the area the lifeguards patrol and have judged safest that day. Bondi is known for its rips, which shift with conditions, so swimming between the flags keeps you in the safest water and in the lifeguards' sight.

items.q: Can you smoke or vape on Bondi Beach?
items.a: Keep it off the sand — smoking and vaping aren't welcome on the beach. It's both etiquette and health on a crowded family beach, and butts are a real pollution problem for the ocean.

items.q: What's the most common tourist mistake at Bondi?
items.a: Two stand out: getting badly sunburnt on day one, because the Australian UV is stronger than most expect, and swimming outside the flags. Sort those and you're ahead of most first-timers.

blocks.text: Everyone assumes you have to pay to park at Bondi. You don't — and this is the local secret I share with visiting friends every summer.

The spot is the residential streets north of Blair Street — that is, the blocks heading away from the beach. Punch "Blair Street" into your maps app, then simply head north (away from the water) and start looking. The parking here is free and unrestricted around the clock, no meters, no time limits.

On weekdays there are spaces until late afternoon, when residents start arriving home from work. On weekends it's busier, but the constant coming and going means you can usually snag something if you're patient — and much more easily if you're early.

From about 9am on a Saturday or Sunday, parking anywhere near Bondi becomes a genuine challenge. Beat the rush: get here early, grab a free spot north of Blair Street, and enjoy a quiet morning on the sand before the crowds roll in.

One caveat — always read the signs. As you get closer to the beach you'll hit timed and permit-only zones, so keep heading north until the restrictions drop off. For every other way to get to Bondi (train, bus, and the rest), see my full guide to parking and getting here.

items.q: Where is the free parking at Bondi Beach?
items.a: The residential streets north of Blair Street, heading away from the beach. It's free and unrestricted 24 hours, roughly a 5–7 minute walk to the sand.

items.q: What time should I arrive for a free spot?
items.a: Before 9am on weekends. Weekdays are easier until the late afternoon, when residents return home.

blocks.text: I've lived alongside this stretch of sand for years, and what still surprises me is how much history is packed into one kilometre of coastline. Bondi isn't just a pretty beach — its name means the sound of the surf, it's home to Australia's first surf lifesaving club, the whole place is on the National Heritage List, and there's a winter swimming pool you can only truly belong to after five years of Sunday races. Here are the facts about Bondi that genuinely surprise the people I show around.
The name itself means the sound of the waves

This is my favourite one to open with. "Bondi" comes from the Aboriginal word usually written as "Boondi", and the meaning most often given is tied to the sound and motion of water tumbling over rocks — the noise of the surf breaking on the shore. Sources vary on the precise translation, but the through-line is lovely: the beach is essentially named after the sound you hear the moment you arrive. Stand on the promenade at dawn and you're hearing the very thing the name describes.
Bondi is where Australian surf lifesaving began

The red-and-yellow flags feel timeless, but they had to start somewhere — and that somewhere was here. The Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club was formed in February 1907 and is recognised as Australia's first surf lifesaving club, born out of the urgent idea that ocean bathing needed people trained to pull swimmers out of trouble. Everything that spread up and down the coast, and the culture the world now associates with our beaches, traces back to that decision on this sand.

items: The Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club (1907) is regarded as Australia's first.
The whole beach was added to the National Heritage List in 2008.
It's one of the most filmed beaches in the country, thanks in no small part to 'Bondi Rescue'.

blocks.text: Want the history without the crowds? Walk the promenade early — before about 8am in summer — and you'll have the lifesaving murals, the Pavilion and the whole sweep of the beach almost to yourself, in the best light of the day.
Black Sunday and a pool that takes five years to belong to

Two stories always stop visitors in their tracks. The first is Black Sunday, in February 1938, when freak waves dragged a huge number of bathers — reportedly around 250 people — off the sandbank in minutes. What followed became one of the most famous mass rescues in surf lifesaving history. It's a sobering reminder that even a beach this beloved has to be respected.

The second is happier but almost as demanding. At the Bondi Icebergs, the winter swimming club at the southern end, tradition holds that earning lifetime swimming membership means competing on three Sundays out of every four, right through the cold months, for five straight years. Five winters of ice blocks dropped into the pool before the season starts, just to belong. If you ever needed proof Bondi locals are a certain breed, that's it.

blocks.title: Volatile facts change — check before you plan
blocks.text: Session times, entry fees and membership rules at venues like the Icebergs can change. I've kept the surprising history here and left the day-to-day specifics to the official sources listed below, so always confirm current details on the venue's own website first.

One quick myth-buster: you'll sometimes read that Bondi once hit a scorching 47 degrees. Sydney did record extreme heat in early January 2018, but that headline reading belonged to Penrith in the city's west — the ocean keeps Bondi much milder than inland suburbs.

items.q: What does the name 'Bondi' mean?
items.a: It comes from the Aboriginal word 'Boondi'. The meaning most commonly given relates to the sound and motion of water breaking over rocks — essentially the noise of the surf. Different sources record slightly different translations, but they share that connection to the waves.

items.q: Is Bondi really the birthplace of surf lifesaving?
items.a: The Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club was formed in 1907 and is recognised as Australia's first, so Bondi has a strong claim as the home of the movement in this country.

items.q: What was Black Sunday at Bondi?
items.a: In February 1938, freak waves swept a large group of bathers — reported as around 250 people — off the sandbank. Lifesavers rescued the vast majority in what's remembered as one of the great mass rescues in surf lifesaving history.

items.q: How do you become a member of the Bondi Icebergs winter swimming club?
items.a: By tradition, earning lifetime swimming membership means competing on three Sundays out of four through winter for five consecutive years. Check the Icebergs website for current membership details before counting on specifics.

items.q: How long is Bondi Beach?
items.a: It's about one kilometre of sand — surprisingly compact given how internationally famous it is, which is partly why it feels so busy on a hot summer day.

blocks.text: That's what I love about this place: you can come for a swim and leave with a head full of stories. A beach named after the sound of its own waves, the cradle of Australian surf lifesaving, heritage-listed sand, and a pool you earn over five winters. Bondi rewards anyone curious enough to look past the postcard.

blocks.text: Bondi's Icebergs gets all the postcards, but if you ask me, Bronte Baths just down the coast is the more soulful swim. It's a saltwater pool carved straight into the sandstone at the southern end of Bronte Beach — free, unpretentious, and my favourite place for an early lap when I want to skip the crowds.

Bronte sits on the Eastern Beaches strip between Bondi to the north and Coogee to the south. The pool is cut into the rock shelf at the southern headland, so it fills and refreshes with the ocean — you're swimming in the sea, just with a wall between you and the swell. There's a shallower end that's good for kids, and it's a genuine lap-swimmer's pool the rest of the time.
Getting there

items: On foot — it's right on the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk, one of the best ways to arrive.
Public transport — train to Bondi Junction, then a bus down to Bronte. Easy and it skips the parking headache.
By car — there's parking around Bronte Road and the park, but it's limited and fills fast on a nice day, so come early.

blocks.title: Check before you go
blocks.text: Bronte Baths has been through staged upgrade works (over recent winters), and ocean pools are also periodically drained for cleaning — so it can be closed, especially in the cooler months. Check Waverley Council's ocean-pool status before you make a special trip.
Is it free? And can anyone use it?

Yes on both counts — Bronte Baths is completely free and open to the public, no entry fee. There are showers and changing facilities nearby (some may be coin-operated). It's an easygoing, welcoming spot for locals and visitors alike.

blocks.title: A word on the water
blocks.text: Bronte is a beautiful beach but a serious one — it's known for a strong permanent rip (the "Bronte Express"). The pool is calmer than the open beach, but conditions in and around it still change with the surf and tide. On the beach, swim between the red and yellow flags when lifeguards are patrolling, and check Beachsafe for current conditions.

items.q: Is Bronte Ocean Pool free?
items.a: Yes — Bronte Baths is completely free and open to the public. Showers and changing facilities nearby may be coin-operated.

items.q: Where is the Bronte Ocean Pool?
items.a: It's carved into the rock at the southern end of Bronte Beach, in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs, right on the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk.

items.q: Is the Bronte pool open all year?
items.a: It's generally open year-round in daylight hours, but it closes periodically for cleaning and has had staged upgrade works, mainly in winter. Check Waverley Council's ocean-pool status before a special trip.

blocks.text: Pack your bathers, walk a stretch of the coast to get there, and have a dip in one of Sydney's loveliest ocean pools. Bronte doesn't shout about itself — which is exactly why I love it.

sources.label: Waverley Council — ocean pools & cleaning schedules (status/closures)

blocks.text: The short answer: the best car park at Bronte Beach is the Bronte Cutting, the council-run metered area right beside the sand — but on a warm weekend it fills by mid-morning, so either roll in before 9am or be ready to work the back streets. I've circled this valley for years, and the good news is Bronte is genuinely easier to park at than its famous neighbour Bondi, once you know how the meters work.
The Bronte Cutting: your first choice

The Cutting is the ribbon of metered parking running through the middle of the park, from Bronte Road down toward the beach and pool. It's the spot everyone wants — you can practically fall out of the car onto the grass. It's Waverley Council pay parking with pay-by-plate meters, so note your number plate before you walk off. Pay at the machine or, more usefully, through the Park'nPay app, which shows live space availability so you know whether it's worth heading down the hill.

blocks.title: Check the sign, not your memory
blocks.text: Rates, time limits and operating hours are set by Waverley Council and do change. Rather than trust a number you read online, check the meter signage on the day or the Park'nPay app — always the current source of truth.

My morning trick: get there before 9am, especially in summer and on weekends. The sunrise-lap crowd is leaving just as the day-trippers arrive, so you'll often slide into a Cutting bay someone's vacating. Late afternoon is the mirror image — from about 3–4pm the beach thins and spaces open again.
Working the back streets

When the Cutting is full, I head uphill. Unlike Bondi, where a legal kerbside spot near the sand can feel mythical, Bronte's surrounding streets give you a real shot within a short walk. The catch is the maze of restrictions: metered sections, timed zones and permit-only blocks sit next to each other, and Waverley's officers enforce them.
The streets I'd point a first-timer toward:

items: Bronte Road — the main spine down to the beach; metered nearer the bottom, timed and permit zones as you climb.
Macpherson Street — a short, mostly flat walk in from the Charing Cross side.
Pacific Street and the cross-streets above the park — a decent bet if you don't mind a stroll downhill (and the climb back up).
The quieter streets further up the hill — read every sign; many are permit-only and will earn you a fine, not a park.

blocks.title: Read the whole sign before you lock the car
blocks.text: Bronte's restrictions flip from one pole to the next — a 2-hour zone can become resident-permit-only a few metres along. Check the arrows and fine print for your exact bay, and don't assume a free-looking stretch stays free all day.
If you come here often

If Bronte is your regular, it's worth looking at Waverley Council's beach parking permit, which lets you park in the metered beach areas — including the Bronte Cutting — instead of feeding the meter. Eligibility and pricing vary, and residents and ratepayers generally pay less, so check the current terms on the council's permit page before you apply.
The honest answer: leave the car at home

My favourite way to reach Bronte on a busy day is to not drive at all. Buses run from the Bondi Junction interchange (an easy train hop from the city) to the Bronte terminus right by the park, and on a packed summer Sunday they beat the parking lottery every time. Use the Transport for NSW trip planner for routes and times — the difference between starting your day relaxed on the sand and doing laps of the hill.

items.q: Where is the closest car park to Bronte Beach?
items.a: The Bronte Cutting — the council-run metered area running down the middle of the park to the beach and pool. It's pay-by-plate (meters plus the Park'nPay app) and the first place to try.

items.q: How much does parking at Bronte Beach cost?
items.a: The rates are set by Waverley Council and change, so I won't quote a figure that might be stale. Check the meter signage or the Park'nPay app for the current rate and any daily cap.

items.q: What's the best time to get a park at Bronte?
items.a: Before about 9am, or from mid-to-late afternoon (roughly 3–4pm on). On summer weekends everything fills through the middle of the day, so early or late is your friend.

items.q: Is there free parking near Bronte Beach?
items.a: Some surrounding streets have timed or unmetered sections, but they're tangled up with enforced permit-only zones. Read every sign for your exact bay — the safest, closest option is still the metered Cutting.

items.q: Can I avoid parking altogether?
items.a: Yes, and on a busy day I'd recommend it. Take the train to Bondi Junction and a bus down to the Bronte terminus by the park. Check the Transport for NSW trip planner for current routes and times.

blocks.text: Bronte rewards a little forward planning. Arrive early, use the Park'nPay app before you commit, respect the back-street signs, and keep the bus in your back pocket for the busiest days. Do that and you'll spend your day in the water and on the grass — not grinding up and down the hill for a bay.

The safest place to swim at Bondi Beach is between the red-and-yellow flags, and — nine days out of ten — that means the calmer northern end of the beach. The flags aren't decoration: the lifeguards plant them each morning over the water they've judged safest that day, and move them as the surf shifts. Swim between them and you're swimming where trained eyes are watching.

items.label: Avoid if unsure
items.value: The southern end near the rocks

blocks.text: Why the flags matter more than the spot

People often ask me to point at a fixed "safe corner" of Bondi, but the honest answer is that the safe zone moves. The ocean here changes hour to hour — a gentle shore break at breakfast can turn into churning white water by lunchtime. That's why the lifeguards re-set the flags through the day. The safest place isn't a GPS pin; it's wherever those flags are standing right now.

blocks.title: Bondi's rips are the real danger
blocks.text: Most rescues here involve people caught in rip currents — fast, narrow rivers of water pulling straight out to sea. Bondi's most notorious is the 'Backpackers' Express', which usually forms toward the southern end near the rocks. If you're ever caught in one, don't fight it: stay calm, keep floating, raise an arm for the lifeguards, then swim across it parallel to the beach back toward the flags.
North end vs south end

As a rule I send families and less-confident swimmers to the northern end, up toward North Bondi. It's the more sheltered stretch, the water tends to be shallower and gentler, and it's usually where the flags go. The southern end — down by the rocks and the Icebergs headland — is where the surf is punchier and rips set up along the rocks. That end draws surfers and strong swimmers; it's not where I'd wade in if I wasn't sure of myself.

Before you get changed, walk down to the flags and watch the water for two minutes. A darker, flatter channel with fewer breaking waves cutting out through the surf is often a rip, not a safe lane. When in doubt, ask a lifeguard — they'd far rather point you to the right spot than pull you out of the wrong one.
The safest swim of all: the North Bondi children's pool

If you've got little ones, skip the open surf entirely and head to the far northern end, where there's a small, shallow, sandy-bottomed children's pool tucked in beside the Wally Weekes tidal pool. It's sheltered from the waves, gentle, and by a distance the most relaxed place at Bondi to let small kids splash about — it's my first recommendation for anyone travelling with toddlers.

blocks.title: Supervision still comes first
blocks.text: Even in the calmest, shallowest water, young children need an adult within arm's reach. Drowning is silent and fast — it can happen in seconds and in surprisingly little water. Stay off your phone, stay close, and take turns watching if you're in a group.
A few habits that keep you safe

items: Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags, and follow whatever the lifeguards tell you.
Never swim alone, at night, or after drinking alcohol.
Check the day's conditions on Beachsafe before you go in — surf, wind and hazard warnings change constantly.
If you're not a strong ocean swimmer, stay where you can comfortably touch the bottom.
If you get into trouble, don't wave and thrash — float, stay calm, and raise one arm to signal for help.

items.q: Where exactly is the safest place to swim at Bondi?
items.a: Between the red-and-yellow flags, which the lifeguards set up over the safest water each day. That's usually toward the calmer northern end of the beach. For young children, the small sheltered children's pool at the far north end is safer still.

items.q: Is the north or south end of Bondi safer for swimming?
items.a: The northern end is generally the more sheltered, calmer stretch and is where I'd send families and casual swimmers. The southern end, near the rocks and the Icebergs headland, has stronger surf and is where rips commonly form, so it suits surfers and confident swimmers.

items.q: What is the 'Backpackers' Express' at Bondi?
items.a: It's the nickname for Bondi's most infamous rip current, which typically forms toward the southern end of the beach near the rocks. Swimming between the flags keeps you clear of it and in view of the lifeguards.

items.q: What should I do if I'm caught in a rip current?
items.a: Don't fight it. Stay calm, keep floating and raise one arm to signal the lifeguards. Let the rip carry you until it weakens, then swim across it — parallel to the shore — back toward the flags.

items.q: Is Bondi Beach patrolled by lifeguards all year?
items.a: Yes — Bondi is patrolled by professional lifeguards year-round, with longer hours over the warmer months. Times vary by season, so check current hours before an early or late swim and always stay between the flags.

blocks.text: Bondi is one of the great swims on earth, but it's a serious ocean beach too. Read the water, swim between the flags at the calmer north end, keep the kids in the shallow children's pool, and never take your eyes off the little ones. Do that, and you'll get the postcard swim without the scare.

sources.label: Beachsafe (Surf Life Saving Australia) — Bondi Beach conditions

blocks.text: Christmas Day at Bondi Beach is exactly the Aussie summer Christmas the postcards promise — sunshine instead of snow, Santa hats over swimmers, and the sand packed with families, backpackers and homesick travellers all sharing the same patch of coast. If you're weighing up whether to come down on the 25th, my short answer is yes: it's one of my favourite days of the year here. But there are a few things I always tell people first, because a Bondi Christmas rewards anyone who turns up prepared.
What Christmas Day actually feels like here

The beach doesn't run on a schedule on Christmas Day — people drift down from mid-morning and stay until the light goes. You'll see picnics and beach barbecues (seafood and salads far more than roast turkey), pick-up volleyball games, surfers in Santa hats, and groups of travellers who've adopted each other for the day. If you're far from home and feeling it, this is the place to be — almost everyone around you is too, and Bondi's come-as-you-are spirit makes it easy to fall in with a crowd.

For a quieter version of the day, walk it off — the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk is stunning in the morning light, and the northern end of the beach near the children's pool is usually calmer than the busy middle.

blocks.title: Bondi is an alcohol-free zone
blocks.text: Bondi Beach is an alcohol-free zone under Waverley Council rules, and glass is a no-go on the sand. Police and rangers do patrol on Christmas Day. Plan for a booze-free beach day and keep the celebrating for a licensed venue or a private place afterwards — check Waverley Council for the current alcohol-free zone details.
Swim safety comes first

Bondi is patrolled every day of the year by Waverley Council's professional lifeguards, and through summer they're backed up by volunteer surf lifesavers. Wherever you swim, get in between the red and yellow flags — that's the stretch the lifeguards have judged safest and are actively watching. If there are no flags up, the message is simple: don't swim.

blocks.title: Alcohol and the ocean don't mix
blocks.text: Every Christmas the lifeguards deal with avoidable rescues, and alcohol is behind a lot of them — it slows your reactions and clouds your judgement, and even confident swimmers get caught out. If you've had a drink, stay out of the water.

The Sydney sun in late December is fierce — much stronger than a northern-hemisphere winter sun, and it catches visitors out. Slip on a shirt, slop on SPF50+ and reapply every couple of hours, grab a hat, and bring your own shade and water. An umbrella and a full bottle will save your whole afternoon.
What's open (and what to plan around)

Christmas Day is a public holiday in New South Wales, so treat the surrounding shops, cafés and venues as closed or on reduced hours unless you've confirmed otherwise. Don't count on grabbing lunch or a coffee on the strip — bring what you need with you. Public transport also runs to a holiday timetable, so check Transport for NSW before you set out.

The famous Bondi Icebergs pool and its restaurant keep their own festive-season hours, which change year to year — check the Icebergs website directly if you're hoping to swim laps or book a table over Christmas.

items: Pack in: sunscreen, hat, water, snacks or picnic food, shade, a rubbish bag.
Leave at home: alcohol and anything glass — both are prohibited on the beach.
Arrive earlier for parking and a good spot; it fills up fast on a warm 25th.
Bin your rubbish or take it with you — the clean-up after big beach days is brutal.

items.q: Can I drink alcohol on Bondi Beach on Christmas Day?
items.a: No. Bondi Beach is an alcohol-free zone under Waverley Council rules, and glass isn't allowed on the sand either. Police and rangers patrol on Christmas Day, so keep any celebrating to a licensed venue.

items.q: Is it safe to swim at Bondi on Christmas Day?
items.a: Yes, if you swim between the red and yellow flags where the lifeguards are watching, and only if you're sober. Bondi is patrolled year-round, but rips are real — if there are no flags, don't swim.

items.q: Will cafés and shops be open?
items.a: Assume most are closed or on reduced hours, since Christmas Day is a NSW public holiday. Bring your own food and water rather than relying on grabbing something nearby.

items.q: How do I get to Bondi on Christmas Day?
items.a: Public transport runs to a holiday timetable, so check Transport for NSW before you travel. If you're driving, arrive early — parking near the beach disappears fast on a warm Christmas.

items.q: What's the one thing first-timers forget?
items.a: Sun protection. The late-December Sydney sun is much stronger than a European winter sun. Bring SPF50+, a hat, shade and water, and reapply sunscreen every couple of hours.

blocks.text: That's the whole trick to a Bondi Christmas: come prepared, respect the ocean and the sun, take your rubbish with you, and let the day carry you. Local or traveller far from home, Christmas on Bondi has a way of becoming one you remember for all the right reasons.

sources.label: Waverley Council — Alcohol Free Zones and Alcohol Prohibited Areas

blocks.text: If you only do one thing at the southern end of Bondi, make it Icebergs — the cliff-hugging ocean pool where waves crash straight over the lap lanes and swimmers plough on regardless. It's part public pool, part winter-swimming institution, part fine-dining destination, and after years living around the corner I still rate it the most photographed 50 metres of water in Australia. Here's how I'd tackle the whole complex: pool, bistro, and the famous dining room upstairs.

items.label: Where
items.value: 1 Notts Ave, southern end of Bondi Beach

items.label: Closed
items.value: Thursdays for cleaning (tides permitting in summer)

items.label: Best for
items.value: Ocean swims, sunset drinks, a special-occasion lunch

blocks.text: The pool: where locals actually swim

The Bondi Baths are carved into the rocks at the beach's quiet southern corner, and the setup is simple: a full 50-metre saltwater lap pool refreshed by the ocean, plus a smaller shallow pool that's perfect for little kids. Lifeguards are on duty during opening hours, there's a sauna and hot showers, and towel and locker hire if you've turned up empty-handed. On a big swell the sea washes over the eastern wall — which is why the underwater footage from here goes viral every winter.

Admission is refreshingly cheap for something this iconic — a small single-visit fee, with concession rates for kids and families and multi-visit passes if you're staying a while. Prices and hours shift seasonally and the pool closes Thursdays for cleaning, so I always check the official Pool Conditions page the morning of a swim rather than trust a number read online months ago.

Go early. I love a 7am lap when the sun is coming up and the pool is nearly empty — by mid-morning in summer the deck fills with sunbathers and the lanes get busy. The pool also closes for swim-club events on some weekends, so check the club's site first.

blocks.title: Pool and dining room are different bookings
blocks.text: The pool is walk-up entry (no booking). The upstairs Dining Room and Bar is a separate business with its own reservations — you don't need to swim to eat there, but you can't wander up in your swimmers for a table.
A club born in winter

The Bondi Icebergs Swimming Club was founded in 1929 by local lifesavers who wanted to stay fit through the cold months, and winter swimming has been its heart ever since. Membership famously hinges on turning up to swim right through the Sydney winter — the stubborn, salty tradition that makes Bondi, Bondi. On opening day each season, members still toss chunks of ice into the pool to earn the name. You don't need to be a member to swim, though — the pool is open to all.
Eating and drinking: the dining room vs the bistro

There are two ways to eat here, and people mix them up constantly. Upstairs is Icebergs Dining Room and Bar, the glass-walled modern-Italian restaurant opened by restaurateur Maurice Terzini in 2002. It's a proper special-occasion room — floor-to-ceiling views down the length of the beach, a serious wine list, and prices to match. Book ahead, dress up a little, and aim for a window table at golden hour. Menus change often, so I check idrb.com for the current offering before promising anyone a specific dish.
If you want the same view for a fraction of the price, the club's own bistro downstairs is the local's move — relaxed, family-friendly and easy on the wallet.

For the postcard photo of the pool with the whole beach curving behind it, walk up onto the start of the Bondi to Bronte coastal path. That elevated clifftop angle is the shot everyone recognises — and it's free.

items.q: Do I have to be a member to swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: No. The pool is open to the public for a modest entry fee, with concession rates for kids and families. Membership of the Icebergs Swimming Club is a separate thing tied to winter-swimming commitments — you don't need it to swim.

items.q: How much does the Icebergs pool cost and what are the hours?
items.a: It's inexpensive — a small single-visit fee with cheaper rates for kids and families. Because prices and hours change seasonally, and the pool closes Thursdays for cleaning (tides permitting in summer), check the official Pool Conditions page at icebergs.com.au before you go.

items.q: Is the swimming pool the same as the famous restaurant?
items.a: No — they're separate. The Dining Room and Bar is the upmarket modern-Italian restaurant upstairs (book at idrb.com); the pool is the walk-up ocean baths below. There's also a casual, cheaper club bistro if you just want lunch with the view.

items.q: Is Bondi Icebergs good for kids?
items.a: Yes. Alongside the 50-metre lap pool there's a smaller, shallower children's pool, and lifeguards are on duty during opening hours. The casual bistro is family-friendly too, though the pool gets crowded on hot summer afternoons.

items.q: When is the pool closed?
items.a: Icebergs typically closes on Thursdays for cleaning (with summer exceptions when tides permit), and occasionally for swim-club events or heavy seas. Check the official Pool Conditions page the day you visit.

blocks.text: That's the whole complex: swim the ocean pool, warm up in the sauna, grab a bistro lunch, then linger over a drink as the light turns gold over Bondi — which is exactly why Icebergs stays my favourite corner of the beach.

The short answer: Bondi Beach is the sand — the world-famous coastal strip you picture when someone says "Bondi" — while Bondi Junction is a busy inland shopping and transport hub about 2 kilometres uphill, with no beach in sight. They're two separate suburbs, roughly a 10–15 minute bus ride apart, and mixing them up is the single most common mistake I see visitors make when they book accommodation or plan their day.

I've lived around here long enough to have given these directions more times than I can count — usually to someone standing at Bondi Junction with a suitcase, wondering where the ocean went. So here's how the two differ and, more usefully, which one you actually want.

items.label: Bondi Beach
items.value: Coastal suburb — the sand, surf & promenade

items.label: Bondi Junction
items.value: Inland shopping & transport hub, ~2 km uphill

items.label: Apart
items.value: About 2 km / a 10–15 min bus ride

items.label: Train station
items.value: Bondi Junction only — Bondi Beach has none

blocks.text: Bondi Beach: the one you've seen on postcards

Bondi Beach is the coastal suburb about 7 kilometres east of Sydney's CBD. This is the crescent of golden sand, the Icebergs pool, the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk, Campbell Parade's cafés and the surf culture the name is famous for. It's low-rise, salty and relaxed — people come here to swim, sunbake, surf, walk the cliffs and eat with a sea view.

Crucially, Bondi Beach has no train station. You reach it by bus, car, bike or on foot. So if your reason for coming to Sydney is the beach, this is the suburb you want to be near — ideally within walking distance of Campbell Parade or Bondi Road.
Bondi Junction: the shopping and transport hub

Bondi Junction sits inland, roughly 2 kilometres up the hill from the sand and about 6–7 kilometres from the CBD. It's the urban, high-rise end of "Bondi": office towers, apartment blocks and the enormous Westfield Bondi Junction shopping centre. There is no beach here — just a genuinely excellent place to shop, and the main gateway you pass through on the way to the coast.

What makes the Junction matter to visitors is transport. It's the eastern terminus of the T4 Eastern Suburbs line, so trains from Central and the city terminate here, and the bus–rail interchange fans out to the beaches. In practice, most people arriving by train ride to Bondi Junction and then hop on a bus for the final leg down to the sand.

blocks.title: Getting from the Junction to the Beach
blocks.text: From the interchange above Bondi Junction station, frequent buses run down to Bondi Beach — the 333 is the fast, limited-stops service most visitors use. The ride is short, but times shift with traffic, so check live routes and departures in the Transport for NSW trip planner before you head down.
So which one do you actually want?

It comes down to why you're here. If you've come for sand, surf and the coastal walk, base yourself at Bondi Beach — waking up a two-minute stroll from the water beats a daily bus commute every time. If you're after big-brand shopping, a train connection into the city, or simply cheaper, quieter accommodation with easy transport, Bondi Junction is a smart, practical base.

items: Here for the beach, surf or coastal walk → stay at Bondi Beach.
Here for shopping, city train links or better-value stays → Bondi Junction works well.
Arriving by train → you'll pass through Bondi Junction and bus down to the beach.
Driving → the beach has limited, pricey parking; the Junction's Westfield car park is larger.

blocks.text: Double-check your booking says "Bondi Beach" and not "Bondi Junction" if the beach is your priority. I've met travellers who booked a Junction hotel expecting to open the curtains to the ocean — and got a shopping-centre view and a bus timetable instead.

items.q: How far is Bondi Junction from Bondi Beach?
items.a: About 2 kilometres — a short bus ride, a quick drive in light traffic, or a 25–30 minute downhill walk. Frequent buses, including the 333, connect the two; check the Transport for NSW trip planner for current routes and times.

items.q: Does Bondi Beach have a train station?
items.a: No. Bondi Beach has no train station. The nearest is Bondi Junction, the terminus of the T4 Eastern Suburbs line, and from there you take a bus down to the sand.

items.q: Can you walk from Bondi Junction to Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes. It's about 2 kilometres, mostly downhill toward the water, and takes roughly 25–30 minutes. It's an easy walk down; the uphill return is a bit more of a workout, so many people bus back.

items.q: Should I stay in Bondi Beach or Bondi Junction?
items.a: Stay at Bondi Beach if the ocean and beach lifestyle are the point. Choose Bondi Junction if you want major shopping, a direct train line into the city, or more affordable, transport-friendly accommodation.

items.q: Is Bondi Junction the same as Bondi Beach?
items.a: No — they're two distinct suburbs. Bondi Beach is the coastal one with the sand and surf; Bondi Junction is an inland shopping and transport hub with no beach, about 2 kilometres away.

blocks.text: Once the map's straight in your head, the two work brilliantly together: shop and catch your train at the Junction, then ride ten minutes downhill to swim and walk the cliffs. Same name, two very different Bondis — and now you know which is which.

Ask me where to eat in Bondi and I'll give the same answer every time: the best table is one where you can smell the salt and hear the surf. From Sean Moran's dining room above North Bondi to a wood-fired pizza on Hall Street, here's my personal top ten — the places I send hungry friends to.

One honest caveat first: Bondi's food scene moves fast, and hours, menus and prices shift with the seasons. I've linked each venue's own site below — check the details there before you set your heart on a booking. Now, the good stuff.
The special-occasion tables
1. Icebergs Dining Room and Bar

Perched above the ocean pool at the south end, this is the Bondi view everyone pictures — the pool below, the whole crescent of beach beyond. It's polished Italian and a genuine occasion. Book ahead and dress up; if the budget's tight, come for a drink at the bar and soak up the same view.
2. Sean's

Sean Moran has cooked on this North Bondi corner since 1993, and Sean's is still my sentimental favourite. The menu is short, handwritten and driven by whatever's best that week, much of it from his own farm in the Blue Mountains. It feels less like a restaurant than being fed generously in someone's home.
3. North Bondi Fish

Right on Ramsgate Avenue with the sand at your feet, this is where I bring visitors who want seafood with a proper beach view. Oysters, whole fish, a crisp glass of white — long lunches here slide happily into the afternoon.
Brunch, pizza and the everyday classics
4. bills, Bondi

Bill Granger's ricotta hotcakes and creamy scrambled eggs more or less wrote the rulebook for Sydney brunch, and the Hall Street room is bright, buzzy and reliably lovely. Yes, it's popular; yes, it's worth it.
5. Da Orazio Pizza + Porchetta

Da Orazio is back on Hall Street, now with the little wine bar Orazietto next door. Blistered wood-fired pizza, that legendary porchetta and a properly Italian racket of a room — my go-to for a lively group dinner.
6. Bondi Trattoria

The "Tratt" is a Campbell Parade institution — pasta, pizza and people-watching from tables that spill toward the beach. It isn't reinventing anything; it's just a warm, dependable Italian that's fed locals for decades. I love it for an unfussy weeknight spaghetti.
Cafés, casual bites and something sweet
7. Speedo's Cafe

Tucked at the quiet north end, Speedo's is the classic post-swim café — acai bowls, big breakfasts and a health-leaning menu, steps from the sand near Ben Buckler. Grab a table outside and watch the ocean-pool crowd stroll by.
8. Porch and Parlour

Just around the corner, Porch and Parlour has done generous, produce-led breakfasts and lunches for years. It's my pick when I want somewhere calmer than the main drag but still unmistakably North Bondi.
9. Totti's Bondi
The Merivale crowd's Bondi trattoria is all about pillowy wood-fired bread and a table full of Italian sharing plates. A fun, boisterous room — best with friends and no plans for the afternoon.
10. Gelato Messina
No Bondi food day of mine ends without gelato, and Messina's Hall Street scoop shop is the reward after a long beach walk. The flavour board changes constantly, so just ask what's new.

For beachfront tables at the popular spots — weekend brunch at bills, a sunset seat at North Bondi Fish — book a few days ahead or arrive on opening. Walk in at 12:30 on a sunny Saturday and you'll join the queue with everyone else.

blocks.title: Check before you go
blocks.text: Opening hours, session times and menus in Bondi change often. I've linked each venue's official site in the sources — always confirm current details and book directly there rather than trusting a number in any guide, including this one.

items.q: What is the most famous restaurant in Bondi Beach?
items.a: Icebergs Dining Room and Bar is the most iconic, thanks to its perch above the ocean pool and its sweeping view across the beach. Sean's and bills are close behind as long-standing institutions.

items.q: Where's the best breakfast or brunch in Bondi?
items.a: bills on Hall Street is the classic for hotcakes and scrambled eggs. For somewhere quieter, Porch and Parlour and Speedo's Cafe at the north end do generous, produce-led breakfasts near the sand.

items.q: Do I need to book restaurants in Bondi?
items.a: For the sit-down favourites — Icebergs, Sean's, Da Orazio and Totti's — yes, especially on weekends and in summer. Cafés like Speedo's and Porch and Parlour are walk-in, but expect a wait at peak brunch times.

items.q: Where can I eat with a beach view in Bondi?
items.a: North Bondi Fish sits right on the sand at Ramsgate Avenue, and Icebergs overlooks the ocean pool at the south end. Bondi Trattoria's front tables also look out to the water.

items.q: Is there good pizza in Bondi?
items.a: Da Orazio Pizza + Porchetta on Hall Street is the local benchmark for wood-fired pizza. Bondi Trattoria and Totti's are also solid for a relaxed Italian dinner.

blocks.text: That's my ten — splurge-worthy views, honest neighbourhood classics and a scoop of gelato to finish. Eat from the north end to the south and you'll have tasted the real Bondi, salt air and all.

If you only have time for one stretch of Sydney coastline, make it the Eastern Suburbs beaches — Bondi, Tamarama, Bronte, Clovelly, Gordons Bay, Coogee and Maroubra, strung along about six kilometres of headland. I've walked this coast in every mood, and the short version I give friends is: Bondi for the buzz, Bronte for a swim with the kids, Clovelly and Gordons Bay for snorkelling, Coogee to finish with a beer. Here's how I'd actually spend the day.

items.label: How I get around
items.value: The clifftop coastal walk on foot

blocks.text: Start at Bondi — the famous one, for good reason

Bondi is the beach that ends up on the postcards, and I never tire of it — a wide sweep of pale sand with a flagged swimming area, a busy café promenade and a sea pool at each end. The Icebergs pool at the southern tip is the iconic one; swimming a few laps there with waves crashing over the wall is a rite of passage. Sessions and lane availability change seasonally, so check the Icebergs website before you go rather than trusting a timetable I might have out of date.
Bondi's parking is a headache on any warm weekend. I'll often park near Coogee or take the bus, walk north to Bondi, then stroll back — you get the whole coast twice and never circle a car park.
The walk south: Tamarama, Bronte and the sea baths

From Bondi's southern end the coastal walk begins — my favourite way to see the lot. First up is Tamarama — locals call it 'Glamarama' — a small, pretty pocket beach hemmed by cliffs. It's beautiful, but the surf can be powerful and the rips serious: swim only between the flags when it's patrolled, and if in doubt, just press on.

A little further on is Bronte, which might be the most complete beach on the coast for a family day: a patrolled surf beach, a grassy park with barbecues and shade, a kiosk row, and the Bronte Baths carved into the rocks for a sheltered swim when the shore break is dumping. It's the classic midpoint of the walk.

blocks.title: Read the beach before you swim
blocks.text: Conditions on this coast change fast — Tamarama, Bronte and Maroubra can all throw strong rips. Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags at a patrolled beach, and check the daily surf report on the Beachsafe app (Surf Life Saving Australia) before you get in.
The snorkelling middle: Clovelly and Gordons Bay

This is the part visitors often miss, and I'd send you here first. Clovelly isn't a wide sandy beach at all — it's a long, narrow bay between two rock shelves, with flat concrete edges to lay a towel on and steps into calm, clear water. Because it's so sheltered it's brilliant for kids learning to snorkel, with plenty to see from little fish to the resident blue gropers. Around the headland, Gordons Bay is a quiet cobbled cove with a marked underwater nature trail for snorkellers and divers. Both sit inside the Bronte–Coogee Aquatic Reserve, so it's look-don't-touch — no fishing or collecting.
Finish at Coogee (with Maroubra as a bonus)

Coogee is where I like to end up: a friendly, family-sized beach with a Norfolk-pine promenade made for an evening walk and pubs and cafés a block back for a well-earned feed. It's also home to a cluster of ocean pools — Wylie's Baths on the southern headland, and McIver's Baths, a historic women-and-children's swimming spot. Entry fees and hours for the tidal pools change, so check locally on the day. If you've still got legs, Maroubra sits further south — a long, surf-serious beach that's less crowded, with a skate park and playground.

items.q: What's the best order to visit the Eastern Suburbs beaches?
items.a: I walk north-to-south: Bondi, Tamarama, Bronte, Clovelly, Gordons Bay, then Coogee, with Maroubra as an optional extra beyond. Finishing at Coogee means plenty of pubs and cafés for a late lunch or sunset drink.

items.q: How long is the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk?
items.a: It's roughly six kilometres one way and most people take about two hours at a relaxed pace, longer with swims and coffee stops. It's a sealed clifftop path with some stairs — just bring water, sun protection and decent shoes.

items.q: Which beach is best for snorkelling?
items.a: Clovelly and Gordons Bay. Clovelly's sheltered channel is calm and easy for kids, while Gordons Bay has a marked underwater nature trail. Both sit inside the Bronte–Coogee Aquatic Reserve, so it's look-but-don't-take.

items.q: Which beaches suit young families?
items.a: Bronte and Clovelly are my picks — Bronte has a grassy park, barbecues and the sheltered Bronte Baths, and Clovelly's calm water is ideal for little swimmers. Coogee is gentle too.

items.q: Do I need to pay or book anything?
items.a: The beaches and the coastal walk are free. Some ocean pools charge a small entry fee and hours vary seasonally, so check on the day. Parking is the real cost on warm weekends — buses or an early start save the stress.

blocks.text: That's the whole coast in a day: Bondi's energy, the cliff path through Bronte's parkland, the clear water at Clovelly and Gordons Bay, and Coogee as the light goes gold. Bring a towel, sunscreen and time to spare — it's the stretch of Sydney I never tire of showing people.

sources.label: Destination NSW — Bondi to Coogee Coastal Walk
Randwick City Council — Beaches and coast

blocks.text: Here's my honest answer to the question I'm asked most about Mackenzies Bay: it's real, it's genuinely magic, and there's a good chance it isn't there right now. "Maccas", as we call it, is a tiny cove tucked between Bondi and Tamarama that only becomes a golden-sand beach in certain years — then vanishes back to bare rock, sometimes for the better part of a decade. If you catch it with sand, you've caught one of Sydney's true hidden gems.

items.label: Where
items.value: Between Bondi & Tamarama, on the coastal walk

items.label: Sandy?
items.value: Only in certain years — highly unpredictable

blocks.text: The beach that comes and goes

Most years, most of the time, Mackenzies is a rugged little rock platform you'd stroll straight past. Then, every so often, the ocean quietly rebuilds it: sand gets carried in from nearby sandbanks and piled into the cove until — seemingly overnight — there's a proper beach where there was bare stone. It's the same spot; it just changes costume. One season it's a sunbathing pocket, the next a rocky enclave good for peering into tidal pools.

Coastal scientists put it down to a recipe of waves in the right size and direction, a nearby supply of loose sand, and calm-ish conditions to let it settle. Low-pressure swells, offshore winds and stretches without big storms all help it pile up — and El Niño years, which bring less storm activity, have lined up with some of its appearances. A serious storm can strip the same sand just as fast.
How long has it been gone this time?

The bay keeps no schedule. It's often quoted as appearing "every seven years or so", but that's a rough average, not a promise. A cyclone stripped the sand in the late 1990s and it reportedly stayed bare rock until around 2007, when it returned briefly as a wide sweep of sand before winter gales carried it off within months. Because it's this fickle, I never claim it's here right now — check a recent photo or a local's Instagram before you make the trip.

blocks.title: This is not a swimming beach
blocks.text: Mackenzies isn't an official, patrolled beach — there are no lifeguards, access is over slippery rock, and the cove is known for unpredictable surges and rips. Even when the sand looks inviting, treat the water with real caution and never turn your back on it, because unexpected waves can wash right across the rocks. For a swim, walk the few minutes to patrolled Bondi or Tamarama instead.
How to find it (and when to bother)

There's no road to Maccas — the only sensible way in is on foot along the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk. From the southern end of Bondi, follow the path past the Icebergs and over the headland toward Tamarama; Mackenzies is the little cove between the two, below the track. The last scramble down is over rock and can be slick, so wear proper shoes and skip it in the wet.

Even without sand, this stretch of the coastal walk is worth doing for the clifftop views alone. Go early for soft light, fewer people, and easy parking before Bondi fills up. If you're chasing the sand, a lower tide gives you the best look — a high tide can hide what little there is.

Part of the charm is the crowd, or lack of one. Because it's off the radar and unpatrolled, Maccas draws a small, easygoing group of locals rather than the crowds of Bondi — and yes, plenty of dogs. Just know that dog rules on Waverley's beaches and reserves are set and enforced by the council, so check their current signage and website before you bring the pup rather than assuming it's a free-for-all.

items.q: Is Mackenzies Bay there right now?
items.a: Impossible to promise. It's a rocky inlet most of the time and only becomes a sandy beach in certain years, sometimes vanishing for years in between. Before you go specifically for the sand, check a very recent photo or ask a local — its status can even change with the tide.

items.q: Where exactly is Mackenzies Bay?
items.a: It's the small cove between Bondi and Tamarama beaches, tucked below the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk. There's no road access — you reach it on foot from the walking track.

items.q: Can you swim at Mackenzies Bay?
items.a: It's not recommended. There are no lifeguards, access is over slippery rock, and the cove is known for rips and unpredictable surges. Swim at patrolled Bondi or Tamarama instead, both only minutes away.

items.q: Why does the beach disappear?
items.a: The sand is delivered by the ocean under the right mix of swell, wind and calm conditions, then carried away again by storms. There's no fixed pattern — it's at the mercy of the weather.

items.q: Can I bring my dog?
items.a: You'll often see dogs there because the cove is unpatrolled, but dog access on Waverley's beaches and reserves is governed by council rules. Check the council's current signage and website before you go rather than assuming it's allowed.

blocks.text: That's what I love about Maccas: it refuses to be pinned down. In a city full of famous, reliable beaches, here's one that shows up on its own terms and slips away when it feels like it. Catch it with sand and it feels like a secret the ocean let you in on. Catch it as bare rock and, well — that's just an excuse to try your luck another year.

sources.label: Waverley Council Library — Mackenzies Bay, the disappearing beach
Time Out Sydney — Sydney's disappearing beach

blocks.text: Here's the honest answer I give every visitor who asks: you can legally fly a drone in the Bondi area, but almost certainly not the way you're imagining — hovering low over the sand, the surf break or the Icebergs pool full of swimmers. On a normal Bondi day the beach is a crowd, and Australia's drone rules don't allow flying over people, so the classic "buzz the beach" shot is off the table. The good news: with a bit of planning you can still get jaw-dropping aerial photos and stay on the right side of the law.
What Australia's drone rules actually say
Drones are governed nationally by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA). If you fly recreationally, these core rules apply at Bondi just as they do everywhere else:

items: Stay at or below 120 metres (400 ft) above ground level.
Keep the drone at least 30 metres away from other people — and never fly directly over anyone.
Don't fly over crowds, gatherings, sporting events or a busy beach.
Fly only one drone at a time, in daylight, and always within your visual line of sight.
Don't fly near where emergency operations (like a surf rescue) are underway.
Keep well clear of controlled airspace and away from helicopters and other aircraft.

blocks.title: Check before you launch
blocks.text: To know whether the airspace above you is open, use a CASA-verified drone safety app (the "Can I fly there?" tools). It shows restricted zones and airport buffers in real time — which matters in Sydney, where airspace changes quickly.
The Bondi problem: it's almost always a crowd

The biggest thing that trips people up isn't the height limit — it's people. A patrolled, populated beach counts as a populous area, so the 30-metre rule and the no-flying-over-people rule make a full beach on a sunny Saturday a no-go for casual flying. Bondi also sits under busy Sydney airspace with helicopters passing along the coast, which is why keeping clear of aircraft and staying in line of sight isn't optional.
Where you take off and land matters too

On top of CASA's air rules there's a second layer people forget: the ground. The beach, promenade and surrounding parks are Waverley Council land, and councils can restrict or prohibit launching, landing and operating drones from their reserves — often with on-site signage. So even when the airspace looks clear, you may still not be permitted to take off from the sand or the park.

blocks.title: Obey the signs and the council
blocks.text: Before you fly, read any on-site signage and check Waverley Council's current position on drones on council land. Anything commercial — paid photography, film or media — will generally need a council permit and, depending on the job, CASA accreditation. When in doubt, ask the council first.
Whales, wildlife and your neighbours' privacy

From roughly May to November the humpbacks migrate past Bondi, and it's tempting to chase them with a drone. Don't. NSW has strict approach distances for marine mammals, and a drone diving in on a whale is both illegal and a fast track to serious social-media backlash from locals. Keep your distance, check the current NSW National Parks marine mammal rules, and give sunbathers the same courtesy: no one wants a camera over their towel.

My move for a clean Bondi aerial: get down for a weekday sunrise before the beach fills up, launch from a quiet, open spot away from people, and shoot out over the empty water toward the headland rather than back over the sand. Early light on the pool and the curve of the bay does the work for you.

items.q: Can I legally fly a drone over Bondi Beach?
items.a: Not when the beach is populated, which is most of the time. CASA rules ban flying over people and require you to stay 30 m from them, so hovering over a busy beach isn't allowed. You can fly in the wider area if you keep clear of people, stay under 120 m and in line of sight, and check that both the airspace and the council land you use permit it.

items.q: Do I need a licence to fly a drone for fun at Bondi?
items.a: For purely recreational flying within CASA's standard rules you generally don't need a licence, but you must follow all the operating conditions. Anything commercial — paid photos, film or media — usually needs a Waverley Council permit and, depending on the job, CASA accreditation.

items.q: Can I film the whales migrating past Bondi with my drone?
items.a: No. NSW sets minimum approach distances for whales and other marine mammals, and flying close to them is against the rules. Watch from the clifftops instead and check the current NSW National Parks guidance first.

items.q: How do I get a great Bondi aerial shot without breaking the rules?
items.a: Go at a quiet time like a weekday sunrise, launch from open ground away from people, stay under 120 m and in sight, and shoot out over open water rather than the sand or crowd. Check airspace with a CASA-verified app and obey on-site signage first.

blocks.text: Bondi from the air really is something special — the pool, the sweep of the bay, the light at dawn. Earn it the responsible way: right time, right place, clear of people and wildlife, and a quick check of the rules before you launch. Nail the shot and tag @visitbondibeach and #visitbondibeach so we can all admire it.

sources.label: CASA — Can I fly there? (drone safety apps)
