blocks.text: The short answer: Bondi Beach sits about 7 km east of the Sydney CBD and roughly 14 km from Sydney Airport, and from either you're realistically 30 to 60 minutes away, depending on how you travel. Here's my local take on how far Bondi really is — and the smartest way to close the gap.

The single most important thing to know: there's no train station at Bondi Beach itself, and the name catches a lot of visitors out. The closest station is Bondi Junction, about 3 km up the hill, and from there you hop on a bus down to the sand.
The Bondi Junction hop (how nearly everyone arrives)

Bondi Junction is the eastern terminus of the T4 Eastern Suburbs & Illawarra line, so trains from the CBD and the airport line all funnel through it. Follow the signs upstairs to the bus interchange and jump on a 333, 380 or 381 — each runs frequently down Bondi Road to Campbell Parade, right along the beachfront.
The 333 is the one I steer people towards: a limited-stops express that runs from the CBD through Bondi Junction to the beach, so you can often skip the train and stay on one bus.

Tap on with a contactless card or your phone — you don't need a physical Opal card anymore, and the daily and Sunday fare caps apply just the same. One tap covers the train, a second the connecting bus. Child and concession fares still need a physical card.
From Sydney Airport

Bondi is one of the closer beaches to the airport, around 14 km by road. A taxi or rideshare is usually 25 to 40 minutes, though the Eastern Distributor can bunch up in peak hour, so leave a buffer if you've got a flight. On public transport, take the airport train to Bondi Junction — the airport stations charge a separate access fee on top of the normal fare — then a beach bus down — slower than a car, but cheap.

blocks.title: Check live times before you commit
blocks.text: Bus and train frequencies shift by time of day, and roadworks around the Eastern Suburbs come and go. For an exact door-to-door time, plug your start point into the free Transport for NSW Trip Planner — it accounts for the current timetable and any disruptions.
From the CBD, Opera House and Circular Quay

This is the easy one. Catch the 333 straight to the beach, or take a T4 train to Bondi Junction and change to a bus — either way, generally 30 to 50 minutes. The 333 starts near Circular Quay, so after the Opera House you can go from harbour to surf without working out a connection.
From Manly and the Northern Beaches

Manly and Bondi are Sydney's two most famous beaches, on opposite sides of the harbour, so this is the longest common trip — comfortably over an hour on public transport. My favourite way is also the most scenic: catch the Manly ferry to Circular Quay, then pick up the 333 out to Bondi, turning a slog into one of the best half-days in the city.
By car you cross the Harbour Bridge or the tunnel — genuinely unpredictable, so I'd budget 45 to 75 minutes.
A quick word on driving and parking

You can drive, but I rarely recommend it unless you're staying out this way. Street parking around Campbell Parade is metered, time-limited and fiercely contested, especially on warm weekends — nine times out of ten the train-and-bus combo is faster and far less stressful than circling for a space.

items.q: Is there a train station at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No — the name trips a lot of visitors up. The nearest is Bondi Junction on the T4 line, about 3 km from the sand. From there a 333, 380 or 381 bus runs down to the beachfront.

items.q: How far is Bondi Beach from Sydney city centre?
items.a: About 7 km east of the CBD. The 333 express runs from the city straight to the beach, or take a T4 train to Bondi Junction and change to a bus — usually 30 to 50 minutes.

items.q: How do I get from Sydney Airport to Bondi Beach?
items.a: It's roughly 14 km. A taxi or rideshare is quickest at around 25 to 40 minutes. By public transport, take the airport train to Bondi Junction (a station access fee applies at the airport) and connect to a beach bus.

items.q: What's the best way to get from Manly to Bondi?
items.a: My pick is the Manly ferry to Circular Quay, then the 333 to Bondi — scenic and simple. Allow well over an hour, since you have to cross the harbour either way.

items.q: Do I need an Opal card?
items.a: Not necessarily. You can tap on with a contactless card or a phone, and the fare caps still apply. A physical Opal card is only essential for child, concession or senior fares.

blocks.text: Bondi feels like its own world once your toes are in the sand, but it's genuinely well connected — a short bus from a major train station, an easy hop from almost anywhere in Sydney. Sort out the Bondi Junction connection, tap on with a card, and the distance takes care of itself.

sources.label: Transport for NSW — Opal fares & travel

blocks.text: Yes — there are free public electric barbecues at all three beaches, and the best of them sit at Bronte Park, Tamarama and the north end of Bondi. They're the push-button kind maintained by Waverley Council, and on a good weekend they're the beating heart of the coast: sausages sizzling, kids everywhere, someone's uncle guarding the hotplate. Here's exactly where I'd send you, and how to actually land one.

items.label: Where
items.value: Bronte Park, Tamarama Beach, North Bondi

blocks.text: Bronte Park — the family favourite

If you only pick one, make it Bronte. The park curves behind the beach in a big green amphitheatre, with the barbecues among picnic shelters and shady grass, and the playground and Bronte Baths a short toddle away. It's my pick for families — you cook, the kids run, and there's a saltwater pool for the post-lunch swim. There are only a couple of hotplates, though, so on a sunny Saturday they go early.

items: Picnic shelters and plenty of shaded grass for the eskies
Playground and the Bronte Baths ocean pool right there
Bronte Gully behind you if you want quieter, leafier tables
The kiosk and cafés on Bronte Road for coffee and forgotten supplies

blocks.text: Bronte is the hardest of the three to park near. Come on the 379 bus, or arrive before 9am and walk in — circling the streets at midday on a hot Sunday is a special kind of misery.
Tamarama — small, scenic and underrated

Little Tamarama — "Glamarama" to the regulars — has barbecue facilities tucked behind the beach, with sheltered tables and that dramatic view up the gully. It's a smaller beach and park, which is exactly why I like it: fewer hotplates, but far fewer people fighting for them than at Bondi or Bronte. There's a little playground in the gully and a grassy slope made for a rug.

blocks.title: Swim between the flags
blocks.text: Tamarama is one of the most powerful little beaches in Sydney and rips are common. It's patrolled, so always swim between the red-and-yellow flags and watch kids in the shallows, even on a calm-looking day.
North Bondi — barbecues with the big view

The northern end of Bondi is where the barbecues cluster, on the grassy foreshore near the children's playground and skate area. It's the spot for a bigger group — the most cooking capacity of the three, ocean pools nearby, and that full sweep of Bondi in front of you. It's also the busiest, so start early.

items: Foreshore BBQs near the North Bondi playground and skate park
A short stroll to the North Bondi end of the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk
Ocean pools and the surf club within easy reach
Cafés and public toilets close by

blocks.text: How to actually get a hotplate

The barbecues are free and there's no booking — genuinely first-come, first-served. On a warm weekend or public holiday the good ones are gone by mid-morning, so if a cook-up is the plan, get there early and hold the fort.

items: Arrive before 10am on weekends and holidays, earlier on a scorcher
Send one person ahead to claim a plate while the others park
Bring your own oil, foil, tongs, paper towel and a rubbish bag
Have a picnic backup in case every hotplate's taken

blocks.title: Leave it clean, and check the fire rules
blocks.text: Rangers patrol these parks, and leaving a filthy hotplate or littering can earn a fine. On extreme-danger days a Total Fire Ban can also change what's allowed in public parks, so check the NSW Rural Fire Service first. For current facilities and any bring-your-own-gas rules, Waverley Council is the source of truth.

Charcoal and wood fires aren't the go in these parks — stick to the council electric plates or a compliant gas BBQ. And pack patience: the push-button plates take a while to heat, so fire them up before you start chopping onions.

items.q: Are the BBQs at Bondi, Bronte and Tamarama free?
items.a: Yes — the electric barbecues in the council parks are free public facilities from Waverley Council. There's no booking, so the only real cost is getting there early enough to grab one.

items.q: Can you book a public barbecue at Bronte or Bondi?
items.a: No — the individual hotplates can't be reserved; it's first-come, first-served. For a larger event, contact Waverley Council about park hire and permits.

items.q: Which spot is best for a family with young kids?
items.a: Bronte Park, for my money — the barbecues sit right by the playground, the Bronte Baths ocean pool and shaded grass. Tamarama is a lovely quieter alternative.

items.q: Can I bring my own gas BBQ or charcoal?
items.a: Charcoal and open fires aren't permitted in these coastal parks. A portable gas BBQ may be allowed in some areas, but check with Waverley Council first — and remember a Total Fire Ban can override everything on extreme days.

items.q: Are dogs allowed near the barbecues?
items.a: Dogs are welcome on-leash across much of the Waverley area, with off-leash times in spots like Bronte Gully, but they're generally kept away from the barbecue, playground and beach areas. Check the council's current dog rules.

blocks.text: That's the local playbook: Bronte for families, Tamarama for a quieter view, North Bondi for a big group. Get there early, cook something simple, and leave the hotplate cleaner than you found it. See you at the grill.

sources.label: NSW Rural Fire Service — Fire danger & Total Fire Bans

blocks.text: When people ask me for the calmest, prettiest swim near Bondi, I send them over the headland to Nielsen Park and its harbour cove, Shark Beach — a netted, gentle-water beach in Sydney Harbour National Park at Vaucluse, wrapped in fig-shaded lawns with the city skyline glinting across the water. It's the antidote to a big surf day: no crashing waves, just clear green water and one of the loveliest views in Sydney.

If you'd tried to visit in the last few years you may have found it fenced off. Shark Beach was closed for a major rebuild of its near-100-year-old seawall and reopened to swimmers on 12 December 2024, with refreshed grounds, extra promenade seating and a wheelchair-accessible ramp down to the sand. It's back — and honestly, better than I remember it.

items.label: Where
items.value: Nielsen Park, Vaucluse (Sydney Harbour National Park)

items.label: Cost
items.value: Free entry to the park and beach

blocks.text: Why I love Shark Beach

Don't let the name spook you — the "shark" here is the net, not the resident. A marine net curves out from the shore in the warmer months, so you swim in a sheltered pocket of the harbour with sailboats and kayaks drifting just beyond it. Because it's harbour rather than open ocean, there's no shore dump and barely a ripple — my go-to when I've got little kids in tow or just want a float rather than a fight with the surf.

Behind the sand is the bit that keeps me coming back: a wide, sloping lawn under enormous Moreton Bay figs and grassy terraces made for a blanket. Above it sits Greycliffe House, a grand 19th-century sandstone mansion — not open as a casual attraction, but a beautiful backdrop for a picnic.

The shark net is a summer fixture — it's typically removed over the cooler months and can come out temporarily after big swells. If a netted swim is the whole point of your trip, check the NSW National Parks alerts page before you commit.
Getting there and parking

By car from Bondi it's a short, pretty run north through Vaucluse — but parking is the catch. There's a limited car park and some accessible spaces off Greycliffe Avenue, and on a warm weekend they fill early. My honest advice: arrive before mid-morning or plan to circle.

By public transport, the 325 bus runs through Vaucluse and stops near the park entrance, and you can connect to it from Bondi Junction or the city. Because bus routes and timetables change, I'd plug your start point into the Transport for NSW trip planner rather than trusting a fixed time — it'll give you the current route and connections.

blocks.title: Come by foot if you can
blocks.text: Nielsen Park sits on the Hermitage Foreshore Walk, an easy harbourside track linking it toward Rose Bay with knockout views of the Harbour Bridge and city. Walking in and swimming to cool off is one of my favourite half-days in the eastern suburbs.
Food, facilities and the kiosk

The historic kiosk has reopened as The Nielsen, a café-restaurant serving casual bites like fish and chips through to a sit-down menu. Hours and menus shift with the season, so check its site before counting on a meal there. There are also public toilets, picnic tables and barbecues around the grounds, so a bring-your-own picnic works just as well.

items: Pack reef shoes or thongs — the sand gives way to some rocky, seagrassy patches near the edges.
Shade goes fast under the figs on hot days; a small sun shelter is worth bringing.
There's no surf patrol like Bondi's — it's calm water, but keep your own eye on young swimmers.

items.q: Is Nielsen Park safe for swimming with kids?
items.a: It's one of the calmer options near Bondi — Shark Beach is a netted harbour cove with no ocean waves, which makes it popular with families. There's no ocean-style lifeguard patrol though, so supervise children closely as you would at any harbour beach.

items.q: Are there really sharks at Shark Beach?
items.a: The name predates the net and refers to the harbour, not a hazard on the day. A marine net is installed over the summer months to create an enclosed swimming area. As with anywhere in the harbour, swim within the netted zone.

items.q: How do I get to Nielsen Park from Bondi?
items.a: By car it's a short drive north through Vaucluse, but parking off Greycliffe Avenue is limited — arrive early. By public transport the 325 bus stops near the entrance; use the Transport for NSW trip planner for current times from your start point.

items.q: Is there food at Nielsen Park?
items.a: Yes — the historic kiosk has reopened as The Nielsen, a café-restaurant serving casual bites through to a dine-in menu. Hours vary seasonally, so check their website. There are also barbecues and picnic tables if you'd rather bring your own.

items.q: When did Shark Beach reopen?
items.a: Shark Beach reopened on 12 December 2024 after a multi-year closure to rebuild its ageing seawall, along with refreshed grounds and a new accessible ramp to the sand.

blocks.text: So if the Bondi surf is pumping and you fancy the opposite — glassy water, a shady lawn and a view worth lingering over — point yourself north to Nielsen Park. It's a joy to have it back.

sources.label: NSW National Parks — Nielsen Park visitor info
NSW Environment — Nielsen Park seawall rebuild project

blocks.text: Are there thieves or pickpockets at Bondi Beach? Honestly, not many — Bondi is a friendly, well-patrolled family beach, and violent theft is rare. What does happen, like at any busy beach, is the opportunist kind: a phone, wallet or bag left on a towel while everyone's in the surf, gone in a heartbeat. You just don't want to hand anyone an easy target.

I've swum here for years, and the pattern is almost always the same. It's not gangs working the promenade — it's someone spotting an unattended bag near the water and helping themselves. The good news: a couple of simple habits make you an unappealing mark.
How common is theft at Bondi, really?

Low, but not zero. Bondi is patrolled by professional lifeguards through the day, there's a police station right by the beach, and the promenade stays busy from dawn to sunset. That crowd is mostly your friend — thieves prefer quiet, unwatched spots. The classic Bondi loss isn't a dramatic snatch; it's the phone that slid out of a bag, or the wallet left visible while you swam. Treat your gear as you would in any big city and you'll be fine.

blocks.title: The one rule that matters most
blocks.text: Never leave valuables unattended on the sand while you swim — not even for "just a quick dip". An unwatched bag by the shoreline is the easiest thing to take. If it can't be watched, it shouldn't be there.
My local playbook for keeping your stuff safe
None of this is complicated — it's just what the regulars do.

items: Travel light. Bring only a card, a little cash, your phone and keys. Leave the passport, spare cards and good jewellery at your accommodation.
Use the buddy system. Take turns — one swims, one watches the towels. It's the oldest trick and still the best.
Set up near the flags and lifeguard tower — more eyes and foot traffic, less appeal for anyone sizing up bags.
Keep valuables on your body. A waterproof pouch around your neck or waist keeps a card, key and phone with you in the water — no beach pile to guard.
Make your bag boring. Tuck phones and wallets deep inside, zipped up, not perched on top of a towel like a shopfront display.
Mind your car. Don't leave anything visible in a parked car around Bondi — bags, cameras and loose change are an invitation.

blocks.text: My favourite low-effort trick: a cheap dry bag or an old-looking supermarket bag. Thieves go for the obvious designer backpack, not a scruffy plastic bag. Camouflage beats a lock.
Lockers and somewhere to stash your bag

If you'd rather not babysit your things, you're near a few options. The Bondi Pavilion sits on the beachfront with change rooms and facilities, and there are private luggage-storage spots and cafés around Campbell Parade. Availability, hours and fees change, so check on the day at the Pavilion, or search "Bondi luggage storage" for current staffed options near the beach. For a swim, though, a waterproof pouch on your body usually beats a walk back to a locker.
If something does get taken

First, don't panic — and act fast on the digital side, where the real damage is. Use Find My iPhone or Find My Device to lock and locate your phone, and call your bank to freeze cards. Then report it: you'll almost always need a report number for insurance or a replacement card.

items.label: Non-emergency report
items.value: Police Assistance Line — 131 444, or report online at police.nsw.gov.au

items.label: Nearest station
items.value: Bondi Beach Police Station, near the beach

items.label: On the sand
items.value: Flag down a lifeguard — they'll point you the right way

items.q: Is Bondi Beach safe for tourists?
items.a: Yes — Bondi is a busy, well-patrolled beach that's very safe for visitors, and serious crime against people is rare. The main risk is opportunistic theft of unattended belongings, which the simple habits above almost entirely prevent.

items.q: Are there pickpockets at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Classic street-style pickpocketing isn't really the Bondi problem. Far more common is unattended items — bags, phones and wallets left on the sand while people swim — being taken. Keep valuables on you or watched and you remove the risk.

items.q: Where can I leave my things while I swim at Bondi?
items.a: Best of all, don't leave them — wear a waterproof pouch with your card, key and phone, or use the buddy system so someone always watches the towels. The Bondi Pavilion and nearby luggage-storage services handle larger bags; check availability and fees on the day.

items.q: How do I report theft at Bondi Beach?
items.a: For a crime in progress or any danger, call Triple Zero (000). To report a theft after the fact, call the NSW Police Assistance Line on 131 444 or report online at police.nsw.gov.au — you'll get a report number for insurance.

items.q: Should I bring valuables to Bondi Beach at all?
items.a: Bring only what you'll actually use — a card, some cash, your phone and keys. Leave your passport, spare cards, laptop and good jewellery at your accommodation. Less to lose means less to worry about.

blocks.text: So — are there thieves at Bondi? Occasionally, in the opportunist sense, like any famous beach. But this is my patch, and I don't spend my swims worrying about it. Travel light, keep valuables on you or watched, and you'll be free to do the only thing Bondi asks: get in the water.

sources.label: NSW Police Force — Report a crime
NSW Police Force — Police Assistance Line (131 444)
NSW Police Force — Bondi Beach Police Station

blocks.text: If you just want to see what Bondi is doing right now, the quickest way is a live surf cam — and my go-to is the Swellnet Bondi camera, which streams the beach in real time along with the current swell and wind. I check it most mornings before I decide whether to bring the board, the towel, or just my coffee. Below I'll walk you through the cams I actually trust, what they can (and can't) tell you, and how to read the picture before you head down.

items.label: Cost
items.value: Free to view (some replays/HD need a subscription)

blocks.text: The Bondi surf cams I actually use
There's no single "official" Bondi cam — a few different feeds point at the beach, and each has its own angle and quirks. These are the ones I keep bookmarked:
Swellnet — my first check. A live HD stream looking across the beach, paired with the current surf report, swell and wind readings. It's the one I'd send a visiting mate.
Surfline — another solid live cam bundled with a multi-day forecast for swell, wind and tide. Handy if you're planning a few days ahead.
Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club — a stream from the club at the south end, near the Icebergs corner where the surfers gather.
North Bondi Surf Life Saving Club — a free community feed looking over the quieter northern end, which is usually the gentler side for a swim.

blocks.title: Streams move around
blocks.text: Cam operators occasionally change hosting, go offline for maintenance, or move a feed behind a subscription. If a link's down, open the club or Swellnet/Surfline homepage and follow their current cam link rather than trusting an old bookmark.
How to read Bondi before you leave home

A surf cam is brilliant for a gut-check, but it flattens the ocean — waves always look smaller on a screen than they feel when you're standing in the shorebreak. Here's how I get more out of the picture:
For surfers

I watch a few sets roll through rather than judging on a single frame, then cross-check the cam against the swell and wind figures on Swellnet or Surfline. Bondi is exposed to south and east swells, and a light offshore (westerly) wind is what cleans it up. The southern end near the point tends to hold the better banks, but it's also the most crowded.
For swimmers and families

Look for the red-and-yellow flags on the cam — that's the patrolled zone, and it's the only place you should swim. If the water looks churned up or you can spot a darker, calmer channel cutting out through the whitewater, that's often a rip. Patrol hours and current flag positions change with the season, so I confirm them on Surf Life Saving NSW's Beachsafe page rather than eyeballing the screen.

Cam glare is real. Around sunrise the low sun blows out the eastern-facing feeds, and after dark most of them are useless. Mid-morning gives the clearest read of both the surf and how busy the sand already is.

blocks.title: A cam is not a lifeguard
blocks.text: Never let a calm-looking screen talk you into swimming outside the flags or when the beach isn't patrolled. Conditions at Bondi can change fast, and rips aren't always visible on camera. When in doubt, ask a lifeguard on the sand.
Pair the cam with a forecast

The cam tells you now; a forecast tells you later. Before a dawn patrol I'll glance at the swell and wind outlook on Swellnet or Surfline, and check the Bureau of Meteorology for Sydney weather, wind and tide times. Tide matters more than people expect at Bondi — the same swell can look playful at one stage of the tide and closed-out at another.

items.q: Where can I watch a live Bondi Beach surf cam?
items.a: The most reliable free live feeds are the Swellnet and Surfline Bondi cams, plus community streams from the Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club and North Bondi Surf Life Saving Club. Each looks at a slightly different part of the beach.

items.q: Is the Bondi surf cam free to watch?
items.a: Viewing the live streams is generally free. Some platforms put HD, replays or detailed long-range forecasts behind a paid subscription, but you don't need to pay just to check current conditions.

items.q: Does the surf cam show how crowded the beach is?
items.a: Yes — that's one of the best uses. A quick look tells you roughly how packed the sand and the car parks are, which is gold on a hot summer weekend or a public holiday.

items.q: Can I rely on the cam to decide it's safe to swim?
items.a: No. Use it as a first look, but always swim between the red-and-yellow flags during patrol hours, and check current patrol times and safety alerts on Surf Life Saving NSW's Beachsafe page. A camera can't spot every rip.

items.q: What's the best time of day to check the cam?
items.a: Mid-morning gives the clearest image. Early sunrise light can wash out the eastern-facing cameras, and after dark most Bondi feeds are too dim to read.

blocks.text: So bookmark a cam or two, learn to read the sets, and back it up with a forecast — then you'll know whether today's a board day, a swim day, or a stay-in-bed day before you leave the house. See you in the water.

North Bondi Surf Life Saving Club — Webcams
Bureau of Meteorology — Sydney forecast & tides

blocks.text: Yes — you can get onto the sand at Bondi in a wheelchair, and get right down near the water. Waverley Council runs a beach-access program at North Bondi with free beach wheelchairs you can book, a firm ramp down to the sand, an accessible shower and toilets, and a long, level promenade to enjoy the view. Here's how I'd plan a smooth, low-stress day — and where to double-check the details that shift with the seasons and the surf.

items.label: Where
items.value: Lockers on the promenade, North Bondi

items.label: Beach ramp
items.value: Northern end, near Wally Weekes Pool

blocks.text: Beach wheelchairs at Bondi

This is the part people are most surprised by. Council keeps beach wheelchairs — one sized for adults, one for children — in lockers on the promenade at the northern end of the beach. Their wide, balloon-style wheels roll over soft sand where an ordinary chair would sink, so you (or someone you love) can actually reach the water's edge rather than watch from the top.

Bookings are essential, and they're free. I'd arrange one ahead rather than turn up hoping a chair is free — there are only a couple, and they go quickly on hot days. Council's beach-wheelchair booking page is the place to start, or you can call the Bondi Pavilion on (02) 9083 8400. Booking methods change, so if in doubt, confirm the current one on Council's Access Bondi page.

The lockers double as secure storage for YOUR own wheelchair while you use the beach chair, so you don't have to leave it unattended on the promenade. And there's an outdoor accessible shower right beside them to rinse the sand and salt off before you transfer back.

blocks.title: Beach matting varies with the surf
blocks.text: Council also rolls out temporary beach-access matting — a firm pathway over the sand — on certain days, but the days and times shift with staffing and surf conditions. Rather than quote a timetable that might be out of date by your visit, check the current schedule on Council's Access Bondi page or ask when you book.
Getting there, parking and step-free access

Bondi doesn't have its own train station — the nearest is Bondi Junction, and from there frequent buses (the 333 and other Bondi Beach services) drop you at the beach. Most Sydney buses are wheelchair-accessible with ramps and priority space, but I'd still plan the exact trip on the Transport for NSW Trip Planner, which lets you filter for step-free journeys and flag any lift outages at Bondi Junction on the day.

If you're driving, there are accessible parking bays in the car parks and streets behind the beach, including up the northern end — which is where the beach wheelchairs, ramp and accessible facilities all cluster together. Spaces near the ramp are limited and go early on sunny weekends, so arriving before mid-morning saves a lot of circling.

items: Head for NORTH Bondi — ramp, beach wheelchairs, accessible shower and toilets are all at that end.
The sand ramp is at the northern end, near the North Bondi Surf Life Saving Club and Wally Weekes Pool.
The promenade runs the full length of the beach on the level — the whole view, no stairs.
Plan the bus trip on the TfNSW Trip Planner and check step-free options and lift status.

blocks.text: Accessible toilets, changing and facilities

There are accessible and ambulant toilets at the North Bondi amenities, right by the wheelchair lockers and outdoor shower — which makes that northern corner the practical base for the day. The restored Bondi Pavilion is worth knowing about too: on the ground floor it has accessible toilets plus an adult change facility with a height-adjustable table and hoist. That change room is fitted with an MLAK (Master Locksmith Access Key) lock, so if you rely on adult change facilities, bring your MLAK key or arrange access in advance.

For a genuinely accessible outing beyond the sand, the promenade north towards Ben Buckler gives you flat, sealed coastal views without the steps of the full Bondi-to-Coogee walk (which turns to stairs before long). It's my go-to for a relaxed roll — ocean on one side, coffee stops on the other.

items.q: Are beach wheelchairs at Bondi free, and how do I book one?
items.a: Yes, they're free. Waverley Council keeps adult and child beach wheelchairs in lockers on the promenade at North Bondi, and bookings are essential. Arrange one ahead through Council's booking page or by phone (Bondi Pavilion, (02) 9083 8400). Numbers are limited, so book early on warm days.

items.q: Can you actually get a wheelchair onto the sand at Bondi?
items.a: Yes. A ramp reaches the sand at the northern end near Wally Weekes Pool, and the booked beach wheelchairs have wide wheels made to roll across soft sand into the shallows. Council also lays temporary access matting on some days — check the current schedule when you book.

items.q: Where are the accessible toilets and showers?
items.a: At the North Bondi amenities, with accessible and ambulant toilets plus an outdoor shower beside the beach-wheelchair lockers. Bondi Pavilion adds accessible toilets and an MLAK-locked adult change facility with a hoist on its ground floor.

items.q: How do I get to Bondi by public transport with a wheelchair?
items.a: The nearest station is Bondi Junction; from there accessible buses such as the 333 run to the beach. Plan the exact step-free route and check for any lift outages at Bondi Junction using the Transport for NSW Trip Planner.

blocks.text: Bondi has come a long way on access, and while there's always more to do, a well-planned day here really can be for everyone. Book your beach wheelchair, aim for the northern end, and give yourself the morning — you'll get the sand between the wheels and the same big blue horizon the rest of us come for. For anything that shifts with the season, the Access Bondi page is the source I trust.
People ask me this more than you'd think, usually with one eyebrow raised: are there snakes in Bondi? I always give the same answer — only one, and his name is Blake.

If you've wandered down Blair Street lately, you might have spotted a curious creature slithering along the footpath. Don't panic — this isn't the sort of snake that sends you running. He's the friendliest serpent in Sydney: Blake the Blair Street Snake, a community art project made entirely of painted rocks.

It starts with a single boulder — Blake's cheerful head, painted minty green with pink and black patches, perched beside a hand-lettered sign that reads: "I'm Blake the Blair St Snake. Add a painted rock to see how long I can get :)"

From there, a colourful line of rocks winds down the stone wall like scales on a giant, happy reptile. Some are splashed in pastels, others flecked with stars or faces, and a few were clearly painted by very small and very enthusiastic hands. Every week Blake stretches a little further as locals and passers-by add to him.
Why I love stumbling across Blake

In a world of "Do Not Touch" signs and endless screens, here's a simple invitation to join in. No permissions, no forms — just grab a rock, grab some paint, and make your mark. I've watched joggers pause mid-stride to admire him before carrying on toward the beach, and I've never once seen someone walk past without smiling.

Each rock tells a tiny story: maybe painted on a rainy afternoon, maybe made at a weekend craft session, maybe left by a visitor who wanted to be part of something local. To me, Blake is like Bondi's community diary — only instead of words, it's written in colour. Bondi's famous for its shimmering water and perfect surf, but this quirky reptile has become just as iconic in his own way.

If you're bringing kids, paint a rock at home the night before and let it dry — then it's ready to add to Blake's tail on the day. A weatherproof outdoor paint or a coat of clear sealer helps your rock survive Bondi's sun and salt air.

items.q: Are there actually dangerous snakes at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Bondi is a busy urban beach, so you're extremely unlikely to encounter a wild snake on the sand or promenade. The only "snake" locals talk about is Blake, the painted-rock art trail on Blair Street.

items.q: Where exactly is Blake the Blair Street Snake?
items.a: Along the stone wall on Blair Street in Bondi. Look for the minty-green painted boulder with the sign inviting you to add a rock — the trail of rocks grows from there.

items.q: Can I add my own rock?
items.a: Yes — that's the whole idea. Paint a rock, bring it down to Blair Street, and add it to the end of Blake's body to help him grow a little longer.

blocks.text: So next time you're wandering Blair Street, keep an eye out. Bring a rock, add your touch, and help Blake slither a little further. Because yes — there is a snake in Bondi. Just one. And he's the kind that makes everyone smile.

The honest answer is that there is no single best time to visit Bondi Beach — it depends entirely on the Bondi you're after. If you want warm water, packed sand and long lit-up evenings, come in summer (December to February). If you'd rather have the coastal walk mostly to yourself, mild sunny days and whales offshore, I'd send you in autumn or winter. After years of watching the beach shift with the seasons, here's how I'd time your trip.
Summer (December to February): peak Bondi

This is Bondi at full volume — warm days generally in the mid-to-high 20s°C, the ocean at its most swimmable, and the sand busy from mid-morning. It's my pick if you love a crackling atmosphere: everyone's out, the promenade hums until late, and the water is genuinely inviting. The trade-off is crowds. Christmas Day and New Year draw huge numbers, and on a hot January weekend the good spots vanish early.

In summer I get down by 8–9am, claim a patch between the red-and-yellow flags, and I'm swimming before the car parks fill. By midday parking near the beach is a lost cause — take the bus, or park up the hill and walk down.

blocks.title: Always swim between the flags
blocks.text: Bondi has rip currents, and they catch strong swimmers too. Swim between the red-and-yellow flags where the lifeguards are watching, and check current conditions with Surf Life Saving before you go in.
Autumn (March to May): my quiet favourite

Autumn is Bondi's best-kept secret. The summer heat eases into mild, settled days, the ocean still holds plenty of its summer warmth well into April, and the crowds thin out noticeably. This is when I do the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk without dodging anyone, linger over a long breakfast, and actually get a table. If you want warm-enough beach weather without the peak-season scrum, this is your window.
Winter (June to August): whales, waves and space

Winter days at Bondi are cooler and the beach empties out, which is exactly why some of us love it. Swimming is bracing (the Icebergs pool crowd will tell you that's the point), but the surf often gets bigger and cleaner, and the light on a crisp morning is beautiful. The headline act is whale watching: humpbacks migrate along the NSW coast roughly May to November, and from the elevated coastal path or Ben Buckler headland you can often spot them without a boat.

Bring binoculars and walk up to the northern headland (Ben Buckler) on a clear winter morning. Look for the puff of a blow or a splash on the horizon, then wait — where there's one whale there's usually another.
Spring (September to November): the sweet spot

Spring is where the balance tips just right — warming days, water climbing back toward swimmable, and crowds that haven't yet hit summer levels. It's also the strongest stretch for events. September brings Festival of the Winds, Waverley Council's free family kite-flying day on the sand, and in October–November the coastal walk between Bondi and Tamarama becomes the open-air gallery of Sculpture by the Sea, the world's largest free outdoor sculpture exhibition.

blocks.title: Event dates move each year
blocks.text: Festival of the Winds and Sculpture by the Sea run on dates that shift annually, and sometimes change format. Before you build a trip around one, confirm the current dates on the Waverley Council and Sculpture by the Sea websites listed in my sources.
So when should you actually come?

If forced to choose, I'd point most first-timers at late spring or early autumn: you get warm, swimmable days and Bondi's easy outdoor energy, but without summer's shoulder-to-shoulder sand. Come in summer for maximum buzz and warmest water, and in winter if you want dramatic surf, whales and a beach that feels like it's yours.

items.q: What is the best month to visit Bondi Beach?
items.a: For the best balance of warm, swimmable weather and manageable crowds, I'd pick March (early autumn) or late October–November (spring). January is warmest and liveliest but by far the busiest, while June–August is quiet and best for whales and surf rather than swimming.

items.q: When is Bondi Beach least crowded?
items.a: Winter (June to August) is the quietest, followed by autumn weekdays. If you want space on the sand and the coastal walk without a warm-weather trade-off you can't accept, autumn is the sweet spot.

items.q: Can you swim at Bondi in winter?
items.a: Yes — plenty of locals do, and the beach is patrolled. The water is cold, so most winter swimmers keep it short or use the Icebergs ocean pool. Always swim between the flags and check conditions with Surf Life Saving first.

items.q: When can you see whales from Bondi?
items.a: Humpback whales migrate along the NSW coast roughly from May to November, with strong sightings through the winter months. You can often see them from the coastal walk or Ben Buckler headland — no boat required, just clear conditions and a bit of patience.

items.q: What are the big events at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Spring is the busiest for events: Festival of the Winds (a free kite-flying day) in September, and Sculpture by the Sea along the Bondi-to-Tamarama coastal walk in October–November. Dates change each year, so check the official sites before planning around them.

blocks.text: If you only have one day at Bondi, spend the morning swimming between the flags at the south end, walk the cliff path toward Tamarama before lunch, and save sunset for the grassy hill above the Icebergs pool — that single loop hits the famous stuff and the quiet corners both. I've wandered this coast for years, so here's my honest, local-first guide: the must-see spots that earn the hype, the hidden gems most visitors walk straight past, and the practical bits that make the day.

items.label: Where
items.value: Bondi Beach, eastern suburbs of Sydney, NSW

items.label: Getting here
items.value: Train to Bondi Junction, then the 333/380 bus

items.label: Patrols
items.value: Lifeguards year-round; swim between the red-and-yellow flags

items.label: Best for
items.value: Swimming, the coastal walk, cafés and people-watching

blocks.text: The must-see spots

Start where Bondi shows off. The southern end, near the Bondi Icebergs, is where the postcard photos happen — the ocean pool sits right on the rocks and the waves wash straight into it at high tide. Icebergs is a working swimming club with a public pool anyone can swim in, but session times and entry change with the seasons, so check the Icebergs website before you build your morning around it.

From there, the Bondi to Coogee Coastal Walk is the one thing I'd never let a first-timer skip. It runs roughly 6 km along the cliff tops, linking Bondi to Tamarama, Bronte, Clovelly and Coogee, with sea views the whole way. You don't have to do all of it — even the first stretch to Bronte is worth it, with ocean pools and cafés to stop at. Wear proper shoes, bring water, and go early in summer.

Back at the beach, the Bondi Pavilion is the grand old building on the promenade — a community and cultural hub with event spaces since its restoration. Wander the promenade for the famous graffiti wall, grab a coffee, and just watch Bondi be Bondi.
Hidden gems the crowds miss

Most visitors cluster in the middle of the beach and never move; the locals I know drift to the ends. North Bondi is calmer, with the free ocean pools (the "kiddie pools") tucked into the rocks — lovely for families and gentler swimming when the surf's up, and my pick for a quiet coffee away from the Campbell Parade bustle.
The Sunday Bondi Markets at Bondi Beach Public School — vintage, jewellery, art and food, and a genuine slice of the local creative scene. Check the Bondi Markets site for current days and hours.
The laneways and walls behind Campbell Parade, where Bondi's ever-changing street art lives — no two visits look the same.
Hall Street and the streets just back from the sand, where the café and food scene is far better value than the beachfront strip.
Ben Buckler, the rocky headland at the far north end, for wide clifftop views and a whale-watching chance in the winter migration months.
Come on a weekday if you can. Bondi on a summer Saturday is a different animal — parking is brutal and the sand fills fast. Midweek mornings you get the same beach with half the people.
Getting here and staying safe

There's no train to the sand itself. Take a train to Bondi Junction, then a short bus (the 333 or 380) down to Campbell Parade — check Transport for NSW for live timetables and to tap on with an Opal or contactless card. Parking near the beach is limited and metered, so I only drive here off-peak.

blocks.title: Swim between the flags
blocks.text: Bondi has real rip currents. Always swim between the red-and-yellow flags, where lifeguards are watching. If you're caught in a rip, don't fight it — stay calm, raise an arm for help, and float or swim parallel to the beach until you're free.

Bondi is patrolled by professional lifeguards year-round, backed by volunteer surf lifesavers in the busy months, but conditions change quickly — if in doubt, ask a lifeguard where it's safest to swim that day.

items.q: What are the absolute must-sees at Bondi Beach?
items.a: The Bondi Icebergs ocean pool at the south end, the Bondi to Coogee Coastal Walk, the Bondi Pavilion and promenade, and a swim between the flags on the main beach. If you add one hidden gem, make it quieter North Bondi.

items.q: How do I get to Bondi Beach from the Sydney CBD?
items.a: Take a train to Bondi Junction, then the 333 or 380 bus down to Bondi Beach. Use an Opal card or contactless payment and check Transport for NSW for current timetables. There's no train that goes all the way to the sand.

items.q: How long is the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk?
items.a: It's roughly 6 km one way along the cliff tops, typically taking a couple of hours at a relaxed pace with stops. You can do just the first section to Tamarama and Bronte if you're short on time.

items.q: Is Bondi Beach safe for swimming?
items.a: Yes, when you swim between the red-and-yellow flags where lifeguards patrol. Bondi is patrolled year-round, but it does have rip currents, so avoid unpatrolled areas and always check conditions before you go in.

items.q: When is the best time to visit Bondi to avoid crowds?
items.a: Weekday mornings, especially outside the peak summer weekends. You get the same beach and cafés with far fewer people and much easier parking.

blocks.text: That's my Bondi — famous for a reason, but far richer once you step past the middle of the beach. Do the walk, find the quiet ends, eat a street back from the sand, and respect the ocean, and you'll leave with the real version, not just the postcard.

sources.label: Sydney.com — Bondi to Coogee Coastal Walk

blocks.text: Ask me where to drink in Bondi and I'll answer before you finish: start beachfront for a sundowner, then wander inland as the night warms up. After years living just back from the sand, these are the ten bars I actually send friends to — ocean-view balconies, a proper microbrewery, cosy locals' corners and one or two that run late.

items.label: Best for views
items.value: Icebergs, North Bondi RSL, Hotel Ravesis

items.label: Getting here
items.value: Bus to Bondi Beach, or the 333 from the city

blocks.text: My beachfront big-hitters
1. Hotel Ravesis

You can't miss the flamingo-pink corner where Hall Street meets Campbell Parade. Ravesis is my pick for the whole spectrum in one building — a schooner or a rosé on the terrace early, then upstairs as the DJs get going and it tips into the small hours. Grab a front-terrace spot for the wide view.
2. Icebergs (the Bondi Bar balcony)

For the postcard, nothing beats the balcony bar at Icebergs, above the famous ocean pool at the south end. It's dress-up-a-little and priced for the view, but a negroni at golden hour is a genuinely Sydney moment. It books out — reserve ahead through the Icebergs site.
3. North Bondi RSL

My tip for the best-value view in Bondi: the RSL at the north end. Sign in as a guest, head to the wrap-around glass balcony and you get the same knockout beach outlook for far less. Check the North Bondi RSL site for sign-in and hours first.

Bondi faces east, so the sun sets behind you over the rooftops, not the sea. The magic is the glow on the water and the headlands — have a drink in hand about half an hour before sunset and watch the beach turn gold.
Craft beer, cocktails and cosy corners
4. Curly Lewis Brewing Co.

Bondi's own microbrewery, just back from Campbell Parade, brews everything on-site, the tanks right behind the bar. I come for a tasting paddle before committing to a pint, usually landing on whatever hazy they've got pouring. Communal tables and an easy beer-garden feel.
5. The Anchor

A small, buzzy agave-and-cocktail spot at the south end of Campbell Parade that locals took to fast. It's tight and loud in the best way, with a margarita list that rewards a bit of adventurousness — great for kicking off a night.
6. Beach Road Hotel

A couple of streets back on Beach Road, this big multi-level pub is the reliable all-rounder — cold schooners, pub classics, live sport, and DJs and bands upstairs on weekends. It's where a lot of Bondi nights quietly end up.
The rest of my ten
These four round out the list — a different mood for each night.

items: The Bucket List — the sprawling open-air bar in the Bondi Pavilion, feet-in-the-sand spritzes and a great afternoon-session spot in summer.
Neighbourhood (Curlewis Street) — a lively little local back from the sand, good for a natural wine with the after-beach crowd.
The Shop & Wine Bar (Curlewis Street) — café by day, snug wine bar by night; my pick for a quiet drink and a cheese plate.
The Stuffed Beaver (Bondi Road) — an unpretentious, good-fun bar for burgers, mezcal and a night that doesn't take itself too seriously.

blocks.title: Summer weekends fill fast
blocks.text: From December through February the beachfront venues can hit capacity by mid-afternoon on a hot day. If a table matters — especially at Icebergs or for a big group — book ahead through the venue's own site and confirm current hours.
How I'd string them together

stops.title: North Bondi RSL
stops.detail: Best-value beach view while the light is still high.

stops.title: The Bucket List / Pavilion
stops.detail: Down to the sand for a spritz as the beach turns gold.

stops.title: Curly Lewis or The Anchor
stops.detail: Head inland — a pint or a cocktail to shift gears.

stops.title: Hotel Ravesis or Beach Road
stops.detail: Finish where the DJs are for a late one.

items.q: Which Bondi bar has the best beach view?
items.a: The balcony bar at Icebergs, above the ocean pool, wins for the postcard shot. For the same outlook at a much lower price, head to North Bondi RSL's upstairs balcony. Ravesis' front terrace pairs the view with a livelier crowd.

items.q: Where can I drink late in Bondi?
items.a: Hotel Ravesis and the Beach Road Hotel reliably keep going into the night on weekends, with DJs upstairs. Closing times vary by season, so check each venue's own site for current hours.

items.q: Is there craft beer brewed in Bondi?
items.a: Yes — Curly Lewis Brewing Co. is Bondi's own microbrewery, brewing on-site just back from Campbell Parade. A tasting paddle is the best way in.

items.q: How do I get to Bondi Beach for a night out?
items.a: The easiest route from the city is the 333 or 380 bus, or the train to Bondi Junction and a beach-bound bus. Check Transport for NSW for timetables and plan your way home before the last service.

items.q: Do I need to book ahead?
items.a: For most pubs and casual bars you can just turn up. For Icebergs, or larger groups on summer weekends, book directly through the venue's site.

blocks.text: That's my ten — enough range for any kind of Bondi night, from a quiet wine after the beach to a full sunset-to-late crawl. Hours and prices move with the seasons, so treat this as the shortlist and confirm details on each venue's own site.

Bondi's dining goes well beyond fish and chips on the sand. There's cliff-top Italian, produce-driven fine dining that's been going since the early '90s, beachfront seafood and a new wave of share-plate spots on Hall Street. Below is the shortlist I'd steer a visitor towards — grouped by the kind of night you're after, with what each place is known for and who it suits. I write as a local curator rather than claiming to have dined at each one this month, so book ahead for the big ones and check current details before you go.

blocks.title: A living guide
blocks.text: Restaurants change — menus, chefs and hours shift, and the best tables book out. I last reviewed this in August 2026; confirm opening days and book ahead on the venue's own channels before a special trip.
Best for a special occasion
Icebergs Dining Room and Bar

Icebergs is the Bondi bucket-list dinner — a glamorous, glass-walled Italian dining room on the southern cliff, looking straight down over the Icebergs pool and the ocean. Overseen by hospitality figure Maurice Terzini, it's polished coastal Italian with one of the best views of any restaurant in Sydney. Best for: a celebration, a long lunch, or impressing visitors — book well ahead, and it's at the premium end. You can pair it with a look at the [Icebergs pool and where to swim](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach) below.
Sean's (formerly Sean's Panorama)

A genuine Bondi institution: chef Sean Moran has run this small, produce-led restaurant on Campbell Parade since 1993 (now simply "Sean's"). The short, hand-written menu changes with what's good, much of it from the chef's own farm. It's understated and beloved rather than flashy. Best for: a considered, ingredient-first dinner or weekend lunch — a small room, so booking is wise.
Beachfront seafood
North Bondi Fish

About as beachfront as dining gets — right on Ramsgate Avenue at the north end, with the sand almost at the door. The menu is easy-going seafood: sashimi, calamari, tacos, and fish and chips, plus cocktails. Best for: a relaxed lunch or early dinner with a view, and a solid choice with kids in tow.
Fish Shop

A casual, nautical-themed seafood spot a short walk back from the beach — the more laid-back, everyday alternative to a big seafood night out. Best for: an unfussy seafood feed without a special-occasion price tag.
Italian & share plates
Totti's Bondi

Totti's, behind The Royal on Bondi Road, is the crowd-pleasing Italian everyone seems to end up at — famous for its pillowy wood-fired bread and generous, family-style plates in a sunny, convivial room. Best for: a group, a birthday, or a long boozy lunch — it's popular, so book ahead.
Newer and something different
LULU

One of the newer names worth knowing, LULU is a funky Pan-Asian bar and kitchen on Hall Street built around share plates — think Vietnamese-style prawn banh mi, Korean fried chicken and fresh sashimi, with drinks to match. Best for: a livelier, share-and-graze dinner away from the beachfront. (As a newer venue, check its days and hours before you rely on it.)
What's changed recently

A couple of things to note for 2026. Hall Street has picked up newer, more casual share-plate venues like LULU, which are worth a look alongside the classics. Sean's Panorama now trades simply as "Sean's" — same chef, same Campbell Parade address, so don't be thrown by the shorter name. And the refurbished Bondi Pavilion has reopened on the beachfront with its food and drink line-up reshuffled since the works, so check who's trading there now rather than trusting older guides.
What to know before you go

items: Book ahead for the big ones: Icebergs, Totti's and Sean's fill up, especially for weekend lunch and warm evenings.
Timing: sunset tables with a view (Icebergs, North Bondi Fish) are the most sought-after — reserve early or aim for lunch.
Price: Icebergs and Sean's sit at the premium end; North Bondi Fish, Fish Shop and LULU are more mid-range.
Getting there: it's an easy night out on foot or by bus — see [getting to Bondi](/getting-to-bondi) if you're coming from the city.
Make a day of it: line up a swim or the coastal walk first — see [things to do in Bondi](/things-to-do-in-bondi).

items.a: For a special-occasion dinner with a view, Icebergs Dining Room and Bar is the classic pick. For understated, produce-driven cooking, Sean's on Campbell Parade has been a favourite since 1993.

items.a: North Bondi Fish is the most beachfront option, on Ramsgate Avenue at the north end. Icebergs sits above the pool on the southern cliff with the best elevated view.

blocks.text: Here's the honest answer to "where do I park at Bondi Beach?" — yes, there is free, unrestricted parking, but it's in the residential streets north of Blair Street, a 5–7 minute walk from the sand, and on a sunny weekend you need to be in it before about 9am. Everything closer than that is paid or time-limited. I've circled these blocks more times than I'd like to admit, so below is every option — free streets, the beachfront car park, the meters, accessible bays and the park-and-ride — with straight talk on what each one is actually good for.
The free parking that actually exists

My go-to on a busy day is the residential grid north of Blair Street — the streets heading away from the water and up the hill: Warners Avenue, Brassie Street, Niblick Street, Patterson Street, Oakley Road, O'Donnell Street, the top of Gould Street, Knowles Avenue, Frederick Street, Wairoa Avenue and Mitchell Street. Those streets are genuinely free and unrestricted around the clock: no meters, no time limits. A trick I use to get my bearings: drop "74 Blair Street" into Google Maps and it drops you right at the edge of the zone — then park in the streets just north of there. (Blair Street itself isn't part of the free area — start one block north of it.) The trade-off is the walk (roughly 5–7 minutes down to the sand) and the timing. On weekdays the bays hold until residents come home in the late afternoon; on a sunny weekend they fill from mid-morning, which is exactly why arriving early matters so much.

The one thing that catches people out: the closer you get to the beach, the more the free bays give way to timed and permit-only zones. Waverley Council runs Resident Parking Schemes across Bondi, so a free-looking bay near the water can quietly be permit-only. My rule is simple — keep heading north until the restriction signs drop off, then park. The streets up the hill behind the southern end are my quiet secret too: everyone aims for the middle of the beach, so those blocks often have room when the north end is chaos.

Read the closest sign every single time, even if the car in front of you is parked there. Time limits, permit zones and no-stopping lines change street by street in Bondi, and inspectors patrol hard on weekends. Blocking a driveway is one of the costliest tickets you can collect — never worth it for a five-minute dash.
Paid parking, closest to furthest
When I've got beach gear, kids, or it's just too hot to walk, I pay. Roughly in order of how close they sit to the sand:

items: Queen Elizabeth Drive car park — Waverley Council's own metered car park running right behind the beach. It's the closest and most convenient, and the first to fill on a nice day, so treat it as an early-morning play.

Campbell Parade meters — the paid on-street bays opposite the beach. Handy for a quick visit, but time-limited and the priciest per hour, so they suit a coffee-and-a-swim rather than a full beach day.
The Notts Avenue / Icebergs (south) end — metered street parking down toward the pool. Limited and sought-after, but a lovely spot to land if you time it right.
Side streets a block or two back — often overlooked once the beachfront meters are full; check the posted rates and time limit at the sign before you leave the car.

blocks.text: Waverley Council's beach meters are pay-by-plate, so there's no paper ticket — you enter your number plate at the machine or, far easier, pay from your phone through the PayStay app (the meters also accept the NSW Park'nPay app). The beach meters operate well into the evening, especially in summer, so an evening visit is rarely free at the beachfront — read the hours on the sign. On rates: I'm not going to bake a dollar figure into this page, because Waverley reviews meter prices and charges more for beach-adjacent bays in summer than for streets further back. Check the current rate on Waverley Council's parking page and budget for a daily total before you go.

blocks.title: Staying all day, often?
blocks.text: A Waverley Council beach parking permit lets you park for extended periods in the metered beachfront bays around Queen Elizabeth Drive without feeding the meter. Residents and ratepayers pay a lower rate, and eligibility and fees are set by the council — if you're a Bondi regular it can pay for itself, so check the current terms on the council's beach parking permit page.
Accessible parking and the busy-day plan

There are designated accessible parking bays around the beachfront, including near Queen Elizabeth Drive and the Bondi Pavilion, and a valid Mobility Parking Scheme permit gives concessions on time limits in metered and timed bays. Because the exact bay locations and any current works can change, I'd confirm on Waverley Council's parking page or with the Pavilion before relying on a specific spot.

And if it's a perfect summer Saturday? Don't fight it. Drive to Bondi Junction, park there, and jump on the 333 or another Bondi Beach bus down to the sand — it's a short ride and on a hot weekend it's genuinely faster than doing laps for a beachfront bay. Tap on with an Opal card or contactless, and check Transport for NSW for live timetables.

items.q: Is there free parking at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes — the residential streets north of Blair Street, heading away from the water, have free, unrestricted bays about a 5–7 minute walk from the sand. Watch for permit-only and timed zones closer to the beach, and get in before about 9am on sunny weekends.

items.q: What's the closest car park to Bondi Beach?
items.a: Waverley Council's Queen Elizabeth Drive car park, the large metered car park right behind the beach. It's the first to fill on a nice day, so arrive early or have a backup ready.

items.q: How much does it cost to park at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Waverley Council sets the meter rates and charges more for beach-adjacent bays in summer than for streets set further back. Rates change, so check the council's parking page for the current figure and daily budget rather than trusting a fixed number.

items.q: How do I pay the parking meters at Bondi?
items.a: The beachfront meters are pay-by-plate — enter your number plate at the machine, or pay from your phone using the PayStay or NSW Park'nPay app. There's no paper ticket to display.

items.q: When should I arrive to actually find a spot?
items.a: Before about 9am or after about 4pm on busy weekends and holidays. The 9am–3pm window is the hardest; if you're arriving then, plan on a paid meter, the South Bondi streets, or the Bondi Junction park-and-ride.

blocks.text: Parking at Bondi rewards planning far more than luck. Come early, know your free streets north of Blair, keep a paid meter and the Bondi Junction bus as backups, and always read the sign. Do that and you'll spend the day in the water — not behind the wheel.

I've talked friends and visitors through this reservation more times than I can count, so here's exactly how I'd go about it, without the midnight stress.

Totti's sits inside The Royal Bondi on Bondi Road, a short stroll up from the sand, and it has become one of those Sydney rooms everyone wants a piece of — sun-warmed, loud in the best way, and built around that famous woodfired bread. That popularity is exactly why a little planning goes a long way.

blocks.text: Booking online: the reliable way in

Reservations run through Merivale's own booking system on the Totti's venue page — that's the one platform I'd point anyone to. Tables are released a set window ahead of time, so the trick is simply to be ready when your date first becomes available rather than trying weeks later once the prime slots are gone. Because that release window can change, I'd open the booking calendar, scroll to the furthest bookable date, and work backwards from there rather than trusting a number you read on a blog.

items: Jump on the booking page the day your date opens — lunch and prime dinner slots go fast.
Have your details (name, phone, card if requested) ready so you're not fumbling as tables vanish.
Set a phone reminder for the morning the window opens, then book first, deliberate later — you can always adjust.

blocks.text: Keep a browser tab on the Totti's booking page even after you've missed out for your ideal night. Totti's is a largely outdoor venue, so when Bondi's weather turns, last-minute cancellations reappear online — I've grabbed a Saturday table on the Thursday before simply by refreshing at the right moment.
Be flexible — it's your biggest advantage

If you can bend on timing, the whole thing gets easier. An earlier lunch or a later dinner sitting is far more likely to have space than the 7pm-on-a-Saturday sweet spot everyone else is chasing. Midweek is calmer than the weekend, and smaller groups of two or three slot in where a table of eight simply won't. None of this is a secret — it's just how a busy room breathes.

blocks.title: Larger groups and special occasions
blocks.text: Big tables, birthdays and set-menu events work differently from a regular booking, and Totti's has a private dining option too. For anything beyond a standard table, contact the venue directly on +61 2 9114 7371 or use the enquiry form on Totti's private dining page rather than the standard online booking.
No booking? You still have options

Don't write off a spontaneous visit. Same-day walk-ins are welcome at Totti's, with a limited number of tables held back each day — your odds are best if you turn up early rather than at peak, keep the group small, and are happy to perch wherever they can seat you. A weekday afternoon is your friend here. And if it's genuinely last-minute, a quick phone call the morning of can turn up a cancellation the website hasn't caught up with yet.
Book if you can, walk in if you can't, and either way — order the bread.

One last piece of honesty: opening hours, menus and the exact booking window all shift from season to season, so before you build a whole day around it, check the current details on the official Totti's page. Get the reservation sorted, arrive a touch early to soak up the courtyard buzz, and the hard part's done.

items.a: Through Merivale's online booking system on the Totti's venue page (merivale.com/venues/tottis). You can also phone the venue on +61 2 9114 7371. Booking online is the most reliable route for a standard table.

items.a: Keep watching the online booking page — Totti's is largely outdoor, so cancellations reappear when the weather turns. You can also call the venue on the day to ask about no-shows and last-minute openings.

items.a: Inside The Royal Bondi at 283 Bondi Road, Bondi, a short walk up from the beach. Check the official Merivale page for current opening hours before you go, as they change seasonally.

blocks.text: Bondi packs one of Sydney's best café scenes into a few walkable streets behind the beach — beachfront brunch rooms, serious coffee windows, and a run of newer openings worth knowing about in 2026. Below is the shortlist I'd hand a visitor: what each place is known for, roughly where it is, and who it suits. I write these as a local curator rather than claiming to have eaten at every one this week, so treat the details as a well-researched starting point and check current hours before a special trip.

blocks.title: A living guide
blocks.text: Bondi's café scene moves fast — hours, menus and even owners change. I last reviewed this in August 2026; confirm anything time-sensitive on the venue's own channels before you go.
Best beachfront cafés for brunch
Speedos Café — North Bondi

Speedos sits up at the quieter North Bondi end (Ramsgate Avenue) with some of the best ocean views of any café on the beach. It's the classic post-swim spot — health-leaning brunch, bowls, pancakes and juices, with window benches looking straight out to the water. Best for: a relaxed, view-first breakfast at the north end.
Chapter One — Campbell Parade

Right on Campbell Parade opposite the sand, Chapter One is a café-meets-wine-bar that's been going since 2012, pouring Allpress coffee alongside an all-day menu. It's an easy, central choice if you want to be directly across from the beach. Best for: an all-rounder in the middle of the action.
bills — Hall Street

The Sydney institution founded by Bill Granger has been on Hall Street (number 79) since 2014, and it's still open and busy. Come for the dishes that made it famous — ricotta hotcakes and sweetcorn fritters — in a light, airy room. Best for: a benchmark Bondi brunch and a bit of Sydney food history.
Best for specialty coffee
Harry's Bondi — Wairoa Avenue

Harry's has been caffeinating Bondi since 1997 and is my pick if coffee is the point. It grew from a hole-in-the-wall into a full café, with batch brew, espresso and cold drip plus a following for its matcha and specialty lattes. Best for: coffee-first locals and a quick, quality cup.
Sonoma — bakery coffee

Sonoma is the well-known Sydney sourdough bakery with a Bondi outpost — a reliable stop for a proper coffee and a pastry or bakery-driven breakfast without the full brunch sit-down. Best for: a quick, high-quality grab-and-go.
Gertrude & Alice — Hall Street

Genuinely one of a kind: a second-hand bookshop and café on Hall Street where you can settle in with Campos coffee, a Middle Eastern-leaning breakfast and a stack of books. It's the antidote to Bondi's see-and-be-seen rooms. Best for: a slow, quiet morning and something different.
Strong all-rounders just back from the sand
Blackwood — Glenayr Avenue

An Eastern Suburbs brunch staple a couple of streets back, Blackwood is known for a seasonal menu that blends Mediterranean and Asian influences — ricotta pancakes, chilli scrambled eggs — with carefully made coffee. Best for: a considered brunch away from the beachfront crush.
Porch and Parlour — North Bondi

A long-running North Bondi favourite (Ramsgate Avenue) built around local produce, with its well-known pea pancakes and a reliably buzzy weekend. It's also one of the better-known dog-friendly spots. Best for: a neighbourhood brunch with the dog in tow.
Newer and more unusual spots
Cafe Bondi — North Bondi (new)

One of the more recent openings, Cafe Bondi is on Campbell Parade at the North Bondi end and opens early for coffee, sunshine and an easy all-day menu. Best for: an early start at the quieter north end. (As a newer venue, double-check its days and hours before you rely on it.)
Up South — Bondi Road

Further up Bondi Road, Up South made its name on playful matcha creations and a rotating treats cabinet — the spot for a strawberry or pistachio matcha and a photo. Best for: matcha fans and a sweet mid-morning stop.
Lox, Stock & Barrel — bagels & deli
A Bondi take on a Jewish deli, known for artisan bagels and generous, deli-influenced brunch plates. Best for: a bagel-led breakfast or an easy weekday lunch.
Makaveli & Pocket — café by day, bar by night

From the same team, Makaveli (Glenayr Avenue) and Pocket (Campbell Parade) both work the café-to-cocktail-bar angle — pastries, loaded sourdough and coffee in the morning, share plates and drinks later. Best for: a laid-back start that can roll into the afternoon.
What's changed recently

Two things worth flagging for 2026. First, there's genuine new blood at the north end — Cafe Bondi being the clearest recent opening. Second, the former Hall Street all-day spot Bondi Hall has closed, so ignore older lists that still feature it. The refurbished Bondi Pavilion has also reopened with food and drink operators on the beachfront; those line-ups have shifted since the works, so check who's trading there now rather than trusting an older guide.
What to know before you go

items: Timing: arrive close to opening or after about 2pm to dodge the worst queues; weekend mornings are the busiest.
Booking: most Bondi cafés are walk-in, though a few take reservations for larger groups — check ahead if there are more than four of you.
Dogs: several are dog-friendly, with Porch and Parlour the best-known; outdoor tables are your friend.
Reusables: bring a keep-cup — some cafés knock a little off for it.
Make a morning of it: pair a café with the Saturday [Bondi Farmers Market](/whats-on/markets), or a swim first — see [where to swim at Bondi](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach).

blocks.text: Every year I get asked the same thing the moment the mornings turn crisp: when is whale season at Bondi? The short answer is roughly May to November — and the best part is you don't need a boat. Some of the finest whale watching in Sydney happens for free, right from the headlands either side of the beach. This is my local guide to when the humpbacks pass, where I stand to watch them, and how to give yourself the best chance of a breach.
When whales pass Bondi

Sydney's whale-watching season runs from around mid-May to early November as tens of thousands of humpbacks migrate along the NSW coast. It splits into two acts. On the northbound leg — roughly May to July — the whales head to warmer breeding waters and travel with real purpose, so June and July are wonderful for sheer numbers. On the southbound return — around September to November — mothers bring their new calves back toward Antarctic feeding grounds, often hugging the coastline and moving slower, which for my money makes the most tender sightings of the year.

I always aim for the first couple of hours after sunrise on a clear, calm day. The light is behind you, the sea is glassier so spouts and breaches stand out, and the crowds haven't arrived. A gentle offshore wind and low swell make an enormous difference.
The best land-based spots near Bondi
You genuinely don't need to pay for a cruise to see whales here. These are the free vantage points I return to, all within a short walk of the beach:

items: Ben Buckler Point (North Bondi) — Bondi's most easterly headland and my first choice. It sits high above the water at the end of Ramsgate Avenue, with an open outlook over the Pacific where locals gather with binoculars all season.
Mackenzies Point — the small headland between Bondi and Tamarama, with a wide southern view that's ideal for scanning.
Waverley Cemetery clifftop — a dramatic, unobstructed stretch of the coastal walk perched right above the ocean.
The Bondi to Bronte (and on to Coogee) coastal walk — not one spot but a whole string of them; I walk slowly and stop wherever I see others looking out to sea.

blocks.title: Mind the edge
blocks.text: These clifftops are stunning but the rock is uneven and the drops are real. Stay behind fences and well back from wet or crumbling edges, keep an eye on children, and never turn your back on the ocean to line up a photo. No whale is worth a slip.
Cruises from nearby Sydney

No whale-watching cruises leave from Bondi Beach itself — the boats depart from Sydney Harbour, mostly Circular Quay and Darling Harbour, and head out through the Heads to the migration route. If you'd rather get close, a half-day tour is a lovely way to do it. For current departure times, durations and prices, which change every season, check the operators' own websites — Destination NSW's Sydney.com whale-watching page is a good starting point.
How to actually spot one
The trick is learning what to look for. Whales usually give themselves away before you see the animal itself:
A blow — a puff of white mist hanging above the water is often the very first sign.
A breach — the full-body leap and enormous splash that everyone hopes for.
A tail or pectoral fin slapping the surface, and dark backs rolling as they travel.

Scan the horizon slowly and let your eyes settle rather than darting about; binoculars help enormously. Give it time — sightings come in waves, and the people who see the most are the ones who stayed longest. If the sea is rough and grey, spotting is hard, so I'll happily come back another morning rather than strain for nothing.

items.q: When is the best time for whale watching at Bondi?
items.a: The season runs roughly May to November. June and July bring the biggest northbound numbers, while September to November is best for mothers with calves travelling close to shore. Early morning on a calm, clear day is ideal.

items.q: Can you see whales from Bondi Beach for free?
items.a: Yes — that's the beauty of it. Head to a headland like Ben Buckler Point at North Bondi, Mackenzies Point, or anywhere along the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk. No ticket required, just bring binoculars and a bit of patience.

items.q: What kind of whales pass Bondi?
items.a: The vast majority are humpback whales, with occasional southern right whales, and tens of thousands migrate along the NSW coast each season.

items.q: Do whale-watching cruises leave from Bondi?
items.a: No cruises depart from Bondi Beach itself. Boats leave from Sydney Harbour — mainly Circular Quay and Darling Harbour — and head out through the Heads. Check the operator's website for current times and prices.

items.q: What should I bring for land-based whale watching?
items.a: Binoculars, warm layers and a windproof jacket (headlands are exposed and cool in winter), sun protection, and patience. A thermos never hurts.

blocks.text: There's something I never tire of: standing on Ben Buckler with the wind off the water, waiting — and then that first white blow appears and the whole headland goes quiet. Pick a calm morning between May and November, wrap up warm, and give yourself an hour. Bondi will do the rest.
