blocks.text: Yes — kids can absolutely swim at Bondi Icebergs, and it's one of my favourite spots to bring young families in Bondi. Alongside the famous 50-metre ocean pool you've seen on a thousand postcards, there's a separate, shallower children's pool, and lifeguards are on duty during opening hours. It's a public pool, not a members-only club, so you and the little ones can buy a day pass and jump straight in.

That said, this is real ocean swimming, not a heated leisure centre. The water is pumped straight in from the surf, so it's bracingly cold in winter and lively when a big swell is running. Below I'll walk you through the kids' pool, safety, costs and the practical tips I share with visiting families.
The children's pool: a gentler place to start

The reason I happily recommend Icebergs for families is the separate kids' pool that sits beside the main lap pool. It's smaller and shallower, which keeps little swimmers out of the deep water and away from the serious lap-swimmers ploughing up and down the 50-metre pool. For a first taste of ocean swimming it's ideal — the salty, sun-on-the-water Bondi experience without the deep end, literally.

Because both pools are fed by the sea, the kids' pool is unheated and its temperature shifts with the ocean through the year. On a warm summer morning it's glorious; in winter it's genuinely chilly, so I always pack extra layers for afterwards.

blocks.title: Watch the swell and the wall
blocks.text: On big-surf days waves can wash right over the pool's ocean edge, and the pool sits below the promenade with steps down. Keep young kids close, hold hands on wet edges, and if the sea looks wild, the flagged lifeguard-patrolled area on Bondi Beach itself may be the safer call.
Safety and supervision

Lifeguards are on duty at the pool during opening hours, which is a big part of why I trust it with families. But lifeguards are a backstop, not a babysitter — the water is real ocean, cold enough to take a small body's breath away, so active adult supervision is the golden rule.

items: Stay within arm's reach of young or non-swimming children the whole time.
Ease kids in slowly — cold saltwater is a shock after a warm beach.
Mind the slippery pool edges and the steps down from the promenade.
Check the day's conditions before you commit little ones to the water.

blocks.text: Go early on a summer weekday if you can. The pool is calmest, the deck is quiet, and you'll have space to help a nervous swimmer find their feet before the crowds and the lap-swimming regulars arrive.
Costs, hours and what to bring

Entry is by day pass and it's an affordable outing for a family. Prices and hours change with the season, so treat everything below as a rough guide and confirm the current figures on the official Icebergs pool page before you go.

items.label: Entry
items.value: Day passes for adults, children and families; multi-visit passes too. Check current rates on the official pool page

items.label: Hours
items.value: Early morning to evening most days — confirm the day's hours on the official page

items.label: Cleaning day
items.value: Closed one weekday each week (traditionally Thursday); double-check before you go

items.label: Water
items.value: Unheated, ocean-fed saltwater that tracks the sea temperature

blocks.text: The one that catches people out is the weekly cleaning closure — I've watched families arrive with towels and toddlers only to find the gates shut, so check the pool page the day before. Towel and locker hire are usually available for a small charge if you travel light.

For a family swim I'd pack: warm layers and a spare towel each (that ocean chill lingers), rashies and sunscreen for the exposed deck, water and snacks, and thongs for the walk down. The deck offers little shade and the glare off the water is fierce.
Frequently asked questions

items.q: Can toddlers and young children swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: Yes. There's a separate, shallower children's pool beside the main lap pool that suits young and less-confident swimmers, but it's unheated ocean water, so keep toddlers within arm's reach and supervise them closely at all times.

items.q: Is Bondi Icebergs pool heated?
items.a: No. Both the main pool and the kids' pool are filled with seawater straight from the ocean, so the temperature changes with the sea — pleasant in summer and very cold in winter. Pack warm layers for afterwards.

items.q: How much does it cost for a family to swim?
items.a: Entry is by day pass, with separate adult, child and family rates and cheaper multi-visit passes available. Prices change from time to time, so check the official Icebergs pool page for current rates before you visit.

items.q: When is the pool closed?
items.a: The pool closes one weekday each week for cleaning (traditionally Thursday), and it can also close during rough surf or maintenance, so always check the day's pool conditions before setting out.

items.q: Are there lifeguards on duty?
items.a: Yes — lifeguards are on duty during opening hours. They're there for emergencies, but parents and carers remain responsible for actively supervising their own children in and around the water.

blocks.text: Bottom line: Icebergs is a wonderful introduction to ocean swimming for kids, as long as you go in clear-eyed about cold water and changing conditions. Pick a calm summer morning, bring the layers, keep the little ones close, and you'll have one of those salty Bondi mornings the whole family remembers.

blocks.text: Yes — anyone can swim at the Bondi Icebergs pool. It's a public ocean pool open seven days a week, and you don't need to be a club member to jump in. It's the one you've seen a thousand times on Instagram: two turquoise pools carved into the rocks at the southern end of Bondi, waves crashing straight over the edge. I swim here often, so here are the questions I get asked most, answered honestly — and where a price or time is the sort of thing that changes, I'll point you at the official page rather than risk something stale.
Getting in: hours and fees

The pool opens early — dawn starts most days — and runs into the early evening, seven days a week. It's typically closed on Thursdays for cleaning, though in summer, when the tides cooperate, it often stays open. Opening and closing times shift with the seasons, races and the surf, so rather than quote a clock time that might be stale, I check the official Pool Conditions page at icebergs.com.au the morning I'm heading down.

Entry is casual — no booking, just pay at the kiosk and walk down to the water. There are single passes for adults, children and families, and multi-visit passes that bring the per-swim cost down for regulars. For the current dollar figures, check the Pool Conditions page — prices are exactly the kind of thing I won't quote from memory.

blocks.title: The tide calls the shots
blocks.text: Entry can be affected by tides, swimming races and event days, so the pool occasionally closes to public swimmers at short notice. If you've travelled across town for it, a quick look at the official pool status saves a wasted trip.
What it's actually like to swim here

Two pools sit side by side: a 50-metre lap pool and a smaller, shallower one that's gentler for little kids. The water is ocean-fed and unheated, so the temperature tracks the sea — glorious in late summer, bracing in the best way come winter. On a big swell, waves break clean over the sea wall and wash through the lanes, which is precisely the drama people come for. Lifeguards are on duty during opening hours, but respect the conditions: when it's pumping, the far lanes get lively.

Go early. I love a dawn swim before the crowds — soft light, calm lap lanes, and that postcard shot with the waves over the wall and almost nobody in it. Towel and locker hire are on-site for a small fee, but it's easier to pack your own.
Is there a sauna?

There is, and it's included with your pool admission — a proper reward after a cold-water lap. Sessions are time-capped in the shared space, so don't plan to linger, and you'll want your own towel. It's my favourite winter ritual: freezing dip, warm sauna, repeat.
The club, the restaurant and the history

The pool sits beneath the Bondi Icebergs Club, and the two are separate. Upstairs is the members' club — a relaxed bistro and bar with one of the best views in Sydney, open to visitors as a guest (bring photo ID). Higher still is Icebergs Dining Room and Bar, the fine-dining restaurant that books out well ahead. You can swim without setting foot in either, but that view over a cold drink is hard to beat.

The club dates to 1929, founded by a group of local life savers who wanted to stay fit through winter. Its famous "Rule 15B" required members to swim three Sundays out of four for five years to earn lifetime swimming membership — a wonderfully hard-earned badge of honour. The club bills itself as the only licensed winter swimming club in the world, and the premises you see today reopened after a major redevelopment in the early 2000s.

items.q: Can anyone swim at Bondi Icebergs, or do I need to be a member?
items.a: Anyone can swim. The pool has public entry seven days a week (subject to tides and races) — you just pay at the kiosk. Club membership is a separate thing and isn't needed for a casual swim.

items.q: How much does it cost to swim?
items.a: It's a modest single-visit fee, with cheaper multi-visit passes for regulars. Because prices change, check the official Pool Conditions page at icebergs.com.au for the current figures rather than rely on a number that might be stale.

items.q: Is the pool heated?
items.a: No. Both pools are ocean-fed and unheated, so the water temperature follows the sea — warm in summer, seriously refreshing in winter.

items.q: Why is the pool closed on Thursdays?
items.a: Thursday is the usual cleaning day. In summer, when tides permit, it often stays open on Thursdays too — check the pool status before you go.

items.q: How do I join the Icebergs Winter Swimming Club?
items.a: The winter club is a serious commitment — an induction, a swim time trial and a qualifying season of Sunday swims, not a walk-up membership. If you're keen, contact the club directly through icebergs.com.au for the current process and dates.

blocks.text: That's the honest rundown — whether you're here for one bucket-list dip or a winter regular, the Icebergs lives up to every photo. Pack a towel, check the tide, and I'll see you in the slow lane.

Everyone who visits Bondi finds the beach, the surf and the crowds on Campbell Parade — but the Bondi I love is the one just off the main drag. Here are ten hidden-ish gems I send friends to first: quiet headland lookouts, a free gallery, a Saturday market, a sauna most people walk straight past, and a few pockets of calm the day-trippers never find.

items.label: My tip
items.value: Go early — Bondi belongs to the locals before 9am

items.label: Getting here
items.value: 333/380 bus or a short walk from Bondi Junction

blocks.text: The headland, the views and the wild edges
1. Ben Buckler headland and its lookouts

At the beach's northern tip, the Ben Buckler headland strings together little lookouts — Ray O'Keefe Reserve and Sam Fiszman Park among them — staring down the length of Bondi. It's my favourite sunrise spot: rugged, usually empty and free. Follow the footpath up from North Bondi towards the point.
2. Tamarama, the beach next door

Walk south on the coastal path about ten minutes and you drop into Tamarama — 'Glamarama' to locals — a tiny, dramatic cove between the cliffs, a fraction of Bondi's size and crowd. The surf can be punchy, so read the flags and swim between them.
3. Public art along the coastal walk

Everyone knows Sculpture by the Sea, the free open-air show that lines the Bondi-to-Tamarama walk each spring (dates shift year to year — check the official site). Fewer notice the art that stays: near Marks Park is 'Rise', the permanent Bondi Memorial to victims of gay-hate violence.
Walk the coast south-to-north in the late afternoon: the light's behind you, Bondi opens up as you round the last headland, and you finish right where the good coffee is.
Culture, shopping and a proper market
4. Bondi Pavilion

The Pavilion reopened after a major multi-year restoration, yet most beach-goers still treat it as somewhere to change and grab an ice cream. Go inside: a free art gallery, the Bondi Story Room on local history, a theatre and a pottery studio. Hours vary by space, so check the Waverley Council page first.
5. Gould Street's independent boutiques

One block back from the sand, Gould Street is where locals actually shop — small Australian labels and independent design stores instead of chain-store sameness. An easy, low-pressure browse away from the promenade crush.
6. Bondi Wash flagship

Also on Gould Street, the Bondi Wash flagship is worth a detour even if you buy nothing. Founded by a local, it builds its home and body products around native Australian botanicals, with fresh natives dotted about so you can smell the plants behind each scent.
7. The Saturday Farmers Market

Every Saturday morning the grounds of Bondi Beach Public School on Campbell Parade fill with a farmers market — produce, bread, cheese, flowers and coffee. It runs from around 9am, but confirm current times on the official listing, then cross the road to the sand.
Calm, water and a warm-up
8. The Icebergs sauna

You've seen the Icebergs ocean pool in a thousand photos, but here's what visitors miss: your pool admission also covers the sauna and hot showers on the deck. After a cold swim it's blissful. Fees, hours and closures change (Thursdays are often maintenance days), so check the Icebergs Club site.
9. North Bondi's early-morning café scene

The northern end has a gentler rhythm than the tourist strip. Get there before 9am on a weekday and you'll find the real Bondi — surfers checking the sets, dog-walkers, people reading over a coffee. Speedos and the North Bondi cafés shine in that quiet window.
10. A green escape at Waverley Community Garden

When I need a break from salt and sunscreen I head up to the Waverley Community Garden at Clementson Park, near Bondi Junction — plots, native borders and shade most visitors never realise is there. It's a Council-run community space, so treat it gently.

blocks.title: A note on the 'secret' Bondi
blocks.text: Half of what makes these spots special is that locals use them daily. Take your rubbish, keep the noise down at the lookouts early, and swim between the flags — the friendlier you are, the more the neighbourhood opens up.

items.q: What's the best hidden gem in Bondi that's actually free?
items.a: The Ben Buckler headland lookouts at the northern end — free, uncrowded and the best sunrise view over the beach. The Bondi Pavilion's art gallery and Story Room are free too, and perfect if the weather turns.

items.q: Is there a sauna at Bondi Icebergs, and can the public use it?
items.a: Yes — a sauna and hot showers on the pool deck come with public pool admission. Fees, hours and maintenance closures change, so check the official Icebergs Club site before you go.

items.q: When is the Bondi Farmers Market on?
items.a: Saturday mornings at Bondi Beach Public School on Campbell Parade, typically from around 9am. Confirm current times on the official listing, as they can change.

items.q: Where can I go in Bondi to escape the crowds?
items.a: Head for the edges: Tamarama just south along the coastal walk, North Bondi early in the morning, and the Ben Buckler lookouts, usually near-empty at sunrise.

blocks.text: That's my short list, but Bondi keeps handing out new favourites the longer you slow down. Step one street back, beat the crowds, and you'll find a suburb far more than its famous sand.

If you want to watch English football in Bondi, your two most reliable bets are The Royal Bondi and the Beach Road Hotel — both proper pubs with big screens, cold taps and a crowd that cares. I've watched more late-night Premier League here than I'd like to admit, so here's my honest local rundown, plus the thing that catches every visitor out: the kickoff times.

blocks.title: The rights have changed — this matters in 2025/26
blocks.text: Optus Sport shut down in August 2025. The Premier League and the Emirates FA Cup are now shown in Australia by Stan Sport, with a handful of marquee matches also free-to-air on the Nine Network. So when you ask a venue "are you showing the football?", you're really asking whether they've got the Stan Sport (or Nine) feed on that night. Always confirm the specific fixture before you head down.
The two pubs I'd actually send you to
The Royal Bondi

Up on Bondi Road, The Royal is the closest thing Bondi has to a dedicated footy local — a Merivale pub with a classic front bar, plenty of screens and a live-sport schedule they publish online — so you can check whether your team's game is going up before you leave the house. It gets loud and good-natured on a big matchday, which is half the fun. See their live-sport page (linked in my sources) for what's on.
Beach Road Hotel

A couple of blocks back from the sand, the Beach Road Hotel is the big, buzzy option — multiple bars over multiple levels, so there's usually room even when something major is on. It leans party-pub later in the night, which suits those late European kickoffs. Check their socials or ring ahead to confirm your match is being screened, since which games go where can vary week to week.

items.label: Broadcaster (AU)
items.value: Stan Sport; select games free-to-air on Nine

items.label: Golden rule
items.value: Confirm the exact fixture before you go

blocks.text: Mind the time difference — this is the real catch

Here's what nobody tells visitors: Sydney is roughly nine to ten hours ahead of the UK, so English football rarely lands at a civilised hour here. A Saturday 3pm kickoff in England is around midnight in Bondi, and early kickoffs can mean the small hours. Only the biggest late-window games fall at a friendly Bondi evening time — so I check the local kickoff first, then check the venue is open and putting that game on.

For the truly antisocial kickoffs, ask the pub directly whether they're opening early or staying open late for that fixture — some will, some won't, depending on the match. A quick call or DM the day before saves a wasted 2am trek across Bondi.
Prefer to watch it from your Bondi apartment?

If you're staying nearby and the kickoff is brutal, streaming from the couch is a perfectly good shout. In Australia the Premier League lives on Stan Sport, so a subscription plus decent WiFi is all you need. Grab a few things from the bottle shop on the way home and you've got your own Bondi viewing party — without the 3am walk back up the hill.

blocks.title: A note on the other spots you'll see listed
blocks.text: Older guides point at various beachfront bars and clubs. Plenty of Bondi venues will put a big game on if you ask early enough, but few commit the way a sports-focused pub does. If watching your team is the whole point of the night, start with The Royal or Beach Road and treat everywhere else as a bonus.

items.q: Where's the best place to watch the Premier League in Bondi?
items.a: For a reliable big-screen atmosphere, I'd point you to The Royal Bondi on Bondi Road or the Beach Road Hotel. Both are proper pubs that regularly show live football — confirm your fixture is going on before you head down.

items.q: How do I watch English football in Australia now that Optus Sport has closed?
items.a: From August 2025 the Premier League and FA Cup are shown in Australia by Stan Sport, with select matches also free-to-air on the Nine Network. Optus Sport has shut down, so pubs will be running the Stan Sport or Nine feed.

items.q: What time do Premier League games kick off in Bondi?
items.a: Sydney is around nine to ten hours ahead of the UK, so most matches fall late at night or in the early morning here. A UK Saturday 3pm kickoff is roughly midnight in Bondi. Always check the local kickoff time and whether your venue is open for it.

items.q: Do I need to book or call ahead?
items.a: You don't usually need a booking, but I'd always call or message ahead for anything other than a marquee fixture. Which games go on which screens varies, and some pubs only open early or stay late for bigger matches.

items.q: Can I watch the football at my Bondi accommodation instead?
items.a: Yes — with a Stan Sport subscription and reliable WiFi you can stream every Premier League match from your apartment, which is often the sanest option for a 2am kickoff.

blocks.text: That's my playbook: pick The Royal or Beach Road, confirm the exact game and the local kickoff time, and remember the rights now sit with Stan Sport rather than Optus. Do that and you'll be shoulder-to-shoulder with fellow supporters when the whistle blows — or on the couch with the surf just down the road. Up the football.

blocks.text: The City2Surf draws tens of thousands of runners every August for its atmosphere, its city-to-sea course, and one very famous hill. Whether it's your first or you're chasing a personal best, a bit of preparation goes a long way. Here are the ten things I'd tell any mate before they line up.
1. Know the course

It's 14 km from the CBD to Bondi. The opening kilometres are fast and net downhill, then around the middle you hit Heartbreak Hill — roughly a 2 km climb from Rose Bay to Vaucluse. Knowing where the hill sits helps you save energy for it instead of blowing up early.
2. Enter early and pick the right wave

Entries open earlier in the year and sell out — the 2026 event sold out well before race day. Register as soon as entries open, and choose a start wave that matches your realistic finish time so you're not weaving through slower runners (or holding up faster ones).
3. Train for the hill

Heartbreak Hill is what people remember. Add hill repeats to your training once a week in the lead-up so both your legs and your head know what a sustained climb feels like. It's the single best thing you can do for your time.
4. Build up gradually

Increase your weekly distance slowly rather than cramming. A mix of one longer run, some faster efforts and easy recovery jogs beats a couple of heroic long runs. Consistency is what gets you to 14 km comfortably.
5. Sort your hydration and fuelling

Hydrate in the days before, not just on the morning. Have a light, familiar breakfast a couple of hours before the start. Whatever gels or drinks you plan to use, practise with them in training first.
6. Gear you've tested — and sunscreen

Wear well-broken-in shoes and light, moisture-wicking clothing. Nothing brand new on race day. And even in August, put on sweat-resistant sunscreen before the start — the sun really shows up by the time you reach Bondi.
7. Plan your transport

Roads close and the nearest stations fill early. Give yourself a solid hour of buffer to get to the start, find the gear check, queue for the loo and warm up. Public transport beats driving every time on race day.
8. Check the weather

Early-August Sydney can swing from cool and grey to surprisingly warm. Check the Bureau of Meteorology forecast and dress accordingly — a cheap layer you can shed at the start line is a good friend on a cold morning.
9. Pace it in thirds

Start conservatively, run the hill on effort rather than staring at your pace, and use the downhills to recover without over-striding. Break the run into thirds and reassess how you feel at each. Negative-splitting the City2Surf feels a lot better than fading.
10. Recover and celebrate

Keep walking for a few minutes after the line rather than stopping dead, grab water and a snack, and agree a meeting spot with your crew in advance — phone signal gets patchy in the crowd. Then reward yourself: brunch, a swim, or a dip at the Icebergs pool. You've earned it.

items.q: How long is the City2Surf and how hilly is it?
items.a: 14 km, and hillier than first-timers expect. The main climb is Heartbreak Hill, about 2 km from Rose Bay to Vaucluse near halfway, with a few more short rises after it.

items.q: Do City2Surf entries sell out?
items.a: Yes — it's very popular and sells out ahead of race day, so enter early through city2surf.com.au and pick a start wave matching your expected finish time.

items.q: What should I not do on race day?
items.a: Don't wear or eat anything you haven't tested in training, don't go out too fast, and don't skip sunscreen — the Sydney sun is strong by the Bondi finish.

blocks.text: If you're feeding a family near Bondi and the bill keeps making you wince, here's the good news: yes, kids really can eat free across Sydney's Eastern Suburbs, most often on a quiet weeknight when one free children's meal comes with each adult main. From Double Bay to Coogee there's a solid dozen pubs and clubs running some version of the deal — the catch is the exact night, time and fine print change often, so the most useful thing I can tell you is to confirm the current terms with the venue before you pile everyone in the car.

I've watched these offers come and go for years as a local parent, and the pattern is remarkably consistent even when the details aren't. Here's how the deals work, the venues worth checking, and the traps that catch families out.
How kids-eat-free deals usually work here
Almost every Eastern Suburbs offer follows the same shape, which makes them easy to plan around — the specifics vary by venue, but the structure rarely does.

items: One free kids' meal per adult main purchased — so two adults ordering means two free kids' meals
Children roughly 12 and under, ordering from a dedicated kids' menu (not the full à la carte list)
Dine-in only, and usually a set weeknight or a Sunday rather than every day
Some venues are members-only or need a quick sign-up at the door
School holidays are frequently excluded — the deals fill quiet trading nights

blocks.title: Always ring ahead — these change constantly
blocks.text: Kids-eat-free nights are among the most volatile things a pub markets. Nights get moved, offers get paused over holidays, and some quietly disappear. Treat any specific day or time you read online (including here) as a prompt to check the venue's own website, not a guarantee.
Eastern Suburbs venues worth checking

These are real, well-established family spots across the Eastern Suburbs. I'm deliberately not printing a night against each one, because that's the detail that drifts — click through to each venue to see what's on right now.
Closest to Bondi Beach

items: Easts (Bondi Junction) — big family bistro and the easiest bet a short bus or walk from the beach
Bondi Trattoria, Campbell Parade — a beachfront Italian institution that's long looked after families
The Clovelly Hotel — a relaxed pub an easy hop down the coast, popular with local parents

blocks.text: A little further afield

items: The Golden Sheaf, Double Bay — the standout, with a genuine Sunday kids-eat-free offer
Watsons Bay Hotel — harbour views and a family-friendly setup that runs a kids' offer with an adult main
Coogee Pavilion — a Merivale mega-venue with a dedicated kids' playroom upstairs
Matraville Hotel and other local leagues and bowling clubs, which regularly run family nights

blocks.text: The one deal I'd bank on is The Golden Sheaf in Double Bay: kids eat free all day every Sunday with the purchase of any adult main, and during school holidays they stack it with a free kids' activity program (think face-painting and craft). Get there early on a sunny Sunday — the beer garden fills fast. Confirm the current details on the Sheaf's own Kids Eat Free page before you go.
Getting the most out of the deal

A few habits save my family real money and stress. Book a table where you can — free-kids nights get busy. Ask at ordering whether the offer needs membership or a minimum adult spend, as that's the usual small print.
My honest take: pick one reliable local, get to know its family night, and you'll eat out with the kids far more often than you'd think — without the end-of-month bill shock.

items.q: Where do kids actually eat free near Bondi Beach?
items.a: The closest options are the big family bistros just inland and along the coast — Easts at Bondi Junction, Bondi Trattoria on Campbell Parade and The Clovelly Hotel. For a confirmed offer, The Golden Sheaf in Double Bay runs kids-eat-free every Sunday. Check each venue's current deal before you go.

items.q: What day is the Golden Sheaf kids-eat-free deal?
items.a: Every Sunday, all day, with any adult main meal, and during school holidays it comes with a free kids' activity program. It's the most dependable Eastern Suburbs offer I know of — confirm the current terms on the Sheaf's website.

items.q: Is there usually an age limit?
items.a: Yes — most kids-eat-free deals apply to children around 12 and under, ordering from a set kids' menu rather than the main menu. The exact age cut-off varies by venue, so ask when you book.

items.q: Do kids-eat-free deals run during school holidays?
items.a: Often not. Because these offers exist to fill quiet trading nights, many venues pause or exclude them over the holidays. If you're planning a holiday outing, ring ahead to check that week specifically.

items.q: Do I need to be a member?
items.a: Sometimes. A handful of clubs limit the deal to members, though sign-up is usually free or a token few dollars at the door. Others have no membership requirement — it's worth asking when you order so there are no surprises on the bill.

blocks.text: Bottom line: feeding kids out in the Eastern Suburbs doesn't have to be expensive. There's a genuine spread of free-kids nights from Double Bay to Coogee — just treat the specific night as something to confirm, not assume.

blocks.text: Here's my honest answer to the question everyone asks before their first City2Surf: no, you don't need to be a fitness freak to beat Heartbreak Hill — just a handful of weeks of steady, unglamorous practice on gentle hills. It's a long grind rather than a wall, but a little prep turns dread into a shrug.

I've walked, jogged and occasionally staggered up that hill more times than I'd like to admit, and I've watched plenty of first-timers who "hadn't run since school" reach the top grinning. The trick isn't speed — it's showing up a few times a week and letting your legs get used to going uphill.
First, what Heartbreak Hill actually is

Heartbreak Hill is the roughly 2km climb along New South Head Road between Rose Bay and Vaucluse, around the halfway mark of the 14km City2Surf course that runs from the city out to Bondi Beach. It climbs steadily at a gentle-to-moderate average gradient — it earns its name from length, not steepness. The upside for us mortals: once you're over the top, the back half trends downhill toward the coast.

items.label: Character
items.value: Long and steady, not a sprint wall

items.label: You need
items.value: A few weeks of easy hill practice

blocks.text: A relaxed way to prepare (no gym required)

You don't need a rigid program. What works is repetition on small hills, time on your feet, and a couple of simple strength moves — stretch or shorten it to fit your weeks before race day. Step-ups in particular mimic exactly what a climb asks of you.
1. Build the habit

For the first couple of weeks, forget hills and just move four or five days a week. Walk-jog intervals work well: jog 30 seconds, walk 90, repeat for 20–30 minutes. The goal is just to make moving normal again.
2. Add gentle hills

Once that feels easy, find a hill that takes one to two minutes to climb and go up it four to six times, strolling down to recover. Do this once or twice a week — it's the most useful thing you can do, because hills get easier fast when you practise them.
3. Stretch out one longer session

Keep one weekend walk-jog that slowly grows — 4km, then 6km, then 8km — ideally over undulating ground. You're teaching your body to be comfortable on its feet for a couple of hours, which is what a fun run really is.
4. A tiny strength set, twice a week

items: 10 squats
10 lunges per leg
10 step-ups per leg on a park bench or stair
A 20–30 second plank

blocks.text: Train on terrain that isn't boring and you'll actually turn up. The Bondi to Bronte coastal walk has stairs and rises with an ocean view, and Centennial Park's rolling paths suit long walk-jogs. To rehearse the real thing, jog the Rose Bay to Vaucluse climb once before race day.

blocks.title: Check the official details before you commit
blocks.text: Entry dates, prices, start-group waves and the exact course change year to year. Confirm this year's specifics on the official City2Surf website rather than trusting a number you read anywhere, including here.

blocks.title: A quick sensible caveat
blocks.text: This is general encouragement from a local, not medical advice. If you're new to exercise, carrying an injury, or have any heart or health concerns, chat with your GP before you start training.
Race-day tactics for the hill

items: Start slower than feels natural — the hill arrives around the middle of the course, so don't burn your matches early.
Walk it if you want — it's a fun run, and brisk walking uphill is barely slower than a labouring jog.
Shorten your stride, keep your steps quick, and let your arms swing — small steps beat big heavy ones.
Look up the road, not at your feet, and soak up the crowd. The atmosphere genuinely carries you.

blocks.text: You're stronger than you think — the hill is long, but almost nobody around you is really racing it.

items.q: How hard is Heartbreak Hill really?
items.a: More tiring than terrifying. The gradient is gentle-to-moderate; what makes it tough is that it runs around 2km, mid-course, when your legs are already warm. Pace yourself early and plenty of first-timers walk it happily.

items.q: Can I walk City2Surf and still finish?
items.a: Absolutely. Plenty of people walk part or all of it, and the back half trends downhill toward Bondi. Just keep moving.

items.q: How long do I need to train?
items.a: If you can already walk comfortably for an hour, a few weeks of walk-jogs plus a short hill session or two each week makes a real difference. Consistency beats any single long session.

items.q: Where can I practise hills near Bondi?
items.a: The Bondi to Bronte coastal walk has stairs and rises with a view, Centennial Park offers rolling terrain, and the Rose Bay to Vaucluse climb lets you rehearse the real hill.

items.q: Where do I find this year's entry and course details?
items.a: Check the official City2Surf website for the current year's date, entry fees, start groups and course map — those details shift year to year.

blocks.text: So no, you don't have to be a fitness fanatic. Put in a few weeks of easy practice, start race day slower than your ego wants, and let the crowd and the downhill carry you home to Bondi. See you at the finish.

blocks.text: Here's the short version if you're eyeing the Bondi to Bronte for your first proper ocean swim: it's a point-to-point race of roughly 2 km that starts on my home beach at Bondi, rounds the rocks at Mackenzie's Point, and finishes in the cove at Bronte. And yes, a first-timer can do it — provided you can already swim a couple of kilometres in open water non-stop.

It's run by Bronte Surf Life Saving Club alongside World Series Swims, and it's one of the oldest, best-loved races on Sydney's calendar. What makes it special isn't the distance — it's the water: real swell, the odd rip, deep stretches over reef, and that slightly intimidating moment when you round the headland and Bronte comes into view.

items.label: Route
items.value: Bondi Beach → Mackenzie's Point → Bronte Beach

items.label: Organiser
items.value: Bronte Surf Life Saving Club / World Series Swims

items.label: Season
items.value: Sydney summer — check official site for the date

blocks.text: The course, and why it earns its reputation

You start on the sand in front of the Bondi Pavilion. Your first landmark is Mackenzie's Point, the rocky headland between the beaches — keep it on your left and follow the coast down, over reef, until you drop into Bronte's surf zone. The official course details put it at 2.0 to 2.4 km depending on where the buoys sit.

The honest truth is that it swims harder than its distance suggests. With swell running, the middle past the headland gets lumpy, and the finish funnels you into a smaller, punchier beach. That's exactly why it's such a satisfying first race — a genuine adventure, not a lap of a pool.

blocks.title: Be honest about your ability
blocks.text: This is an ocean race, not flat water. You should be able to swim 2 km continuously in open water, stay calm when you can't touch the bottom, and signal for help if you need to. If that's not you yet, build up over a season.
Training as a beginner

Ocean swimming is a different sport to pool swimming, and the gap catches people out — you can be fit in the pool and still feel wobbly the first time there's swell and no black line to follow. Give yourself a solid run-in, and make sure some of it happens in the sea.

items: Build a pool base: two to three swims a week, mixing distance with intervals so 2 km stops feeling long.
Get in the ocean weekly: nothing replaces real swell, sighting off landmarks, and colder water.
Practise sighting: lift your eyes every few strokes to spot a buoy or headland so you swim straight, not zig-zag.
Rehearse the surf: wade out through small waves and body-surf one in, since the start and finish undo most beginners.
Dress-rehearse: one continuous 1.5–2 km ocean swim before race week, so the distance is nothing new.

blocks.text: The best free training partner is the coastal path — walk it before you swim it. Seeing Mackenzie's Point, the reef and the finish from above makes the course far less daunting at water level. And join a local ocean swim squad if you can; swimming with others builds confidence fast.
Race day, entries and spectating

Entries open online at bonditobronte.com.au, and a popular swim like this can fill before race day — so enter early rather than banking on the morning. There are often shorter options too; check the official entries page for the current distances, categories and fees, which change season to season.

On the day, get there early — parking around Bondi and Bronte is tight on a summer weekend, so walk, bus or train if you can. Warm up with an easy few hundred metres, start a little wider than the pack, and follow the lifesavers' directions at the finish.

If you're not swimming, Bronte is the place to watch. Take a spot on the grassy hill above the beach, bring coffee, and you'll catch the whole drama of the finish — the sprint up the sand and the salty, happy faces.

items.q: How far is the Bondi to Bronte swim?
items.a: It's a point-to-point ocean course of roughly 2 km — the official course details list 2.0 to 2.4 km depending on where the buoys sit. Train for about 2 km and be ready for it to swim slightly longer.

items.q: Do I need to be a competitive swimmer?
items.a: No, but you do need to be a confident open-water swimmer. If you can comfortably swim 2 km non-stop in the ocean and stay calm out of your depth, you're the right kind of prepared. It's about water confidence, not speed.

items.q: When is the Bondi to Bronte swim held?
items.a: It runs during Sydney's summer ocean-swim season, but the date moves year to year — check bonditobronte.com.au for the current one.

items.q: How do I enter, and can I enter on the day?
items.a: Enter online at bonditobronte.com.au. Don't count on race-morning entry — it can sell out, so register early.

items.q: Is it safe for a first-timer?
items.a: It's professionally run and well patrolled by surf lifesavers with rescue craft on the course. The main risk is overestimating yourself, so be sure you can genuinely swim the distance in open water first.

blocks.text: Done the training and picked your date? Then back yourself, round Mackenzie's Point, and enjoy that grin when your feet hit the Bronte sand — a rite of passage for a reason.

blocks.text: Here's the short answer if you're reading this on the plane: to avoid taxi scams at Sydney Airport, ignore anyone who approaches you inside the terminal offering a ride, walk straight to the official taxi rank outside your arrivals hall, and make sure the meter is running before you pull away. Do those three things and you've sidestepped almost every rip-off I hear about. The horror stories from travellers heading to Bondi nearly always start the same way — with a friendly stranger in the baggage hall.
The scams I hear about most
None of these are exotic — they're the same handful of tricks, and once you can name them they lose their power.

items: The terminal tout. Someone approaches you at the carousel asking "Taxi? Best price?" Genuine Sydney taxis never solicit inside the terminal — they wait at the rank. Anyone touting is almost certainly unlicensed, uninsured and unmetered.

"The meter's broken" flat fare. A driver claims the meter is out or won't take cards, then quotes a fat flat rate. In a NSW rank-and-hail taxi the meter must run unless you've agreed a set fare in advance.
The scenic route. A jet-lagged passenger who isn't watching the map is easy to loop around extra kilometres or unnecessary tolls.
Invented surcharges. Real fees exist — an airport pick-up fee and tolls among them — but "baggage handling" charges and mystery add-ons are not.
The card-machine "failure". At drop-off the terminal suddenly won't work, pushing you into cash at a rounded-up number.

blocks.title: The golden rule
blocks.text: A licensed Sydney taxi will never chase you for business inside the terminal. If someone offers you a ride before you've reached the rank, that alone is your signal to say no thanks and keep walking.
How to catch a taxi the right way

The official ranks are supervised and easy to find — signposted outside T1 (International) and between T2 and T3 (Domestic). Follow the "Taxi" signs on the arrivals level and join the queue; marshals are on hand at busy times.

items: Use only the official rank — don't accept a lift arranged elsewhere in the building.
Confirm the meter is on before you move, or agree a set fare up front and hold them to it.
Glance at your maps app now and then — Bondi is roughly 20–30 minutes away in normal traffic.
Pay by card where you can and ask for a receipt — it's your evidence if anything's off.
Trust your gut. If a driver won't run the meter, take the next cab — there's always another.

items.label: Where to queue
items.value: Official rank on the arrivals level, outside each terminal

items.label: Meter
items.value: Must be running (or a set fare agreed first)

items.label: If something's wrong
items.value: Get the receipt; report to NSW Fair Trading

blocks.text: Fares to Bondi are metered, not a fixed CBD flat fare, so the cost shifts with traffic, tolls and time of day. Screenshot an estimate from your maps app before you land, and you'll know instantly if a driver's quote is out of line. For current regulated rates, check the Transport for NSW taxi fares page.
Cheaper, calmer alternatives
A taxi is easy but rarely the cheapest way to Bondi. If you're watching the budget or want zero negotiation, you've got options.

items: Train. The T8 Airport Line runs from stations right under the terminals; change at Central onto the T4 for Bondi Junction, then a short bus or cab to the beach. There's a station access fee on top of the fare at the airport stops — check Transport for NSW for current pricing.

Rideshare. Uber, Ola and others use designated pick-up zones — follow the app's directions rather than the taxi rank. The price is fixed in-app before you commit, which removes the meter argument entirely.
Pre-booked transfer. Pricier, but a named driver with a set price is genuinely reassuring after a long-haul flight.

items.q: Are the taxis at Sydney Airport safe?
items.a: The licensed taxis waiting at the official ranks are regulated, metered and insured — safe and fine to use. The risk comes from unlicensed touts who approach you inside the terminal. Stick to the official rank and you're on a properly regulated service.

items.q: How much is a taxi from Sydney Airport to Bondi?
items.a: It's a metered fare, not the fixed CBD flat fare, so it varies with traffic, tolls and time of day. Check an in-app estimate before you land, and see the Transport for NSW fares page for current regulated rates.

items.q: What should I do if a driver refuses to use the meter?
items.a: Politely decline and take the next taxi from the rank. In a NSW rank-and-hail taxi the meter must run unless you've agreed a set fare first — no need to argue, just step out and grab another cab.

items.q: How do I report a dodgy taxi driver?
items.a: Keep your receipt or note the cab's plate, then lodge a complaint with NSW Fair Trading or the taxi network. Paying by card and asking for a receipt gives you the paper trail.

blocks.text: Don't let any of this put you on edge — most Sydney drivers are honest and most arrivals are completely uneventful. Know the rank, insist on the meter, keep half an eye on the map, and your first ride into Bondi will be the easy, sunny start to your trip that it should be.

blocks.text: Driving to Tamarama, Coogee or Clovelly on a warm weekend? Here's the short version: on-street parking is free at all three but tightly time-limited, and it fills scandalously early — so arrive before 9am, or don't drive at all. Below, here's where the bays are, how long you can stay, and when to just catch the bus.

items.label: Tamarama
items.value: Waverley Council — very limited on-street bays

items.label: Best free lot
items.value: Clovelly's car park, southern side of the beach

items.label: Pay by
items.value: PayStay app at the metered Coogee car parks

blocks.text: Tamarama: the trickiest of the three

Tamarama is my favourite little cove and the hardest place to park in this whole stretch. It sits in the Waverley Council area, and there simply isn't much room — a handful of bays on the streets around Tamarama Park and Tamarama Marine Drive, and no council beach car park at all. On a sunny Saturday those bays are gone by mid-morning, and circling for one wastes a good beach day.
Most bays in Waverley's beach precincts carry a daytime limit (often signposted 2P), so read the sign before you walk off — limits and hours are actively enforced.

Honestly, I rarely drive to Tamarama. It's about a 10-minute stroll along the coastal walk from Bronte (park up there instead), and the 381 loop from Bondi Junction stops right by the beach — check Transport NSW for times. Either way, you skip the parking lottery entirely.
Coogee: free 4P on-street, plus metered car parks

Coogee and Clovelly both sit in Randwick City Council, which back in January 2021 brought in a 4-hour limit (signed 4P) across its beachside streets. The upshot: on-street parking near Coogee Beach is free, but capped at four hours during enforced hours — fine for a swim and lunch, not a whole lazy day.

items: Free 4P bays run through the streets around the beach — Arden, Beach and Brook Streets and the surrounding grid.
The Coogee Beach and Coogee Oval car parks are metered via the PayStay app — pay only for the time you use and top up from your phone.
Come early. In peak summer the closest bays are taken by 9–10am and you'll be walking in from several blocks back.

blocks.title: Rates change — check before you pay
blocks.text: I won't quote a metered hourly rate, since Randwick reviews them — check the current rate on the meter or PayStay app, and read the sign for enforced hours, as overnight rules differ from daytime.
Clovelly: the easiest place to leave the car

Of the three, Clovelly is where I rate your chances. As well as free 4P on-street bays, there's a free car park on the southern side of the beach, by the grassy park and playground. It still fills on a hot day, but the odds beat Tamarama — and you're steps from that flat-water swimming channel that makes Clovelly so good for kids and nervous swimmers.
If the beachside car park and closest streets are full, drive a few blocks uphill and walk down — the 4P bays extend well back, and a five-minute walk beats a 30-minute crawl.

blocks.title: Good news for 2026
blocks.text: In mid-2026, Randwick councillors voted against introducing visitor pay parking at its beaches (Coogee and Clovelly included), so the free 4P system stays for now. Rules can evolve, so I'll keep this page updated — but for this summer, free-but-timed is the deal.
How I'd actually get there

stops.title: Drive if you must
stops.detail: Aim for the Clovelly beachside car park or an on-street 4P bay while they're still open.

stops.title: Park & walk
stops.detail: Grab any 4P bay a few blocks back and walk in — far less stressful than chasing the front row.

stops.title: Skip the car
stops.detail: Buses run to all three from Bondi Junction; for Tamarama, walk the coastal path from Bronte or Bondi.

items.q: Is parking free at Coogee and Clovelly?
items.a: Yes — on-street parking at both is free, but limited to four hours (signed 4P) during the enforced hours set by Randwick Council. The Coogee Beach and Coogee Oval car parks are metered and paid via the PayStay app. Always read the sign on the pole.

items.q: Where can I park for free at Clovelly Beach?
items.a: There's a free car park on the southern side of Clovelly Beach beside the park, plus free 4P on-street bays through the surrounding streets. Both fill early on hot days, so come before mid-morning.

items.q: Why is Tamarama so hard to park at?
items.a: It's a small cove with only a handful of time-limited on-street bays and no council car park, so on busy days they're taken by mid-morning. I usually walk in along the coastal path from Bronte instead.

items.q: How long can I leave my car?
items.a: Most beachside on-street bays at Coogee and Clovelly are 4-hour (4P) limited during enforced hours; Tamarama's are typically shorter (often 2P). Check the exact limit on the signpost, as they're actively enforced.

items.q: Is it worth driving, or should I catch public transport?
items.a: On summer weekends I'd catch the bus — all three are served from Bondi Junction, and for Tamarama the coastal walk from Bronte beats hunting for a bay. Driving only pays off before 9am.

blocks.text: So there it is — free but timed at all three, easiest at Clovelly, near-impossible at Tamarama on a hot day. Get in early, read the sign, or let the bus do the work.

blocks.text: If you want a scroll from Sundays Bondi without wasting your whole morning in a line, the short answer is this: go early, go on a day they've actually announced they're open, and know exactly what you're ordering before you reach the window. Sundays is the tiny micro-bakery at 211 Bondi Road that founder Laetitia Loefti turned into a genuine phenomenon, and on a good day it can sell out within about an hour of opening. Here's how I'd play it.
First, the thing nobody tells you: check the hours before you leave

This is the single most important tip. Sundays opens a limited number of days a week — usually weekend mornings from 9am until 2pm or until they sell out — but the exact days have shifted since they opened, and I've seen listings disagree on which days they trade. So don't take my word for it or an old blog post's: open their Instagram (@sundaysbondi) the night before and confirm they're baking. It's a two-minute check that saves a wasted trip across town.

blocks.title: They genuinely do sell out
blocks.text: On busy days Sundays has cleared out well before the 2pm close — reports from opening weekend had them gone within the first hour. If you turn up at lunchtime expecting a leisurely scroll, there's a real chance the case is empty. Treat the posted closing time as a maximum, not a guarantee.
What to order

The scrolls here aren't your dense, heavy bakery version — they're light and airy, almost pancake-like, because the dough is cold-fermented overnight and given extra time to rise before baking. That texture is the whole point, so order at least one classic to understand what the fuss is about.

items: Classic cinnamon with cream cheese — the signature and the one I'd never skip. Order it first; it goes first.
Biscoff — one of the core flavours, rich and caramelised if you like things sweeter.
Kinder chocolate — the other regular in the rotation, and a hit with kids (and, honestly, most adults).
Rotating specials like pistachio — these are the ones that vanish fastest, so grab one if it's on the day you visit.
Matcha — Sundays leans hard into matcha, so a matcha scroll or matcha drink alongside your cinnamon is the classic Bondi order.

blocks.text: Prices sit at the premium end for a scroll, which is what you'd expect from small-batch baking with good ingredients. Rather than quote a number that may have moved, I'd just check the board on the day — but go in expecting boutique-bakery pricing, not servo-pastry pricing.

Seating is tiny to non-existent, so I always get mine takeaway and walk the five-ish minutes down Bondi Road to the promenade. A warm cinnamon scroll eaten on the grass above the sand, coffee in hand, is one of my favourite cheap-thrill Bondi mornings.
How I'd time a queue-free-ish visit

stops.title: Check Instagram
stops.detail: Confirm @sundaysbondi is open the next day and note the flavours they're teasing.

stops.title: Arrive before opening
stops.detail: The line starts before the doors do. Being there before 9am is the difference between first batch and no batch.

stops.title: Order everything you want in one go
stops.detail: Know your order before you reach the window — it keeps the line moving and means you won't miss out on a special.

stops.title: Walk it to the beach
stops.detail: Takeaway down Bondi Road to the promenade and eat with a view instead of squeezing inside.

blocks.text: Getting there

Sundays sits at 211 Bondi Road, roughly halfway between Bondi Junction and the beach. Buses run frequently along Bondi Road from Bondi Junction interchange (which connects to the train line), and it's an easy walk up from the sand. Parking is metered and competitive on weekends, so if you can avoid driving, do — plug '211 Bondi Road' into the Transport for NSW trip planner for live bus times.

items.q: What days is Sundays Bondi open?
items.a: It's a limited-days micro-bakery — generally weekend mornings from 9am to 2pm or until sold out — but the days have changed since opening and different listings disagree. Always confirm on their Instagram (@sundaysbondi) before you make the trip.

items.q: What time should I arrive to beat the queue?
items.a: Before 9am. On busy days the first batch can be gone quickly and they've sold out within about an hour, so arriving right at (or just before) opening gives you the best shot at the full range of flavours.

items.q: What should I order at Sundays Bondi?
items.a: Start with the classic cinnamon scroll with cream cheese — it's the signature. The core line-up also includes Biscoff and Kinder chocolate, plus rotating specials like pistachio, and matcha in both scroll and drink form.

items.q: Do they sell out?
items.a: Yes, regularly, often well before the posted 2pm close. Treat closing time as a maximum and go early rather than turning up at lunch and hoping.

items.q: Where exactly is Sundays Bondi?
items.a: 211 Bondi Road, Bondi — about halfway between Bondi Junction and Bondi Beach, walkable from the promenade and served by buses running along Bondi Road.

blocks.text: That's the whole game with Sundays: it's small, it's genuinely good, and it rewards a bit of planning. Check they're open, show up early, know your order, and take it down to the beach. Do that and you'll skip the disappointment I see on faces at 1pm — and you'll understand why the line forms in the first place.

blocks.text: If you're running the Sydney Marathon and basing yourself in Bondi, my advice is simple: keep your carb-loading early, familiar and low-fuss — you needn't leave the beach to eat well. My go-to picks are Pompei's for handmade pasta, Bondi Trattoria for a relaxed sit-down feed, and Sonoma Bakery for portable sourdough the day before. Here's exactly where I'd send a friend for race weekend.

The Sydney Marathon is a big deal now — it joined the Abbott World Marathon Majors in 2025 as the seventh Major. A lot of runners fly in and ask me the same thing: where do I load up the night before? The start and finish are in the city, but plenty stay in Bondi for the sea air and the recovery swim.

blocks.title: Check your race date first
blocks.text: The Sydney Marathon is usually held on a Sunday in late winter or early spring, but the exact date moves year to year — confirm it, along with start times and the expo, on the official TCS Sydney Marathon website before booking dinner.
My favourite carb-loading spots in Bondi
Pompei's — handmade pasta and thin-crust pizza

Pompei's on Roscoe Street is where I'd start. The pasta is made in-house and the pizza bases are thin and crisp rather than heavy — exactly what you want the night before 42.2 kilometres, carbs without the concrete-in-the-stomach feeling. It gets busy, so arrive early on a Friday or Saturday, and check current hours on the Pompei's site before you go.
Bondi Trattoria — the relaxed Campbell Parade classic

Bondi Trattoria is a long-standing institution right on Campbell Parade. It's my pick if you want to sit down, book a table and make a proper evening of it. There's plenty of pasta and the vibe is calm rather than boozy — helpful when you're aiming to be in bed by nine. Book ahead on race weekend; the beachfront tables go fast.
Sonoma Bakery — grab-and-go sourdough

For the day before, when you're grazing rather than sitting down to one big meal, I stock up at Sonoma. Their sourdough, fruit loaf and banana bread are perfect if you're self-catering and want familiar, gentle carbs for breakfast and snacks. Bonus: it's an easy stroll from the beach, so you can pair it with a shake-out walk.

Book your Saturday dinner earlier than feels necessary — a 6pm table beats an 8:30 one when you've got a pre-dawn alarm. And eat the meal your gut already knows; race weekend is no time for a new cuisine or an unfamiliar sauce.
How to actually carb-load (without overdoing it)

The classic mistake is treating carb-loading as one enormous bowl of pasta the night before. It isn't. The idea is to top up your muscle glycogen gradually over the two to three days before by eating a higher proportion of carbohydrate — not to eat until you're uncomfortable. The right amount depends on your training, so for precise numbers see a sports dietitian, not a blog (including mine).

items: Spread carbs across several normal-sized meals over 2–3 days rather than one huge feed.
Choose foods your stomach already tolerates well — familiar beats fancy.
Go easy on high-fibre, very rich or very fatty dishes the night before.
Keep hydration steady, and don't experiment with new supplements or alcohol.
Have a portable breakfast sorted — a bagel, banana bread or toast you know sits well.

blocks.title: Getting to the start line
blocks.text: Race-morning road closures around the CBD are significant and public transport runs to a special timetable. Plan your trip in from Bondi the night before using Transport for NSW and the official race travel information — don't assume your usual bus route will run as normal.

items.label: Race
items.value: TCS Sydney Marathon (Abbott World Marathon Major)

items.label: Best strategy
items.value: Gradual carbs over 2–3 days, not one big meal

items.q: Where's the best place to carb-load in Bondi before the Sydney Marathon?
items.a: For a sit-down pasta dinner I'd book Bondi Trattoria on Campbell Parade or head to Pompei's. For portable, easy-to-digest carbs the day before, Sonoma Bakery's sourdough and banana bread are ideal.

items.q: When is the Sydney Marathon held?
items.a: It's run once a year, usually on a Sunday in late winter or early spring, but the exact date changes annually — confirm it on the official TCS Sydney Marathon website.

items.q: Is the Sydney Marathon a World Marathon Major?
items.a: Yes. In 2025 the Sydney Marathon became the seventh Abbott World Marathon Major, joining Tokyo, Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago and New York.

items.q: Should I eat a big pasta dinner the night before?
items.a: Not one enormous one. Better to raise your carbohydrate intake gradually across the two to three days before, with normal-sized, familiar meals. For personalised numbers, see a sports dietitian.

items.q: Can I stay in Bondi and still get to the start line easily?
items.a: Plenty of runners do, but the start and finish are in the city, not Bondi. Road closures and a special transport timetable apply on race morning, so plan your route ahead using Transport for NSW.

blocks.text: Whatever you choose, keep it boring and keep it early — the exciting part is the finish by the Opera House, not Saturday's dinner. Fuel simply, sleep well and enjoy your run. I'll be somewhere along the way cheering.

People often assume Bondi's story begins with surfboards and suntan lotion, but the beach I love was a gathering place for tens of thousands of years before any of that. Its modern fame — surf lifesaving, the Icebergs, the crowds — is really just the most recent chapter of a very long history on Gadigal Country.
So when visitors ask me how old Bondi really is, I tell them to think in thousands of years, not hundreds. Here's the short version of how this sand became one of the world's most recognised beaches.
First custodians and the name 'Bondi'

Long before the trams and the tourists, this coast was cared for by Aboriginal people — the Gadigal and their neighbours the Bidjigal and Birrabirragal. You can still find traces around the eastern beaches: rock engravings, shell middens, and the distinctive stone tools archaeologists named after this place, the 'Bondi Points'.

The name itself comes from an Aboriginal word. You'll see a few spellings and translations, but it's most commonly understood to describe water breaking over rocks — which, if you've stood at the south end on a big swell, feels right.

blocks.title: A living history
blocks.text: Bondi's Aboriginal heritage isn't a footnote — it's ongoing. The interpretive signage along the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk and Waverley Council's heritage resources are a good, respectful place to learn more.
The birth of a swimming beach

For much of the 1800s, daylight sea bathing was frowned upon and at times restricted. Once those attitudes relaxed in the early 1900s, Sydneysiders poured towards the surf — and Bondi, with its wide sand and easy waves, became the place to be. The catch was that many couldn't swim well, and the rips took a toll.

Out of that danger came something Bondi gave the world. The Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club, which traces its founding to 1906, is recognised as one of the very first surf lifesaving clubs anywhere. The red and yellow flags now seen on beaches globally, and the reel-and-line rescue drills, were pioneered by volunteers here.

items.label: Name meaning
items.value: Aboriginal word, commonly linked to water breaking over rocks

items.label: Surf lifesaving
items.value: Bondi club dates to 1906 — among the world's first

blocks.text: The golden age: Pavilion, Icebergs and 'Black Sunday'

By the 1920s Bondi was booming. Trams carried working Sydneysiders straight to the sand — so much so that 'shoot through like a Bondi tram' became local slang for leaving in a hurry. In 1929 the grand Bondi Pavilion opened, giving the beach its landmark changing rooms, ballroom and promenade.

That same era gave us the Icebergs. In 1929 a group of local lifesavers, wanting to stay fit through winter, formed the Bondi Icebergs Winter Swimming Club at the ocean pool on the south headland. Nearly a century on, they're still plunging into that pool each winter — one of my favourite Bondi traditions.
In about twenty minutes on 6 February 1938, around sixty lifesavers pulled some 250 people from the sea — the largest surf rescue in Australia's history.

It wasn't all sunshine. On that day, remembered as 'Black Sunday', freak waves and a collapsing sandbank swept more than 200 bathers out of their depth in front of a packed beach. Lifesavers rescued the vast majority, but five people lost their lives. It remains a defining moment in Australian surf lifesaving.
From local beach to global icon

Through the decades that followed, Bondi rode every wave of Australian beach culture — post-war holiday crowds, board surfing, beach volleyball, and eventually reality TV and Instagram. That importance was formally recognised in 2008, when Bondi Beach was added to the Australian National Heritage List for both its Aboriginal significance and its role in how the country goes to the beach.

To read Bondi's history straight off the sand, walk from the Icebergs pool at the south end towards the Pavilion. In a few hundred metres you pass the winter-swimming pool, the surf club's turf and the 1929 Pavilion — three chapters in one stroll.

items.q: How old is Bondi Beach?
items.a: As a suburb and swimming beach it took shape in the late 1800s and boomed in the early 1900s. But as a place used by people it's far older — Aboriginal custodians gathered here for thousands of years.

items.q: What does the name 'Bondi' mean?
items.a: It comes from an Aboriginal word most often linked to water breaking or tumbling over rocks. Because it's a transliterated word, treat any single 'official' meaning with caution.

items.q: Why is Bondi so important to surf lifesaving?
items.a: The Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club, which dates its founding to 1906, is recognised as one of the world's earliest. The now-universal red and yellow safety flags and organised reel rescues were pioneered here.

items.q: What was 'Black Sunday' at Bondi?
items.a: On 6 February 1938, freak waves and a collapsing sandbank swept more than 200 bathers out to sea. Lifesavers rescued around 250 people in roughly twenty minutes; tragically five died. It's remembered as Australia's largest surf rescue.

items.q: When did the Bondi Pavilion open?
items.a: The grand Bondi Pavilion opened in 1929 and has been the architectural heart of the beach ever since.

blocks.text: That's what I most want visitors to understand: Bondi isn't famous by accident. It's the sum of a long Aboriginal history, a world-first idea about keeping swimmers safe, and a century of Sydneysiders deciding this was where they'd spend their weekends. Stand on the promenade at sunrise and you're standing in all of it at once.
