blocks.text: The lifeguards you know from Bondi Rescue are real professional lifeguards employed by Waverley Council, not actors — the same crew in blue and yellow who patrol Bondi Beach every day of the year. The TV show made them household names, but their day job is keeping one of the world's busiest beaches safe. Here's who the best-known lifeguards are, some facts about the show, and how to see the team in action. The roster changes over the seasons, so I keep this updated as things shift.

blocks.title: A note I keep current
blocks.text: Lifeguard line-ups rotate and some faces move on, so treat the bios below as the well-known regulars rather than a live roster. I last reviewed this in August 2026.
What is Bondi Rescue?

Bondi Rescue is the documentary series that follows the Waverley Council lifeguards through the Australian summer. It first aired in 2006 on Network 10, is made by production company CJZ, and has run for around 18 seasons — one of Australia's longest-running and most-exported factual shows, screening in dozens of countries. It was rested in 2025 (no new season that year) and, according to its producers, is expected to return, with filming subject to arrangements with Waverley Council. Either way, the lifeguards themselves keep patrolling Bondi.
The Bondi lifeguards you'll recognise
Bruce ‘Hoppo’ Hopkins — head lifeguard

Hoppo is the head lifeguard and the show's steady centre of gravity. He's been part of the Bondi lifeguard service since the early 1990s, and on screen he's the calm, experienced voice coordinating the team through busy days and serious rescues. If there's one name people associate with Bondi Rescue, it's his.
Anthony ‘Harries’ Carroll

Harries is one of the show's most recognisable and charismatic lifeguards — high-energy, endlessly committed on a rescue, and known for his fundraising and community antics off the sand. He's one of the longest-serving faces of the team.
Andrew ‘Reidy’ Reid
Reidy is a seasoned member of the crew, known on the show for his humour and his fitness, with a strong social-media following. He's one of the regulars viewers have followed across many seasons.
Trent ‘Maxi’ Maxwell

Maxi came through as one of the younger lifeguards and became a fan favourite. He's also widely known for working as a firefighter — splitting his time between saving lives on the beach and in the city.
Dean ‘Deano’ Gladstone
Deano is another long-serving member of the team who's featured across many seasons of the show.

Plenty of other lifeguards have featured over the years — you'll hear nicknames like Jesse, Chappo, Whippet, Yatesy, Mouse and Kobi among them. Because the team rotates season to season, I focus above on the best-known regulars rather than trying to list everyone currently rostered.
Interesting facts about Bondi Rescue

items: The lifeguards are real Waverley Council employees — professional, paid lifeguards, not actors and not the same thing as the volunteer surf lifesavers in the red-and-yellow caps.
Bondi is one of the most rescue-heavy beaches in Australia, largely thanks to a notorious rip at the south end nicknamed the ‘Backpackers' Express’.
The show is filmed across the Australian summer, when Bondi's crowds — and the number of rescues — peak.
Bondi Rescue has been sold to dozens of countries, making Bondi's lifeguards internationally famous.

For the full run-down, see our companion pieces on [20 obscure facts about Bondi Rescue](/bondi-blog/2023/9/5/20-obscure-facts-about-bondi-rescue) and [the most dramatic moments on the show](/bondi-blog/2025/1/12/the-20-most-dramatic-moments-on-bondi-rescue).

blocks.text: Key moments from the show

Across its seasons Bondi Rescue has captured everything from huge multi-swimmer rescues on wild-surf days to tense resuscitations, shark alarms clearing the water, and the occasional celebrity spotting on the sand. Rather than rank them here, I've pulled the standouts together in a dedicated guide — see [the 20 most dramatic moments on Bondi Rescue](/bondi-blog/2025/1/12/the-20-most-dramatic-moments-on-bondi-rescue).
Can you meet the Bondi lifeguards?

Yes — the lifeguards are on Bondi Beach every day, based around the lifeguard tower towards the south end near the flags. You'll often see the Bondi Rescue crew there in season. A few things I'd keep in mind: they're working, and their first job is watching the water, so give them space during busy periods and never interrupt a rescue for a photo. Swim between the red-and-yellow flags and you're in the patch they're actively watching. The team also has official merchandise and an active social presence if you want to follow along.

blocks.title: Swim between the flags
blocks.text: The best way to respect the lifeguards' work is simple: always swim between the red-and-yellow flags, where they've judged it safest and are watching. See our guide to [where to swim at Bondi](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach) for the safest spots.

items.q: Are the Bondi Rescue lifeguards real?
items.a: Yes. They're real professional lifeguards employed by Waverley Council who patrol Bondi Beach year-round. The show is a documentary series, not scripted drama, and the rescues are real.

items.q: Who is the head lifeguard at Bondi?
items.a: Bruce ‘Hoppo’ Hopkins is the long-serving head lifeguard and the most recognisable figure from the show, part of the Bondi service since the early 1990s.

items.q: Is Bondi Rescue still on?
items.a: The show was rested in 2025 with no new season that year, but its producers have said it's expected to return, subject to arrangements with Waverley Council. The lifeguards continue to patrol Bondi regardless.

items.q: Are Bondi lifeguards the same as surf lifesavers?
items.a: No. The Bondi Rescue lifeguards are paid, professional council lifeguards. Volunteer surf lifesavers (in the red-and-yellow caps) are a separate service that also patrols, typically on weekends and public holidays.

items.q: Can I meet the Bondi Rescue lifeguards?
items.a: You can usually see the team around the lifeguard tower on Bondi Beach in season. Be respectful — they're working and watching the water — and never interrupt a rescue.

blocks.text: However you know them — from the tower or the TV — Bondi's lifeguards are a huge part of what makes the beach what it is. For more, see the [Bondi Rescue hub](/bondi-rescue), our guide to [where to swim safely at Bondi](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach), and the rest of [things to do in Bondi](/things-to-do-in-bondi).

sources.label: New Idea — Bondi Rescue rested in 2025, expected to return

blocks.text: Yes — anyone can swim at the Bondi Icebergs pool. It's the question I get asked most, usually by someone squinting up at that famous ocean pool and assuming it must be a members-only club. It isn't. The Icebergs Club upstairs has members, but the pool below is open to the public seven days a week — you pay at the door and walk down to the water. Here's what I'd want a friend to know before their first swim.

items.label: Where
items.value: 1 Notts Ave, southern end of Bondi Beach

items.label: Pools
items.value: 50m saltwater lap pool + shallow kids' pool

items.label: Lifeguards
items.value: On patrol during opening hours, year-round

blocks.text: So who can actually swim here?

Everyone. Kids, grandparents, first-timers, serious squad swimmers doing their pre-dawn laps — I've shared the water with all of them. You don't need to be a member of the Icebergs Club and you don't need to book. You simply turn up, pay the entry fee at the kiosk, and head down to the pool deck. There's a 50-metre saltwater lap pool for proper swimming and a smaller, shallower pool that's perfect for little ones and anyone who just wants a gentle dip.

The one thing worth knowing: this is an ocean pool, not a heated indoor lane pool. On a calm day it's glassy and gorgeous. When there's a big swell running, waves break clean over the eastern wall and the water gets lively — bracing, salty and genuinely wonderful, but something to respect if you're not a confident swimmer. Qualified lifeguards patrol during opening hours all year round, so you're in good hands, but always swim within your ability.
Hours, fees and the famous Thursday closure

The pool opens early — from 6am on weekdays and 6.30am on weekends — and runs through to early evening. The catch every visitor needs to hear: Icebergs closes on Thursdays for its weekly clean, when the pool is drained, scrubbed and refilled with fresh seawater. In summer it can reopen once the tide cooperates, but I'd never bank on it. If your only free day is a Thursday, check the official site first.

blocks.title: Don't get caught out on a Thursday
blocks.text: The regular Thursday cleaning closure is the number-one reason visitors turn up to a closed pool. Hours, tide-related closures and swim-race days can all change, so check the current status on the Bondi Icebergs pool-conditions page before you go.

There is a modest entry fee that goes towards maintaining the pool, with separate adult, child and family rates, plus discounted multi-visit passes if you're staying a while. Prices do get reviewed from time to time, so rather than quote a number that might be stale by the time you read this, I'd point you straight to the Icebergs pool-conditions page for the current rates. Towel and locker hire is available on the day if you've travelled light.

Come mid-morning on a clear day and swim east-to-west so you're looking back at the beach and the Icebergs building on your return lap — it's the best free view in Bondi. And go early if you want the deck quiet; by late morning in summer it fills up fast.
What else is down there

Your entry gets you the pools, changing rooms, showers and the sauna (bring a towel; there's a time limit) — a proper treat after a cold-season swim. On the deck overlooking the water is The Crabbe Hole, a tiny café that does excellent coffee and a good post-swim snack. The upstairs Icebergs Dining Room and bar are a separate operation with their own hours if you fancy a longer sit-down with the view.

items: Bring swimmers, a towel, and cash or card for entry
Goggles are worth it — it's saltwater, and the sun sits low over the water morning and evening

items.q: Do you have to be a member to swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: No. The pool is open to the public seven days a week — you just pay the entry fee at the kiosk. Membership relates to the Icebergs Club upstairs, not to using the pool.

items.q: Is Bondi Icebergs pool open every day?
items.a: It's open daily except Thursdays, when it closes for its weekly clean and refill. In summer it sometimes reopens on Thursday afternoon if the tide allows, but that's never guaranteed — check the official pool-conditions page.

items.q: How much does it cost to swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: There's a small entry fee with separate adult, child and family rates and cheaper multi-visit passes. Because prices are reviewed periodically, check the current rates on the Icebergs pool-conditions page rather than relying on an old figure.

items.q: Is the Icebergs pool safe for kids and beginners?
items.a: There's a shallow children's pool alongside the 50m lap pool, and lifeguards patrol during opening hours. It is an ocean pool, though, so on big-swell days waves wash over the wall — keep a close eye on little ones and swim within your limits.

items.q: Is Bondi Icebergs pool heated?
items.a: No — it's an unheated saltwater ocean pool filled from the sea, so it's refreshingly cool. The on-site sauna, included with entry, is the classic way to warm up before or after your swim.

blocks.text: So next time you're on the promenade wondering whether that iconic pool is off-limits — it isn't. Grab your swimmers, check it's not a Thursday, and go have one of the best swims of your life.

blocks.title: 2026 City2Surf results — search here
blocks.text: The 2026 results are live: **[Official City2Surf 2026 results on Multisport Australia →](https://www.multisportaustralia.com.au/races/city2surf-2026)**. Open it, then search by your name or bib number to pull up your finish time, category place and splits.

**Looking for a different year?** The [official City2Surf results portal](https://city2surf.com.au/) and the [Multisport Australia race listings](https://www.multisportaustralia.com.au/) both let you search past City2Surf events — choose the year you ran, then enter your name or bib number. For historical placings and elite times going back to the first run in 1971, the [Ausrunning archive](https://ausrunning.net/misc/city-to-surf/) is the most complete public record. Below: the landmarks that actually matter, and how to read your result like a local.
Where to find your result, year by year

I get asked this a lot, usually by someone who ran once years ago and wants to prove to their kids they did it. The good news: the results don't disappear. Rather than re-type tens of thousands of times and inevitably get one wrong, here's where the accurate records live:

items: Official results search — city2surf.com.au keeps a searchable database of past events. Search by first and last name, or by bib number if you still have it.
Ausrunning's archive — a runner-maintained record of placings and elite times back to 1971, handy for comparing winners and fields across the decades.
Your confirmation email or charity page — if you fundraised through the official platform, your entry and result are usually linked to that account.

blocks.text: Names get entered exactly as you registered them, so if a search comes up empty, try a nickname, a maiden name, or your surname alone. Misspelled and hyphenated names are the top reason people think their result 'vanished'.
The records that have stood the whole time

Here's what surprises people scrolling through 2000 to 2024: the outright course records were both set outside that window and never beaten since. So across every year in this archive, runners were chasing times already on the books.

Susie Power's 45:08 in 2001 sits at the start of this archive's range and remains the women's benchmark. Steve Moneghetti's 40:02 from 1991 — set by one of the race's most dominant men's champions — is the one the elite men still measure themselves against. If you ever want to feel humble about your own time, remember they ran that including Heartbreak Hill.
How the field changed from 2000 to 2024

The bigger story of these years isn't the pointy end — it's the sheer scale. Through the 2000s the event ballooned into the largest timed fun run of its kind in the world, cresting around 80,000 entrants for its 40th anniversary in 2010. Colour-coded start waves, seeded by expected finish time, became the norm because that many people can't all leave the line at once. For most of us the result that matters isn't a podium place — it's beating last year, or finally running the whole hill.

blocks.title: A note on exact yearly times
blocks.text: I haven't reproduced full winner lists or splits for every year here — those numbers shift with re-timings and corrections, and I won't publish a figure I can't stand behind. For the definitive time in any given year, use the official results search or the Ausrunning archive in my sources.
Reading your result like a local

When you pull up an old result, look past the gun time. Your net (chip) time — from when you actually crossed the start mat — is the fairer number if you started in a back wave. Your category placing shows how you fared against your own age group, not the elites. And if you ran more than one year, line the net times up side by side: that's the real story of your City2Surf.

items.q: Where can I find City2Surf results for a specific year?
items.a: For 2026, use the Multisport Australia results page at multisportaustralia.com.au/races/city2surf-2026. For other years, search the official portal at city2surf.com.au or the Multisport Australia race listings, entering your name or bib number and choosing the event year. For historical placings and elite times going back decades, the Ausrunning City to Surf archive is the most complete public record.

items.q: What is the City2Surf course record?
items.a: The men's record is 40:02, set by Steve Moneghetti in 1991; the women's is 45:08, set by Susie Power in 2001. Both were set at or before the start of this 2000–2024 archive and still stand.

items.q: Why can't I find my result in the search?
items.a: Almost always it's a name mismatch. Try your surname alone, any nickname or maiden name you may have registered under, and double-check the year. If you have your old bib number, searching by that is the most reliable method.

items.q: How long is the City2Surf and where does it finish?
items.a: It's about 14 km (officially 13.907 km), running from Sydney's CBD out to the finish at Bondi Beach, with the famous Heartbreak Hill climb near the halfway point.

items.q: How many people run the City2Surf?
items.a: It's grown into the largest fun run of its kind in the world, reaching around 80,000 entrants by its 40th anniversary in 2010, which is why runners set off in staggered, colour-coded start waves.

blocks.text: So whether you're reliving a glory day from 2004 or checking your split from 2023, the records are there and searchable. Find your time, be proud of it, and if it's been a while — maybe this August is the year to add a fresh line to your own archive.

sources.label: Ausrunning — City to Surf rankings and results archive

blocks.text: If you've ever been down at North Bondi on a Friday just after sunrise and spotted a swarm of yellow swim caps bobbing across the bay, you've met the Bondi Salties. They're a free, community ocean-swimming group that meets at the North Bondi Ramp — in front of the North Bondi RSL — at 6:15am every Friday for a soft-sand run and a swim across the bay, and yes, you can absolutely turn up and join them. Here's everything I'd tell a friend before their first Salties morning.

items.label: Where
items.value: North Bondi Ramp, in front of the North Bondi RSL

blocks.text: Who the Salties are

The Salties started in 2013, when a few friends folded a proper ocean swim into their weekly routine. What began as a handful of mates at the ramp is now one of Bondi's warmest little institutions — a friendly, no-egos crowd who show up week after week, big swell or flat, summer or the depths of a Sydney winter. That consistency is the whole point: they pride themselves on being there every single Friday, and it's that turn-up-anyway spirit that gives the group its character.

It's not a formal squad with coaches and lane ropes. It's a community — people of all ages and paces who like starting the last day of the working week in the sea, then grinning over a coffee afterwards. The post-swim coffee, honestly, is half the reason people come back.
What a Friday morning actually looks like

The morning usually runs in two parts. First there's a soft-sand run along the beach — it's encouraged but not compulsory, so if running in sand at dawn isn't your thing, no one's counting. Then everyone gathers for the swim itself, which typically kicks off around 6:30am after the run. You loop the bay from North to South Bondi and back, which comes out at roughly 1.3km of open water.

stops.title: Meet at the North Bondi Ramp
stops.detail: Gather in front of the North Bondi RSL. Get your bearings and say hello — this crowd is easy to talk to.

stops.title: Soft-sand run
stops.detail: A lap of the beach to warm up. Optional, but it's a lovely way to shake off the cold before the water.

stops.title: Bay swim
stops.detail: Roughly 1.3km across the bay and back. Take it at your own pace.

stops.title: Coffee
stops.detail: The best bit for a lot of regulars — post-swim highs and a caffeine hit with good company.

blocks.text: Can visitors join? And is it safe?

Yes — visitors are genuinely welcome to rock up for a one-off swim, and there's no sign-up or fee. Complete your first swim and, when they're in stock, you'll be handed the iconic yellow Salties cap (courtesy of their sponsor, Santa Vittoria) as a little keepsake. They do sometimes run out, so if you miss out, the standing advice from the group is just to keep showing up and one will come your way.

blocks.title: This is unsupervised open-water swimming
blocks.text: The Salties do not provide any water safety or lifeguard cover during their swims. Every swimmer is responsible for themselves. The group asks that you be confident in open water and able to swim at least 1km of continuous freestyle, and comfortable getting in and out through the surf. If that's not you yet, swim between the flags on the patrolled beach instead and build up first.

Bring your own bright cap or tow float for visibility, leave nothing valuable on the sand, and check the swell and conditions before you commit — a 1.3km bay lap feels very different on a big morning than a glassy one. If in doubt, hang back on the shorter, shallower side of the bay for your first go.

And yes, there's marine life. Regulars talk about dolphin encounters — you often hear them before you see them — plus the occasional shark, small stingrays and fish drifting over the sand near shore. It's part of the magic of swimming in real ocean rather than a pool.

items.q: When and where do the Bondi Salties meet?
items.a: Every Friday at 6:15am at the North Bondi Ramp, in front of the North Bondi RSL. The swim itself usually starts around 6:30am after an optional soft-sand run.

items.q: How much does it cost to join?
items.a: Nothing — the Salties are a free community group with no membership fee and no formal sign-up. Visitors and one-off swimmers are welcome.

items.q: How long is the swim?
items.a: A lap of the bay from North to South Bondi and back, which works out at roughly 1.3km of open water.

items.q: Do I need to be a strong swimmer?
items.a: Yes. The group asks that you're confident in open water, able to swim at least 1km of continuous freestyle, and comfortable getting in and out through the surf. There is no water safety provided, so you're responsible for yourself.

items.q: How do I get the yellow Salties cap?
items.a: Complete your first swim and you'll be given one when they're in stock. They occasionally run out, so if you miss out, just keep coming back on Fridays.

blocks.text: For current details and any weather-related changes, check the official Bondi Salties website or follow them on Instagram before you head down. Then set an early alarm, pack a towel and a bit of courage, and come find the yellow caps at the ramp.

The fastest way from Sydney Airport to Bondi Beach is a taxi or rideshare — roughly 30 to 50 minutes door to door depending on traffic — while the cheapest is the train to Bondi Junction and a short bus down to the sand, usually around 60 to 90 minutes all up. I've done this run more times than I can count collecting friends and family off flights, so here's every realistic option compared honestly, and who each one suits.

items.label: You'll need
items.value: An Opal card or a contactless card / phone

blocks.text: The five options at a glance

items: Train + bus via Bondi Junction — cheapest on public transport, ~60-90 min (mind the airport station access fee). Best for solo, light-packing budget travellers.
Taxi — metered, door to door, ~30-50 min. Best for luggage, families and late arrivals.
Rideshare (Uber / DiDi / Ola) — app-quoted, door to door, ~30-50 min. Best value with no surge; check the in-app price.
Pre-booked transfer / shuttle — fixed price confirmed at booking, door to door. Best for groups and very early flights.
Car hire — only worth it if you're touring beyond Sydney; around Bondi parking is tight and metered.

blocks.text: Train to Bondi Junction, then a bus (my pick for value)

Bondi Beach has no train station of its own — the nearest is Bondi Junction, about 3 km up the hill. From the Domestic (T2/T3) or International (T1) terminal, follow the signs to the station beneath the terminal and catch the T8 Airport & South Line towards the city. At Central, change to the T4 Eastern Suburbs & Illawarra Line to Bondi Junction. The T8 runs from early morning until around midnight, so you rarely wait long.

At Bondi Junction, head to the bus interchange above the station and jump on the **333**, **380** or **381** — all three roll down to Bondi Beach in about 10 to 15 minutes. Tap the same Opal or contactless card/phone on and off, and you're on the sand.

blocks.title: Watch the airport station access fee
blocks.text: Both airport train stations add a Station Access Fee per adult on top of your fare. It sits OUTSIDE the daily Opal travel cap, so it's a real chunk of the cost. Check the current amount on Transport for NSW before you budget.

Travelling light? To dodge the airport rail fee, some locals walk a few minutes to a public bus stop outside the terminal, ride to nearby Mascot station, and catch the T8 from there at the ordinary fare — no access fee. Check the current stop and route on the Trip Planner on the day.
Taxi or rideshare (fastest, door to door)

If you've got luggage, kids, or you land late, I'd take a taxi or rideshare — the only truly door-to-door option, dropping you at your accommodation. Taxis queue at the rank outside each terminal; rideshare has its own signed pickup zones, so follow the prompts in your app. Expect 30 to 50 minutes depending on traffic.

Taxis run on a meter; rideshare quotes you before you confirm. I won't name a dollar figure, because both move with traffic and demand — off-peak they're usually a similar ballpark, but rideshare can surge, so check the in-app price first. Taking a taxi? It's worth a two-minute read of my guide to [Sydney Airport taxi scams and how to avoid them](/bondi-blog/2025/6/4/sydney-airport-taxi-scams-how-to-spot-avoid-costly-rip-offs-for-a-hassle-free-arrival) before you get in.
Private transfers, shuttles and car hire

Shuttles and pre-booked transfers suit groups or pre-dawn flights — reserve ahead and the price is locked in. Hiring a car only makes sense if you're touring beyond Sydney; around Bondi, parking is tight and metered, so an idle car is more hassle than help. Prefer to skip the train? A public bus also links the airport to Bondi Junction — check the route on the Trip Planner, then take the 333, 380 or 381.

items.q: Is there a train station at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No. The nearest station is Bondi Junction, around 3 km from the sand. From there it's a 10 to 15 minute bus (333, 380 or 381) or a short taxi ride down to the beach.

items.q: What's the cheapest way from the airport to Bondi?
items.a: Public transport: the T8 train to Central, change to the T4 to Bondi Junction, then a bus to the beach. Just note the airport Station Access Fee adds a fixed charge on top of the fare — check the current amount on Transport for NSW.

items.q: How long does it take?
items.a: Roughly 30 to 50 minutes by taxi or rideshare, and about 60 to 90 minutes by train and bus once you factor in the connection at Central and any waiting.

items.q: Do I need an Opal card?
items.a: No — you can tap on and off with a contactless credit/debit card or a phone/watch. Adult fares are the same either way.

items.q: Can I get a direct bus from the airport to Bondi Beach?
items.a: There's no single bus straight to the beach, but a public bus links the airport to Bondi Junction, where you swap to the 333, 380 or 381. Check the current route on the Transport for NSW Trip Planner.

blocks.text: However you arrive, the moment you crest the hill and Campbell Parade opens onto that big blue arc of beach, you'll know it was worth it. See you down there.

sources.label: Transport for NSW — Getting to and from Sydney Airport

blocks.text: The short answer is 50 metres — the main pool at Bondi Icebergs is a full Olympic-length lap pool, carved into the rocks at the southern end of Bondi Beach. So when people ask me how long it is, I can say it with confidence: it's the same length as the pool you'd swim in at the Olympics, just with a much better view and the occasional wave breaking over the edge.
Two pools, not one

Here's the bit that catches a lot of first-timers out: Icebergs isn't a single pool, it's two. The one everyone photographs — the long, north-facing lane pool that sits right on the ocean's edge — is the 50-metre Olympic pool. That's where the serious lap swimmers, the winter Icebergs members and the sunrise regulars do their thing. Alongside it sits a smaller, shallower children's pool, which is calmer, gentler and perfect for little ones or anyone who just wants a relaxed dip rather than a proper swim.

Both pools are filled with filtered seawater drawn straight from the ocean, which is exactly why the water feels so alive compared to a chlorinated indoor pool. On a big swell the sea washes right over the edge of the main pool, topping it up and giving swimmers an unmistakable salty tang. It's one of my favourite things about the place — you're swimming laps, but the ocean is very much in the room with you.

For the classic photo of the pool set against the ocean, don't get in the water — walk the coastal path just south towards Mackenzies Bay, or grab a window seat upstairs at the club. You get that iconic elevated angle looking straight down the 50-metre lanes to the sea.
Why an Olympic-length pool matters here

The 50-metre length isn't a coincidence. Bondi Icebergs has been a home for winter ocean swimming since the club formed in 1929, and the main pool has long been built to full Olympic lap length. That heritage is why it still draws lap swimmers, triathletes in training and the famous Icebergs winter swimming club, who take the plunge through the coldest months of the year. If you want to actually clock your distance, one length is 50 metres and a there-and-back lap is 100 metres — handy maths if you're setting yourself a target.

blocks.title: It's a working club pool, not a resort
blocks.text: Icebergs is a genuine swimming club and public pool, so it sometimes closes for maintenance (typically a weekday each week) and for the occasional event or competition. Entry fees, opening hours and closures do change, so I'd always check the official Icebergs website or give them a call before you make a special trip.
Planning a swim

You don't need to be a member or a champion to swim here — the pool is open to the public for a small entry fee, and that fee covers both the main pool and the children's pool. Bring goggles if you actually want to swim laps, because the ocean water isn't crystal-clear and the sun glare off the surface is strong. There's a sauna, changing rooms and, up above, the well-known Icebergs dining room and bar if you'd rather admire those 50 metres with a drink in hand than swim them.

items.q: How long is the Bondi Icebergs pool?
items.a: The main pool is 50 metres long — a full Olympic-length lap pool. There's also a separate, smaller children's pool beside it for shallower, more relaxed swimming.

items.q: Is the Bondi Icebergs pool Olympic size?
items.a: Yes. The main lap pool is 50 metres, the standard Olympic length, which is why it's popular with serious swimmers and the club's winter swimming members.

items.q: Are there two pools at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: Yes — a 50-metre main lap pool right on the ocean edge, and a smaller, shallower children's pool alongside it that's better suited to families and casual swimmers.

items.q: Is the pool saltwater or chlorinated?
items.a: Both pools are filled with filtered seawater drawn from the ocean. On a big swell, waves wash straight over the edge of the main pool and top it up.

items.q: Can anyone swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: Yes, it's open to the public for a small entry fee — you don't need to be a member. Hours, fees and maintenance closures change, so check the official Icebergs website before you go.

blocks.text: So next time someone asks you how long the Icebergs pool is, you'll know: 50 metres of Olympic-length, wave-topped seawater, hanging off the rocks at the end of one of the most famous beaches in the world. There aren't many better places to knock out a few laps.

The simplest way to get to Bondi Beach without a car is to catch a train to Bondi Junction and hop on a bus down the hill to Campbell Parade, right across from the sand. It's one of my favourite things about living here: for a beach this famous, Bondi is genuinely easy to reach from almost anywhere in Sydney — no hire car needed.

There's no train station at the beach itself (a common surprise for first-timers), so nearly every public-transport route funnels through Bondi Junction first. Here's exactly how I'd do it, whether you're coming from the CBD, the airport, or driving in for the day.

items.label: Buses to the sand
items.value: 333 from the city; more from the Junction

blocks.text: By public transport (my usual pick)

From the city, take a T4 Eastern Suburbs line train to Bondi Junction — the end of the line and a big interchange. Follow the signs down to the bus stands, where frequent buses run to Bondi Beach and back. The 333 is the one I aim for: it makes fewer stops and drops you on Campbell Parade. Bus numbers can change, so it's worth checking the Transport for NSW trip planner for the current services before you set off.

The 333 also runs all the way from the CBD (Circular Quay through to Bondi Beach), so if you'd rather stay on one bus the whole way you can skip the train entirely. It's slower than train-then-bus, but you get the harbour-to-ocean view for the trouble.

On a hot summer weekend, the bus down from Bondi Junction can crawl and fill up fast. If it's a gorgeous day and you're able, the walk from Bondi Junction to the beach is roughly 25–30 minutes downhill — sometimes genuinely quicker than waiting for a packed bus, and a nice way to arrive.
Paying your fare

You don't need a paper ticket, and drivers don't sell them. Just tap on with an Opal card or any contactless card or phone (Apple Pay, Google Pay and the like) as you board — on buses you tap on only. Opal cards are sold at convenience stores, supermarkets and stations if you'd prefer one, but for most visitors the card already in your pocket is the easiest option. Fares are distance-based with daily and weekly caps — check Transport for NSW for the current amounts before you travel.

blocks.title: Coming from Sydney Airport?
blocks.text: Take the train from the airport to Central, then change to a T4 train to Bondi Junction, and finish on a bus down to Bondi Beach. Note the airport stations charge an extra station-access fee on top of the normal fare — an airport thing, not a Bondi thing.
By car (and the parking reality)

Driving is easy enough — Bondi sits only a handful of kilometres east of the CBD — but I'll be honest about parking, because it's the catch. There's metered street parking around Campbell Parade and the surrounding streets plus a car park behind the beach, but on any warm weekend it fills early and you'll be circling. The metered spots are paid and time-limited, so read the signs carefully and check current rates and time limits with Waverley Council.

If you're set on driving in summer, get there early or you'll spend your morning hunting for a space. Better yet, park at Bondi Junction and bus or walk down — it saves the beachfront scramble entirely.
By rideshare or taxi

Uber, taxis and other rideshare services all serve Bondi and will take you door to sand. It's the most convenient option if you're carrying gear or travelling as a group, though fares climb with demand — expect to pay noticeably more on hot afternoons and event weekends.

items.q: Is there a train station at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No. The closest station is Bondi Junction on the T4 line, a few kilometres uphill from the sand. From there you take a bus down (the 333 is the main one) or walk in roughly 25–30 minutes.

items.q: Which bus goes to Bondi Beach?
items.a: The 333 runs to Bondi Beach from both Bondi Junction and the city (Circular Quay), and it's the fastest as it makes fewer stops. Other routes serve the beach too — check the Transport for NSW trip planner for the current list.

items.q: Do I need an Opal card, or can I tap my phone?
items.a: Either works. You can tap on with a physical Opal card or with a contactless bank card or phone wallet — same fares and the same daily caps. On buses you only tap on.

items.q: How long does it take to get to Bondi from the city?
items.a: Allow roughly 40–50 minutes by train-then-bus from the CBD, longer on busy summer weekends when traffic and crowds slow the buses down. Check Transport for NSW's trip planner for live times.

items.q: Is it worth driving to Bondi Beach?
items.a: Only if you arrive early. Parking is metered, time-limited and fills fast on warm days. Public transport is usually the less stressful choice — or park at Bondi Junction and finish the trip by bus.

blocks.text: However you come, my advice is the same: travel light, go early on a summer weekend, and let the bus or train do the work. Bondi's genuinely one of the easiest world-famous beaches to reach — the hardest part is leaving.

blocks.text: I hear it mangled at least once a day down at the beach, usually from a visitor asking directions. So let me settle it for you: Bondi is said "BON-dye" — the last bit rhymes with "eye", not "ee".

For Australians who grew up with Bondi, there's no question about it — but the spelling trips up overseas visitors, who very reasonably read the "i" on the end as "ee". It isn't. Think "bond" (like a secret agent) followed by "eye", with the emphasis on that first syllable: BON-dye.
What "Bondi" actually means

The name is Aboriginal. Waverley Council, which looks after the beach, records that Bondi comes from a local Aboriginal word meaning "the sound of the waves breaking on the beach" (you'll also see it given as "water breaking over rocks"). Once you know that, the name makes perfect sense — stand on the promenade for a minute and the meaning is all around you.
Easy way to lock it in: it rhymes with "Aussie hi" — Bon-dye, not Bon-dee. Get the ending right and you'll sound like you've been coming here for years.

items.q: How do you pronounce Bondi?
items.a: "BON-dye" — "bond" followed by "eye", with the stress on the first syllable. The "i" at the end sounds like "eye", not "ee".

items.q: Is it BON-dee or BON-dye?
items.a: BON-dye. "BON-dee" is the most common mispronunciation among overseas visitors, but locals say BON-dye.

items.q: What does Bondi mean?
items.a: It's from a local Aboriginal word. Waverley Council records the meaning as "the sound of the waves breaking on the beach" (also commonly translated as "water breaking over rocks").

blocks.text: Hope that helps — now say it with confidence and enjoy the beach.

Yes — Bondi Beach is patrolled by professional lifeguards every single day of the year. These are the same blue-shirted crew you'll recognise from the TV show Bondi Rescue, employed by Waverley Council, and they're on the sand 365 days a year keeping watch over one of the busiest swimming beaches on earth. If you only remember one thing from this guide, make it this: swim between the red and yellow flags, and you're swimming in the safest patch of water on the beach.

items.label: In an emergency
items.value: Raise one arm, stay calm, float

blocks.text: Lifeguards vs lifesavers — who's actually watching?

This trips a lot of visitors up. Bondi has two kinds of guardian. The professional lifeguards wear blue and are paid, full-time Waverley Council staff — on duty here year-round, rain, hail or 40-degree heatwave. The volunteer surf lifesavers wear the iconic red and yellow, are trained through Surf Life Saving, and turn out on weekends and public holidays through the warmer months. On a busy summer Sunday you'll often see both teams working the beach together.
What hours are the lifeguards on duty?

Lifeguards patrol during daylight hours all year, but the exact start and finish times shift with the season — longer through the warmer months (roughly October to April) and shorter through winter. Waverley Council is known for some of the longest patrol hours in the country, but because the times shift seasonally, I won't pin an exact figure here that could be out of date by the time you visit.

blocks.title: Check the current times before you go
blocks.text: For the exact patrol hours on the day you're visiting, check the Waverley Council beach safety page. Times change between summer and winter, so it's worth a 30-second look — especially if you're planning an early-morning or late-afternoon swim.
Swim between the flags — this is the whole game

The two red and yellow flags planted in the sand mark the supervised swimming area. The lifeguards choose that spot deliberately — it's where the conditions are safest that day and where they can see every swimmer. The flags move as the surf and the sandbanks shift, so don't assume yesterday's spot is today's. If you're in the water and you can't see a flag on either side of you, you've drifted too far. Swim back in.

items: Always swim between the red and yellow flags.
Read the beach safety signs at the promenade before you go in.
Never swim alone, at night, or after drinking.
Keep kids within arm's reach in the water at all times.
If you're unsure about conditions, just ask a lifeguard — that's what they're there for.

blocks.text: Rip currents: the real hazard, and how to survive one

Rips are the single biggest danger at any Australian surf beach, Bondi included. A rip is a strong, narrow current that pulls water — and swimmers — away from the shore, often faster than you can swim against it. The classic Bondi rip is the notorious "Backpackers' Express" near the southern end, which catches out visitors who set up their towel by the closest car park and swim straight out in front of it, well away from the flags.

If you get caught in a rip, don't fight it and don't panic — that's what tires people out. Stay calm, float, and raise one arm straight up to signal the lifeguards. A rip won't pull you under, only outward, and the lifeguards are watching the flagged area constantly. Let the current ease, then swim parallel to the beach toward the breaking waves to get back in.

Bondi's other hazards are the ordinary ones of any ocean beach: dumping waves, the odd submerged rock near the headlands, and strong sun. Slip on a rashie, slop on sunscreen, and give the water the respect it deserves. Do that, stay between the flags, and Bondi is a genuinely safe and glorious place to swim.

items.q: Is Bondi Beach patrolled all year round?
items.a: Yes. Professional lifeguards employed by Waverley Council patrol Bondi 365 days a year during daylight hours. Volunteer surf lifesavers in red and yellow add extra weekend and public-holiday coverage through the warmer months.

items.q: What time do the Bondi lifeguards start and finish?
items.a: They patrol during daylight hours all year, with longer hours in the warmer months and shorter ones in winter. Because the times are adjusted seasonally, check the Waverley Council beach safety page for the current hours on the day you visit.

items.q: What do the red and yellow flags mean at Bondi?
items.a: They mark the supervised swimming area the lifeguards have judged safest that day. Always swim between them — that's where the lifeguards are actively watching and where the conditions are best.

items.q: What should I do if I get caught in a rip current?
items.a: Stay calm and don't try to swim against it. Float to conserve energy and raise one arm to signal for help. A rip pulls you out, not under. Once it eases, swim parallel to the beach toward the breaking waves.

items.q: Is it safe to swim at Bondi outside patrol hours?
items.a: It's not recommended. If there are no lifeguards on duty and no flags flying, there's no one watching if you get into trouble. Wait until the beach is patrolled and swim between the flags.

blocks.text: Let me save you the goosebumps: no, the Bondi Icebergs pool is not heated. It's an ocean pool, filled straight from the Tasman Sea, so whatever the water is doing out the front of Bondi that day is pretty much what you'll be diving into. On a still February morning that's glorious. In the depths of a Sydney winter, it's the sort of cold that makes you gasp, laugh, and feel very alive — which, honestly, is the whole point of the place.

items.label: Water
items.value: Natural saltwater, fed by the sea

blocks.text: So how cold does it actually get?

Because the pool takes its water from the ocean, its temperature tracks the sea temperature off Bondi. Broadly, the water is warmest in late summer (roughly December to March) and coldest in winter (around June to August). On a warm, sunny day the shallow ends can take the edge off as the sun works on them, but don't expect a spa — the sea sets the tone here, not a boiler.

blocks.title: Want the real number before you go?
blocks.text: Sea temperature swings from day to day with tides, swell and wind. Rather than trust a figure that's weeks out of date, check the club's own Pool Conditions page, or the Bureau of Meteorology's Sydney sea-temperature charts, on the morning of your swim.

Every so often a big swell washes right over the edge and floods the pool with fresh, cold ocean water — part of what keeps it so clean, and part of why the temperature can shift between visits. It's a living pool, not a climate-controlled one.
Why isn't it heated — and why locals love that

Icebergs earned its name honestly. The winter swimming club that gives the place its identity has been meeting here since 1929, and the tradition is built on cold water: members famously swim right through winter, and the folklore is that they'd drop actual blocks of ice into the pool to keep the season honest. Heating it would rather miss the point. For a lot of us, that bracing hit of cold saltwater — with waves crashing over the sea wall beside you and the whole sweep of Bondi in front — is exactly what makes a lap here feel different from any indoor pool.

If you feel the cold, go for a mid-to-late morning swim on a sunny day, when the sun has been on the water for a few hours and the wind is usually lightest. Bring a towel you can wrap up in fast, and a coffee from the promenade afterwards is non-negotiable.
Warming up: is there anything heated here?

The swimming is cold, but the building above it is not. The Icebergs complex houses a sauna and hot showers, plus the club and the well-known dining room upstairs, so you can thaw out and look back down over the pool you just braved. If a heated indoor swim is what you're truly after, Bondi's ocean pools aren't it — you'd want a standard indoor aquatic centre elsewhere. Icebergs is about the ocean, cold and honest.

items.q: Is the Bondi Icebergs pool heated?
items.a: No. It's an unheated ocean pool filled with natural saltwater straight from the sea, so its temperature follows the ocean — warmest in summer, genuinely cold in winter.

items.q: How cold is Icebergs in winter?
items.a: Cold enough to take your breath away — it mirrors the winter sea temperature off Bondi. For the current conditions on any given day, check the club's Pool Conditions page or the Bureau of Meteorology's Sydney sea-temperature charts before you go.

items.q: Is the water salt or chlorine?
items.a: Saltwater. The pool is fed directly by the ocean rather than treated with chlorine like a suburban pool, which is a big part of its character.

items.q: Is there anywhere warm to recover after a swim?
items.a: Yes — the Icebergs complex has a sauna and hot showers, and the club and dining room upstairs are a lovely spot to warm up with a view over the pool.

items.q: Can I still swim there in winter?
items.a: Absolutely — winter swimming is the whole tradition at Icebergs. The pool is open to the public year-round; just check current hours and any cleaning-day closures on the official Icebergs website first.

blocks.text: My honest advice? Don't let "unheated" put you off. Pick a bright morning, walk down the steps, and take the plunge — cold water and all. It's one of those Bondi experiences that's far better felt than described, and you'll be talking about it long after you've warmed up.

blocks.text: The question I hear most from first-time visitors is a simple one: what's the nearest train station to Bondi Beach? The honest answer is that no train runs all the way to the sand — the closest station is Bondi Junction, about 2 to 3 kilometres uphill from the beach. From there you finish the trip with a short bus ride, a taxi, or a downhill walk. Let me walk you through exactly how I do it.
There's no train to the beach — but Bondi Junction gets you close

Bondi Junction is the terminus of the T4 Eastern Suburbs & Illawarra line, so trains from the city, Central and the southern suburbs run straight there without a change. It's a proper interchange — trains, buses and a big shopping centre all in one spot — which makes it the natural gateway to the beach. What it isn't, despite the name confusion, is walking distance to the water. Bondi Junction sits up on the hill; Bondi Beach is down at sea level, a couple of kilometres east.

If you're coming from the CBD, Circular Quay or Central, catch any T4 train heading to Bondi Junction and ride it to the end of the line. From the platforms, follow the signs up to the bus interchange on the same level as the shopping centre. It's all clearly marked.
From Bondi Junction to the sand
By bus (the usual way)

The buses leave from the interchange right above the station. Routes 333, 380 and 381 all run down to Campbell Parade, the road that hugs the beachfront. The 333 is the frequent prepaid express and is usually the quickest; the 380 and 381 make more stops along the way. It's a short ride down the hill — tap on when you board and tap off when you hop out at the beach.

blocks.title: Summer buses fill up fast
blocks.text: On hot weekends and through the peak of summer, the beach-bound buses can be standing-room-only and you may have to let a full one pass. If you're travelling light and the weather's good, the walk down is often faster than waiting — see below.
On foot

My favourite option on a fine day is to walk. It's a straightforward downhill stroll from Bondi Junction to the beach along Bondi Road, roughly half an hour, past cafés and shops the whole way. The catch is the return leg — it's all uphill back to the station, which is less charming with sandy feet and a towel over your shoulder. Plenty of people walk down and bus or taxi back up.
By taxi or rideshare
Taxis and rideshares are easy to find at both ends. There's usually a rank near Bondi Junction, and at the beach you'll easily get an Uber or cab back up the hill when the buses are packed.

You don't need to buy a paper ticket for any of this. Just tap on and off with a contactless Visa/Mastercard, your phone or watch, or an Opal card — the same tap works across the train and the connecting bus, and the transfer counts as one journey if you keep moving. Grab an Opal card at the station kiosk or a nearby convenience store if you'd rather use one.
Planning your exact trip

Bus routes, timetables and fares do change from time to time, so I always plug my start point into the Transport for NSW trip planner before heading out — it gives you the live next-service times and the current fare for the day you're travelling, so you're never guessing at a platform or a bus stop.

items.q: What is the nearest train station to Bondi Beach?
items.a: Bondi Junction, the terminus of the T4 Eastern Suburbs & Illawarra line. It's about 2–3 km uphill from the beach, so you finish the journey by bus, taxi or on foot — there is no train directly to the sand.

items.q: How do I get from Bondi Junction to Bondi Beach?
items.a: From the bus interchange above the station, take route 333, 380 or 381 down to Campbell Parade at the beach. It's a short ride. You can also walk (about 30 minutes downhill along Bondi Road) or grab a taxi or rideshare.

items.q: Can I walk from Bondi Junction to Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes — it's a pleasant, mostly downhill walk of around half an hour along Bondi Road. The return trip is uphill, so many visitors walk down and catch a bus or taxi back.

items.q: How do I pay for the train and bus?
items.a: Tap on and off with an Opal card or a contactless credit/debit card, phone or smartwatch. The same card works on both the train and the connecting bus. Check current fares on the Transport for NSW website.

items.q: Is it better to take the bus or walk in summer?
items.a: In peak summer the beach buses often fill up, so if the weather's good and you're travelling light, walking down can be quicker than waiting. Save the bus or a taxi for the uphill return.

blocks.text: So while there's no station right on the sand, getting to Bondi is genuinely easy: train to Bondi Junction, then a quick bus, walk or taxi down the hill. Do that and you'll be on the beach before you know it.

sources.label: Transport for NSW — Opal fares & contactless payments

blocks.text: If you only set one early alarm in Bondi, make it for sunrise. Because the beach faces almost due east onto the Pacific, the sun climbs straight out of the ocean — no suburbs or headland in the way, just the horizon and a slow build of colour. Sunset works differently here: the sun drops behind the land to the west, so you won't see it sink into the sea, but the afterglow on the cliffs is worth staying for. Below is where I stand for both.

items.label: Direction
items.value: Faces east — sun rises over the ocean

items.label: Exact times
items.value: Check Geoscience Australia for your date

blocks.text: Where I go for sunrise
The whole eastern edge is a front-row seat, but a few spots lift it from lovely to unforgettable — each with a different foreground.
Mackenzies Point — my desert-island pick

From the clifftop lookout at the southern end — the first headland on the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk — you look back north across the whole arc of sand as the sun lifts over the water beyond Ben Buckler. During the migration months (roughly May to November) you've a real chance of spotting humpback whales offshore.
The Icebergs corner

You don't need to swim to get the shot every visitor wants: the ocean pool in the foreground, waves washing its edge, sky on fire behind. Stand on the promenade above the pool at the south end. If you want to swim laps at first light, check the Bondi Icebergs website for current session times, which change seasonally.
North Bondi and Ben Buckler

The northern end is calmer and far less photographed. The rock shelves below the North Bondi headland and around Ben Buckler give you crashing surf against an open eastern horizon — a peaceful alternative when the south corner gets crowded.
Roughly what time is sunrise?

Sunrise shifts a lot through the year — earliest around midsummer, latest in deep winter, a swing of well over an hour. Rather than trust a number I'd get wrong for your date, I check the free Geoscience Australia sunrise calculator the night before. Whatever it says, arrive 30–40 minutes earlier: the richest colour comes well before the sun clears the horizon, and clifftop parking fills fast on clear mornings.
The best mornings often have a few clouds about, not perfectly clear skies — high cloud holds the pink and gold long after a bare sky goes flat.
Photographing a Bondi sunrise
You don't need a fancy camera — I've shot some of my favourite Bondi frames on a phone. Timing and where you point it matter far more.

items: Shoot the blue hour first — the 20–30 minutes before the sun appears give deep blues and soft pinks, often prettier than the sunrise itself.
Use a foreground: the Icebergs pool, a rock shelf or the promenade rail gives the eye something to hold.
On a phone, tap the bright sky and drag the exposure down, so the colour stays rich and the sand falls to silhouette.
Keep the horizon level and low, and brace your phone on the promenade wall in low light.

blocks.title: Mind the edge and the swell
blocks.text: The clifftop lookouts are unfenced, and the rock platforms below can be swept by sudden waves on a big swell. Stay well back from the edge, keep off wet rock in low light, and never turn your back on the surf for a photo.
What about sunset?

As I said, you won't see the sun sink into the sea here, so chase the afterglow instead. As it drops at your back, the eastern sky turns lilac and rose while the cliffs and the pale Icebergs building light up gold. Marks Park, on the grassy clifftop just past Mackenzies Point, is my go-to — spread a picnic, face the sea, and watch the colour deepen. To watch the sun actually drop below the horizon, Sydney's west-facing harbour spots do it far better.

items.q: Can you watch the sun set over the ocean at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No — Bondi faces east, so the sun rises over the water and sets behind the suburbs to the west. Come at sunrise for the sun-over-ocean show; at sunset, watch the pink afterglow on the eastern sky and cliffs instead.

items.q: What's the best spot for sunrise at Bondi?
items.a: My pick is Mackenzies Point, the south headland at the start of the Bondi to Bronte walk, for the view back across the whole beach. The promenade above Bondi Icebergs is best for the classic ocean-pool photo; North Bondi is quieter.

items.q: What time is sunrise at Bondi?
items.a: It shifts through the year, earliest around midsummer and latest in winter. Rather than guess, check Geoscience Australia's free sunrise calculator for your date, then arrive 30–40 minutes early.

items.q: Might I see whales while watching the sunrise?
items.a: Possibly, roughly May to November during the humpback migration. Mackenzies Point is one of the better clifftop vantage points — bring binoculars and scan the horizon while you wait.

blocks.text: Whichever end you choose, do yourself one favour: put the phone down for the last few minutes. There's a particular hush at Bondi as the sky turns — joggers slow, surfers sit up on their boards, the whole beach holding its breath. That's the bit you'll actually remember.

blocks.text: Bondi doesn't do the glossy, velvet-rope nightlife you might expect from a beach this famous — and that's exactly why I love a night out here. After dark it's more salt-in-your-hair pub sessions, ocean-view cocktails and long tables of people who came for one drink and stayed for five. Here's how I'd map a night, from a golden-hour beer to the last gelato before bed.
Where I start: sunset drinks with a view

The first hour of any Bondi night belongs to the water. My go-to is the bar upstairs at Icebergs on Notts Avenue — it looks straight down the length of the beach, and there's no better place to watch the light go pink over the pool. It's a special-occasion sort of price, so I nurse one negroni and soak it in. For something more low-key, Ravesi's on the corner of Campbell Parade and Hall Street has a classic beachside public bar and a terrace that catches the last of the sun.

Sunset seats at the ocean-view spots go fast on a clear evening. If you want the bar upstairs at Icebergs or a terrace table at Ravesi's, get there a good hour before the sun drops — or book ahead where the venue allows it.
The heart of the night: pubs & bars
This is where Bondi really is itself. A few of my regular haunts:

The Royal Bondi — a grand corner pub on Bondi Road, now run by Merivale. There's regular live music, and the front bar has pool tables and the footy on; upstairs turns into a proper dancefloor on weekends.
Ravesi's — beyond the beachside public bar downstairs, the upstairs bar runs DJ sets on weekends. Check their site for the current line-up before you head up.
Neighbourhood Bondi — exposed brick, good wine and cocktails, and the kind of buzzy-but-not-deafening room where you can actually hear your mates talk.
North Bondi — the northern end has easy, unpretentious spots for a beer close to the sand; it's my pick when I want the beach in view but the fuss dialled right down.

blocks.title: A quick reality check on 'nightclubs'
blocks.text: Bondi isn't a big-club district — the scene is pub- and bar-led, with weekend DJ sets rather than dedicated superclubs. If you want a heavy club night, most locals hop a rideshare to the city or the Inner West. In Bondi, the pubs are the party.
Live music

For live bands, The Royal is the most reliable bet right in Bondi, with regular gigs through the week. A short trip up the hill, the venues around Bondi Junction and Oxford Street add more stages if you're chasing a specific act. Whatever you're into, check the venue's own What's On page for the night you're coming — line-ups change constantly and I never trust a months-old listing.
Late-night eats & getting home

No Bondi night ends without a feed. Gelato Messina is my sweet-tooth default, and the beach end of Hall Street and Campbell Parade keeps a few kitchens going for a post-drinks slice or burger. Hours shift with the season, so don't bank on any one place being open past midnight midweek.

blocks.title: Plan your ride home before you go out
blocks.text: Bondi is not on the train line — the nearest station is Bondi Junction, roughly 3km uphill. Late at night you're relying on night buses or rideshare, and surge pricing on a warm Saturday is real. Check the Transport for NSW trip planner for current night services before you leave.

items.q: Does Bondi Beach have a nightclub scene?
items.a: Not in the big-superclub sense. Bondi's nightlife runs on pubs and bars with weekend DJ sets and live music — places like The Royal and Ravesi's. For a dedicated club night, most people head into the city or the Inner West.

items.q: Which nights are best for going out in Bondi?
items.a: Thursday to Sunday. Weekends bring the DJs and the biggest crowds, while Thursday and Sunday afternoons are great for a more relaxed live-music session.

items.q: Where can I get a drink with a view of the beach?
items.a: The bar upstairs at Icebergs has the standout ocean outlook, and Ravesi's has a beachside terrace on Campbell Parade. Both fill up at sunset, so arrive early on clear evenings.

items.q: How do I get home from Bondi late at night?
items.a: Bondi has no train station — the nearest is Bondi Junction, about 3km uphill. After the last buses, rideshare is the usual option. Check the Transport for NSW trip planner for current night-bus times.

items.q: Is there live music in Bondi?
items.a: Yes — The Royal on Bondi Road hosts live bands several nights a week, and there are more stages up around Bondi Junction. Always check the venue's What's On page for the specific night you're visiting.

blocks.text: That's a Bondi night as I'd do it: a drink with the ocean still glowing, a proper pub in the middle, and something sweet before the walk home. It's not flashy — it's just genuinely good fun, with sand still between your toes. See you out there.

sources.label: Urban List — The Best Bondi Bars

blocks.text: Every August, my end of Sydney turns into a finish line. The City2Surf is the run that ends at Bondi, and whether I'm out on the course or cheering from the promenade, it's one of my favourite days of the year. Here's my local guide to running it well — and enjoying it.

The City2Surf is one of the world's largest fun runs — tens of thousands of people, from elite racers to first-timers in fancy dress, all making the 14 km journey from the city to the sea. It starts near Hyde Park in the CBD (at Park and College Streets) and finishes on the grass above Bondi Beach. Part race, part street party, it's Sydney at its most joyful.
The route — and yes, Heartbreak Hill

From the start you drop down William Street, through the Kings Cross tunnel, then out along New South Head Road with the harbour glinting beside you through Rose Bay. What first-timers never expect is how hilly the whole thing is — there are plenty of climbs before you even reach the famous one. Then comes the bit everyone's heard about: Heartbreak Hill, a roughly 2 km climb from Rose Bay up to Vaucluse. It's twisty and gets steeper in parts near the top, and the truly cruel bit is psychological — just when you're certain you've crested it, it keeps going. From Vaucluse you head along Old South Head Road and Military Road before a glorious downhill toward the coast, a turnaround near Curlewis Street, and the finish on Queen Elizabeth Drive at Bondi.

blocks.title: The local trick: run to the house, not the top
blocks.text: Here's the insider tip I give every first-timer. Somewhere up on the high part of the course there's a striking, futuristic-looking house you can't miss — and it's your signal that the worst of the climbing is behind you. The moment you pass it, the hard hills are done: there's just one last gentle incline before the sharp downhill into Bondi. I stop counting down to the 'top' of Heartbreak Hill and count down to that house instead — it's a much more honest finish line for the climbing.

blocks.title: Two more things that catch people out
blocks.text: Heartbreak Hill still isn't the end of the climbing — there are several short, sharp pinches after it, so keep something in reserve. And whatever you do, don't empty the tank sprinting the final downhill when you spot the water: once you reach the bottom there's still around a kilometre to run, in a nasty flat switchback that doubles you back to the line. More runners than you'd think blow up here because they thought they were finished — save a little for it.
Getting there and home

Public transport is by far the easiest option — roads close across the eastern suburbs and parking near the start or finish is a nightmare. Bring an Opal card or tap on with a card or phone. For the start, trains to St James, Museum or Town Hall put you a short walk from the assembly area. Getting home from Bondi, there are usually free shuttle buses to Bondi Junction where you can pick up the T4 line back to the city. Because the exact shuttle and closure details change each year, I check Transport for NSW's event page in the days before.
My tips for a strong run

items: Train on hills. Even a few weeks of hill repeats makes Heartbreak Hill far less scary.
Go out easy. Aim to run the second half faster than the first — the crowd energy will tempt you to sprint the opening kilometres; don't.
On the hill, shorten your stride and hold a steady effort. People who charge past you early are usually the ones walking it near the top.
Don't experiment on race day — no new shoes, gear or energy gels you haven't tried in training.
At water stations, keep moving through rather than stopping dead; it keeps you and everyone behind you safe.
Sunscreen and a cap. It's August, but the Sydney sun still bites by the time you reach Bondi.

blocks.text: The finish (and the afterparty)

Crossing the line above Bondi Beach, salt air in your lungs and the ocean right there, never gets old. Once you've caught your breath, the celebrating begins — the Bondi pubs and the Pavilion turn on afterparties every year. I've written a separate guide to the best spots to recover and celebrate, and a companion piece on the things I wish I'd known before my first City2Surf.

items.q: How long is the City2Surf?
items.a: 14 kilometres, from Sydney's CBD (near Hyde Park) to the finish above Bondi Beach.

items.q: When is City2Surf 2026?
items.a: Sunday 9 August 2026. The 2026 event is sold out — for entries and future dates, check the official site at city2surf.com.au.

items.q: Where is Heartbreak Hill?
items.a: It's an approximately 2 km climb along New South Head Road from Rose Bay up to Vaucluse, at roughly the halfway mark of the course. It's twisty and steepens near the top, and it tends to keep going just when you think you've finished it.

items.q: How do I know when the hard climbing is over?
items.a: Watch for the striking, futuristic-looking house up on the high part of the course — it's the local landmark that signals the worst of the climbing is behind you. After it, there's only one gentle incline left before the downhill into Bondi. Note that Heartbreak Hill itself isn't the last climb: a few short, sharp pinches follow it.

items.q: Is the finish really downhill?
items.a: Mostly — but don't sprint the final descent with everything you've got. After you reach the bottom there's still roughly a kilometre of flat running in a switchback back to the line, and it catches out runners who spent everything thinking they were done. Save a little in the tank.

items.q: How do I get to the start and back from Bondi?
items.a: Use public transport — roads close and parking is very limited. Trains reach the CBD start; from the Bondi finish there are usually free shuttles to Bondi Junction for the train home. Check Transport for NSW for the current year's details.

blocks.text: Whether you're chasing a personal best or just want to say you've run from the city to the surf, City2Surf is a Sydney rite of passage. Train a little, pace it smart, and I'll see you at the Bondi end.

sources.label: Voltaren City2Surf — official site (dates, entries, waves, results)
Transport for NSW — City2Surf event transport & road closures

blocks.text: If you ask me for the most quietly spectacular spot on the whole Bondi coastline, I'll send you to Waverley Cemetery every time. Perched on the clifftops just south of Bondi, its rows of white marble headstones tumble down toward the Tasman Sea in a way that stops most people mid-stride. Established in 1877, it's one of the great Victorian cemeteries of the world — and it sits right on the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk, so you can wander straight through.

items.label: Where
items.value: Clifftop between Bronte & Clovelly (St Thomas St, Bronte)

items.label: On
items.value: The Bondi to Coogee coastal walk

items.label: Pedestrian access
items.value: Open at all times (per Waverley Council)

blocks.text: A little history on the cliff

Waverley opened its gates in 1877, with the first burial that August, and it's been in continuous use ever since. Spread across roughly 16 hectares of clifftop, it holds tens of thousands of graves and is celebrated for having one of the most intact collections of Victorian and Edwardian monuments anywhere — soaring marble angels, Celtic crosses, draped urns and ornate ironwork, all bleached bright by more than a century of salt and sun.

What I find most moving is who's here. This is the resting place of poet Henry Lawson, whose 1922 funeral drew enormous crowds; Dorothea Mackellar, who gave us "I love a sunburnt country"; cricketing legend Victor Trumper; and Fanny Durack, the first Australian woman to win Olympic gold. Aviation pioneer Lawrence Hargrave is here too. Walking the paths really does feel like leafing through a stone version of Australia's story.

Come in the late afternoon. As the sun drops behind you, it lights the marble to a warm gold and throws long shadows against the deep blue of the sea — the hour photographers dream about, and the crowds have usually thinned.
How to visit — and the walk that runs through it

The easiest way to see Waverley is on foot. From Bondi Beach, pick up the coastal walk at the southern headland and follow it past Tamarama and Bronte; the cemetery sits on the next stretch of cliff, roughly 30–40 minutes' easy walking south. You can also drive or bus to Bronte and stroll in from there. The main entrance is on St Thomas Street.

Waverley Council notes the cemetery is open to pedestrians at all times, while the main gates open for vehicles during daylight hours and the office keeps shorter weekday hours. Because those details can change, I'd check the council's cemeteries page before you rely on a specific time, especially for driving or office visits.

blocks.title: It's a working cemetery
blocks.text: People still come here to grieve and to remember. It's absolutely welcoming to respectful visitors and photographers, but do keep to the paths, keep your voice down near any service, and treat the monuments gently.
Guided tours

The volunteer group Friends of Waverley Cemeteries runs walking tours that dig into the history and the characters buried here — a lovely way to see it if you want the stories behind the stones. Tour days and times do vary, so check the current schedule via Waverley Council rather than turning up on spec.

blocks.title: Mind the cliff edge
blocks.text: This is an exposed, weathered clifftop — a section of it gave way in a 2016 storm and needed major repair. Stick to the marked coastal path and fenced areas, keep kids close, and don't climb monuments or venture past barriers for a photo.
Making a morning of it

stops.title: Start at Bondi
stops.detail: Grab a coffee and set off south along the coastal walk from Bondi's southern end.

stops.title: Bronte for a dip
stops.detail: Pause at Bronte for a swim in the ocean pool or a breather on the grass.

stops.title: Waverley Cemetery
stops.detail: Wander the clifftop rows, find Henry Lawson's grave, and soak up the sea views.

stops.title: On to Clovelly
stops.detail: Continue south to sheltered Clovelly for a snorkel or an early lunch.

items.q: Is Waverley Cemetery free to visit?
items.a: Yes. There's no charge to walk through the grounds, and it forms part of the free public Bondi to Coogee coastal walk.

items.q: How do I get to Waverley Cemetery from Bondi?
items.a: The nicest route is on foot along the coastal walk — head south from Bondi past Tamarama and Bronte, about 30–40 minutes of easy walking. You can also reach it by car or bus to Bronte and enter from St Thomas Street.

items.q: What are the opening hours?
items.a: Waverley Council states the cemetery is open to pedestrians at all times, with vehicle gates open during daylight and the office keeping shorter weekday hours. Check the council's cemeteries page for current times before you go.

items.q: Who is buried at Waverley Cemetery?
items.a: Notable Australians here include poets Henry Lawson and Dorothea Mackellar, cricketer Victor Trumper, Olympic swimmer Fanny Durack, and aviation pioneer Lawrence Hargrave, among many others.

items.q: Can I take photos there?
items.a: Yes, respectful photography is fine and the light on the marble is stunning. Remember it's a working cemetery — keep to the paths, be mindful of anyone attending a service, and don't climb the monuments.

blocks.text: Whether you come for the history, the monuments or that view of headstones against endless ocean, Waverley rewards a slow wander. It's one of those Bondi places that quietly reframes the coast — right there on the walk, waiting.

Yes — you can watch whales right from Bondi Beach, and you don't need a boat to do it. Every year between roughly May and November, tens of thousands of humpback whales pass our coast on their migration between the Antarctic and warmer waters up north, and from the right headland you can watch them spout, roll and sometimes breach without leaving dry land. I've lost count of the mornings my coffee went cold because a whale finally showed itself.
When to come: the two waves

The migration happens in two passes. Heading north — mostly May through August, peaking in the back half of June into July — the whales travel fast and often a fair way out, so you're scanning the horizon for blows. Then from about September into November they come back south, and this is my favourite window: the mums travel with new calves, they dawdle, and they hug the coast much closer in. For the best odds of a close, unhurried sighting, aim for the southbound leg.

blocks.title: Season dates shift a little each year
blocks.text: NSW National Parks and the NSW environment department flag the official start of each migration season. If you're timing a trip, check their current-season notes rather than fixed dates — the whales don't read calendars.
The best vantage points around Bondi
You want height, an open horizon and, ideally, a calm sea. Here's where I go, north to south:
Ben Buckler, the headland at the northern end of the beach, is my first pick — elevated, jutting out, and on a calm day whales can pass surprisingly close. Park up top or walk out along the point.
The Bondi Golf & Diggers clifftop, just north of Ben Buckler, gives you a raised, open outlook over the water (mind the golfers and stay on the public path).
The Bondi to Bronte coastal walk, especially the elevated stretch above Tamarama — the whales sit further out here, but the walk is stunning, so you lose nothing by scanning as you go.
Marks Park, on the clifftop between Tamarama and Bondi, is another clear, high south-side lookout.
The Icebergs pool deck at the south end isn't a dedicated lookout, but plenty of people have caught a distant spout from there mid-swim.

Go early. The sea is usually calmest before the afternoon breeze kicks up, and calm water makes a blow far easier to spot. Bring binoculars if you have them, and once you see one whale, keep watching that patch — they surface several times before moving on.
How to actually spot one

The trick is to look for the blow, not the whale. When one surfaces to breathe it sends up a puff of misty spray that hangs for a second or two — that's usually what catches your eye first. Lock onto that spot and you'll often see the dark back roll through, maybe a tail, occasionally a full breach. If the sea's choppy it's hard work, so come back on a calmer day. And a cluster of whale-watching boats in one area is a good hint there's something worth watching beneath them.
Prefer to get out on the water?

Plenty of operators run half-day whale-watching cruises out of Sydney Harbour through the season, heading offshore to where the whales are moving. Nothing's guaranteed on any trip, but during peak migration you'd be unlucky to come back empty-handed. Book directly with a licensed operator, check their departure point and schedule, and pick a calm-forecast day — responsible skippers keep to the legal minimum approach distances.

items.q: What's the best time of year to see whales at Bondi?
items.a: Roughly May to November. The northbound peak is late June into July when numbers are highest, while September to November brings mothers and calves heading south, often closer to shore and moving more slowly — great for a relaxed sighting.

items.q: Can you really see whales from the beach, or do you need a tour?
items.a: You can genuinely see them from land. Elevated headlands like Ben Buckler give the best free vantage. A boat tour gets you closer, but it isn't necessary.

items.q: What's the single best free spot to watch whales in Bondi?
items.a: Ben Buckler at the northern end of the beach — high, jutting into the ocean, and on a calm day whales pass close in. The Bondi to Bronte clifftop walk and Marks Park are strong south-side alternatives.

items.q: What kind of whales pass Bondi?
items.a: Overwhelmingly humpback whales, which make up the bulk of the migration. Southern right whales are seen occasionally, and they sometimes come in very close to shore.

items.q: How do I actually spot one from the cliffs?
items.a: Scan the horizon for the 'blow' — a puff of misty spray as the whale surfaces to breathe. Once you see it, keep watching that spot; the whale will usually surface again. Calm seas and early morning make spotting far easier.

blocks.text: So grab a coffee, find a high spot on a calm morning, and give the horizon ten patient minutes. Some days you'll see nothing — and some days a humpback breaches clean out of the water and the whole beach gasps at once. That's the magic of a Bondi winter. Happy whale watching.
